pools.title: The Question, and Bodies Before Neurons
pools.covers: reading §4.0 (the unnumbered opening), §4.1.1, §4.1.2 · lecture 4.1 slides one_capacity_three_questions, what_one_neuron_cannot_do, not_a_ladder_again, bodies_before_neurons

items.stem: The chapter opens by setting what one neuron does against what an arrangement of them does. What is the contrast?

options.text: One neuron settles one small question; an arrangement steers an animal, decides what is worth approaching, and holds a state that outlasts the moment that caused it.
options.why: Correct. Those three additions are the chapter's three sections in miniature, and none of them is a property any single cell has.

options.text: One neuron settles one small question; an arrangement settles a great many of them at once and settles each one considerably faster, which is what a body with more cells in it buys.
options.why: Volume and speed are what more cells obviously buy, which is why this is the tempting answer. The chapter's additions are of a different kind — aim, value, and persistence.

options.text: One neuron produces a fixed response; an arrangement produces a response that changes with experience, so the animal improves at what it does.
options.why: Changing with experience is where the weights come from, which the chapter deliberately hands to a later module rather than claiming here.

options.text: One neuron is unreliable on its own; an arrangement averages many of them together, so the whole is accurate where the parts are not.
options.why: Averaging away noise is a real thing circuits do, but it is not the difference the chapter opens on, and it would not produce a verdict about the world.

items.stem: A student writes that the chapter's premise is that a single neuron cannot weigh competing inputs. Why is that wrong?

options.text: A single neuron can do exactly that arithmetic: with an excitatory input from one smell and an inhibitory input from another, its rate climbs with the first and falls with the second.
options.why: Correct. The chapter is careful to concede the arithmetic to the single cell, because conceding it is what locates the real gap elsewhere.

options.text: A single neuron can weigh competing inputs once it has been wired to more than one muscle, which is what the chapter's opening example supplies when it runs the same cell into two different sets of them.
options.why: Wiring to muscles is what turns the rate into a behavior. The weighing happens before that, in the cell's own summing of its inputs.

options.text: A single neuron cannot weigh inputs in a sponge, but can in any animal that has a nervous system, so the claim is true only of the earliest animals.
options.why: Sponges have no neurons at all, and the weighing claim is about what one neuron does rather than about which animals have them.

options.text: A single neuron weighs inputs only when they arrive close together in time, so the claim holds for simultaneous inputs and fails otherwise.
options.why: No timing condition is attached to the claim, and adding one would not rescue the statement the student wrote.

items.stem: The chapter states the claim it inherits from Module 3 "exactly rather than loosely". In a short paragraph, give the claim in that exact form — what a single neuron can do, what it cannot, and what follows.
items.answer: A single neuron can weigh competing inputs. Given an excitatory input from one smell and an inhibitory input from another, its rate climbs with the first and falls with the second, and that arithmetic fits inside one cell. What does not fit inside the cell is the meaning. A rate is only a rate. It becomes approach because of what the cell is wired to, and the identical cell wired to the opposite muscles would produce avoidance instead. So value, goals, and states that outlast their causes are not properties a neuron has; they are properties an arrangement has.
rubric: Concedes that the weighing arithmetic fits inside one cell.
Locates the gap in the meaning rather than in the computation.
Gives the wiring case: the same cell wired to the opposite muscles produces the opposite behavior.
Concludes that value, goals and lasting states are properties of an arrangement.

items.stem: What does the chapter mean by saying that a rate is only a rate?

options.text: The firing rate carries no verdict in itself; it becomes approach or avoidance according to what the cell is wired to.
options.why: Correct. The identical cell, wired to the opposite muscles, would produce the opposite behavior from the same rate.

options.text: The firing rate is too coarse a signal to carry a verdict, so the verdict has to be encoded in the precise timing of the spikes instead.
options.why: Spike timing does carry information, but the chapter's point is about wiring rather than about a richer code in the same cell.

options.text: The firing rate means the same thing in every cell, which is why one cell's output can be read by any other cell that receives it.
options.why: Uniformity of the signal is what makes wiring decisive; the chapter draws the opposite moral from it.

options.text: The firing rate reports only the strength of a stimulus, so a neuron can say how much but never what kind.
options.why: How-much-versus-what-kind is a real distinction, and it is not the one the phrase makes: even a what-kind signal would get its meaning from its wiring.

items.stem: According to the chapter, value, goals, and states that outlast their causes are properties of what?

options.text: An arrangement of neurons.
options.why: Correct. The chapter's whole project is to make that claim mechanical rather than to leave it as a slogan.

options.text: A single neuron, once it is connected to a muscle.
options.why: Connecting one cell to a muscle produces a behavior; the chapter denies that it produces a verdict about the world.

options.text: The chemical that the sensory cell detects.
options.why: If value lived in the molecule, chemistry would be where to study it, and the chapter's opening argues that it is not.

options.text: The animal's body plan, independently of its nervous system.
options.why: Body plan matters a great deal later in the chapter, but it is not what the opening credits with holding value.

items.stem: The chapter names one idea that runs the length of its answer. What is it?

options.text: A nervous system tags the world as good or bad and then acts on the tag, and nothing in the world arrives with either label already on it.
options.why: Correct. Approach and avoidance, weighing a trade-off, hunger changing a verdict and a mood that outlasts its cause all grow out of good and bad.

options.text: A nervous system detects what is in the world accurately and then acts on what it has detected, so better detection produces better behavior.
options.why: Accurate detection is not enough on its own, because detection alone never yields a verdict about whether what was detected is worth approaching.

options.text: A nervous system stores what has happened before and acts on the stored record, so behavior reflects an animal's history rather than its present.
options.why: Storage and learning are deferred to a later module, and the chapter's spine here is value rather than memory.

options.text: A nervous system reduces many signals to a single number, and the size of that number is what determines how strongly the animal acts.
options.why: Reducing many to one is what a unit does, and it still leaves open the question the chapter asks: where the good-or-bad verdict comes from.

items.stem: Why does the chapter insist that nothing in the world arrives labeled good or bad?

options.text: Because a verdict of that kind has to be produced by the animal, which is what makes where it is produced a real question.
options.why: Correct. If the labels came with the world, there would be nothing for a circuit to compute and no place for value to live.

options.text: Because what is good for one animal is bad for another, so any label would be true only relative to a species.
options.why: Relativity across species is real, and the chapter's point is stronger: the label does not exist in the world for any animal until something makes it.

options.text: Because good and bad are human words that cannot be applied to animals without projecting our own experience onto them.
options.why: The chapter applies the vocabulary to worms without apology, and spends its last section arguing that the machinery is shared.

options.text: Because a stimulus can be good in small amounts and bad in large ones, so the label depends on the quantity rather than on the thing.
options.why: Dose-dependence is a genuine complication, but it is not the reason given, and it still presupposes that a label is out there to be found.

items.stem: How does the chapter divide its three sections?

options.text: One per level: why neurons came to be wired into circuits and what steering demands, then the arrangements that meet those demands, then those arrangements in real tissue.
options.why: Correct. It is the second module built this way, so the reader has done a full turn of the wheel already.

options.text: One per animal group: sponges and placozoans, then cnidarians, then bilaterians, following the walk forward through the animal tree that the chapter's first section takes.
options.why: The walk through animal groups is how the first section is organized rather than how the chapter is.

options.text: One per question: where value comes from, how disagreeing signals become one action, and what is different about a hungry animal.
options.why: Those are three of the five reading questions, and each is answered across more than one section rather than owning one.

options.text: One per scale: a single cell, then a small circuit, then a whole nervous system, in increasing order of size.
options.why: Increasing scale is not the organizing principle; all three sections are about arrangements, described at three levels.

items.stem: What is the coordination problem that specialization created in multicellular bodies?

options.text: The cells that sense are not the cells that move, so information has to travel from one to the other.
options.why: Correct. That gap is what the neuron is the animal lineage's answer to, and the chapter resumes the story from there.

options.text: Specialized cells consume more energy than generalist cells, so a body has to decide which of its cells to feed first.
options.why: Energy is what made elaborate cells affordable in the first place; the problem named here is about information rather than about supply.

options.text: Specialized cells divide at different rates, so a body has to keep its tissues growing in proportion to one another.
options.why: Growth regulation is a real problem for a body, and it is not the one the chapter names as the neuron's occasion.

options.text: Specialized cells cannot survive on their own, so a body has to prevent any of them from being separated from the rest.
options.why: Interdependence follows from specialization, but the difficulty the chapter draws out is getting information across the body quickly.

items.stem: The chapter recalls the neuron as the animal lineage's answer to the coordination problem. What three properties does it name for the signal a neuron produces?

options.text: Fast, aimed, and undiminished at the far end.
options.why: Correct. Each is something a chemical signal spreading by diffusion cannot deliver, which is why the trade was worth making.

options.text: Cheap, continuous, and reaching every part of the body at once.
options.why: Those are the properties of the chemical signaling neurons traded away rather than the ones they bought.

options.text: Fast, reversible, and stronger the more urgent the message is.
options.why: Signal strength does not vary with urgency; an all-or-nothing spike is the same size every time, which is what keeps it undiminished.

options.text: Aimed, persistent, and able to be stored for later use by the receiving cell.
options.why: Persistence and storage belong to states and to learning; the signal itself ends with the event.

items.stem: The chapter says the previous module's story stopped in a particular place. Where, and what does this chapter do about it?

options.text: It stopped at a cell type rather than at an animal, with no animal tree drawn; this chapter resumes it by asking what there was to gain by wiring neurons to one another.
options.why: Correct. A worm had already been shown doing things one cell cannot account for, with nothing said about how animals got from the first neuron to that worm.

options.text: It stopped at a single animal rather than at a lineage; this chapter resumes it by setting that animal beside others whose lineages solved the very same problem in some other way.
options.why: The comparative move is Module 2's. What was missing here was any animal at all after the cell type was described.

options.text: It stopped at the algorithmic level rather than the implementational one; this chapter resumes it by supplying the biology that was set aside.
options.why: All three levels were covered for the single cell. The gap was in the biology's history rather than in its levels.

options.text: It stopped at the chemistry of signaling rather than at the cell; this chapter resumes it by building the cell out of that chemistry.
options.why: Building the cell was the previous module's work, and this chapter takes the cell as given.

items.stem: What does a computational question ask, in the form the chapter states it here?

options.text: What problem is being solved, and why solving it was worth what it cost.
options.why: Correct. The cost half matters in this chapter, because everything steering demands has to be paid for.

options.text: What is represented, and by what procedure that representation is transformed.
options.why: That is the algorithmic question, which the chapter's second section asks.

options.text: By what physical means the problem is solved, and at what cost to the animal solving it.
options.why: That is the implementational question, and it is the third section's. The cost clause appears in both, which is why the first half has to be read.

options.text: Which animals solved the problem, and in what order they appeared.
options.why: The walk through animal groups is how the section is organized rather than what the question asks.

items.stem: The chapter re-issues an earlier warning with more force than the previous module needed. What is the warning, and why does this chapter need it more?

options.text: Walking forward through the animal tree reads very easily as walking up it — and this chapter does walk forward, from sponges through cnidarians to bilaterians.
options.why: Correct. A jellyfish is not a rough draft of a worm, and each group has been solving its own problems for as long as any of the others.

options.text: Comparing animals that are distantly related risks mistaking analogy for homology — and this chapter sets side by side animals whose lineages separated hundreds of millions of years ago.
options.why: Homology and analogy are the earlier module's tools, and the warning re-issued here is the anti-ladder one.

options.text: Describing an animal in terms of what it lacks risks defining it by our own body plan — and this chapter describes sponges and cnidarians largely by what they lack.
options.why: The chapter is careful about exactly that, but it is not the warning it names, and it names the ladder explicitly.

options.text: Dating early animal groups from molecular evidence risks treating an estimate as a fact — and this chapter gives several such dates.
options.why: The dating hedges are real and are kept, but they are a separate caution rather than the warning carried forward.

items.stem: An animal with a nerve net is sometimes described as having a primitive nervous system. What does the chapter's framing say about that description?

options.text: Each of these lineages has been solving its own problems for as long as any other, so a nerve net is a solution rather than an early attempt at a brain.
options.why: Correct. The framing is load-bearing later, where anchored cnidarians are presented as successful rather than as unfinished.

options.text: The description is accurate as far as it goes, since a nerve net really is simpler than a centralized nervous system and appears earlier in the record than one.
options.why: Simpler is a description of structure; primitive smuggles in a ranking, which is what the chapter's warning exists to block.

options.text: The description is accurate for cnidarians but not for sponges, since sponges appeared early and are not on the same limb of the tree at all.
options.why: Sponges have no nervous system to rank, and the warning applies across the whole walk rather than to one group.

options.text: The description would be accurate if these animals had gone extinct, but they are still here, so it cannot be applied to them.
options.why: Survival is offered as evidence that these are working solutions rather than as the condition under which ranking becomes legitimate.

items.stem: What makes a sponge an animal, on the chapter's account?

options.text: It is multicellular, it develops from an embryo, and as an adult it is anchored to a surface, drawing water in through its pores and filtering food out.
options.why: Correct. Being an animal is a matter of ancestry and development rather than of having a nervous system.

options.text: It has a nervous system of a very simple kind, built from cells that signal to one another without being fully specialized as neurons yet, which is why no part of one looks like a nerve.
options.why: Sponges have nothing that would count as a nervous system by any definition, which is exactly what makes them useful here.

options.text: It moves under its own power at some stage of its life, which is the property that separates animals from plants and fungi.
options.why: Adult sponges are anchored for life, and the chapter does not make motility the criterion.

options.text: It obtains energy by eating other organisms rather than by making its own food from sunlight.
options.why: Feeding on other organisms is true of sponges, and the chapter's list is about multicellularity, development and mode of life together.

items.stem: What does the sponge case establish about the relationship between behavior and nervous systems?

options.text: A sponge has no neurons, synapses, nerves or ordinary muscle, and it behaves anyway — so behavior does not require a nervous system.
options.why: Correct. Irritate a sponge and it closes its pores and contracts its whole body, in a movement researchers have taken to calling a sneeze.

options.text: A sponge has a minimal nervous system and a correspondingly minimal repertoire of behavior, so the two have scaled together from the very beginning.
options.why: The chapter is emphatic that a sponge has no nervous system at all, which is what makes its behavior interesting.

options.text: A sponge behaves only when it is part of a colony, so coordination rather than the individual animal is what behavior requires.
options.why: No colony condition is described; a single sponge performs the contraction across its own body.

options.text: A sponge's contraction is a passive mechanical response rather than behavior, which is why no nervous system is needed for it.
options.why: The chapter treats the contraction as coordinated across the animal rather than as a passive collapse.

items.stem: The sponge's whole-body contraction takes minutes rather than milliseconds. What accounts for the difference?

options.text: The signal is propagated by chemical and mechanical signals passed from each cell to its neighbors, rather than along anything dedicated to carrying it.
options.why: Correct. It is the previous module's argument about diffusion demonstrated in a live animal rather than calculated on a page.

options.text: The contraction involves a large mass of tissue rather than a single muscle, and a body of that size simply takes longer to move than a small one does, whatever carries the signal.
options.why: Size affects how long the movement takes; the chapter attributes the delay to how the signal travels.

options.text: The sponge has no muscle of the ordinary kind, so the contraction depends on individual cells changing shape one after another.
options.why: Sponges do lack ordinary muscle, but the reason given for the timing is about signal propagation rather than about the effector.

options.text: The sponge is cold-blooded and lives in cold water, which slows every chemical reaction in its body.
options.why: Temperature is not discussed, and the mechanism named is cell-to-cell propagation.

items.stem: Why does the chapter insist that minutes is fast enough for a sponge?

options.text: Because a sponge is fixed to a rock and eats by filtering, so nothing in its way of life turns on a fraction of a second.
options.why: Correct. Slow cell-to-cell signaling is a real way to coordinate a body rather than a failed attempt at a fast one.

options.text: Because a sponge's predators are themselves slow-moving, so the arms race it is caught up in runs at a gentler tempo than a bilaterian's does.
options.why: No predator comparison is offered, and the argument is about the sponge's own mode of life.

options.text: Because a sponge has a large enough surface area that any single injury affects only a small part of it.
options.why: Injury tolerance is not the reason given, and the claim concerns the usefulness of a slow signal rather than the cost of damage.

options.text: Because a sponge's contraction is not a response to anything in particular, so its timing does not matter.
options.why: The contraction is a response to irritation; what the chapter argues is that a slow response to it is sufficient.

items.stem: What is surprising about the molecular equipment sponges carry?

options.text: They have genes for the proteins that make synapses, for receptors, and for the ion channels that do the work of an action potential — with no neurons to put any of it in.
options.why: Correct. That is what shifts the question away from where the pieces came from and onto what had not yet happened.

options.text: They have genes for those proteins but express none of them, so the equipment sits unread in the genome and never appears anywhere in the living animal at all, so its cells have to signal mechanically instead.
options.why: The chapter does not claim the genes go unused; sponges signal chemically between their cells.

options.text: They have receptors and ion channels but nothing resembling a synaptic protein, which is the one part that had to be invented.
options.why: Synaptic proteins are explicitly on the list, which is what makes the case striking.

options.text: They acquired those genes from cnidarians after the two groups diverged, which is why the equipment predates the neuron.
options.why: No gene transfer between groups is described, and the point is that the parts were already present rather than borrowed.

items.stem: If the molecular pieces of a neuron were already lying around, what does the chapter say had not yet happened?

options.text: The arrangement: cells specialized for signaling and nothing else, connected to particular partners rather than to whatever they touch, and carrying signals one way.
options.why: Correct. The step to a nervous system is the arrangement rather than the invention of a new kind of chemistry.

options.text: The concentration: enough of those proteins gathered in one cell for a signal to be produced in milliseconds rather than in minutes.
options.why: Quantity is not what the chapter names, and a sponge's cells already use the equipment they have.

options.text: The insulation: a way of keeping one cell's signal from leaking into every other cell around it as that signal travels the whole length of the animal's body on its way to the far end.
options.why: Insulation is a later refinement of a signal that already travels; the missing thing here is the wiring itself.

options.text: The energy: a supply large enough to pay for cells that do nothing but signal all day.
options.why: The energy revolution happened earlier and is what made elaborate cells affordable, so it is not the missing step here.

items.stem: Sponges have much of the molecular equipment a neuron is built from and no neurons. Explain in a few sentences what the chapter concludes from that, and what it rules out.
items.answer: It rules out the idea that a nervous system had to wait for new chemistry to be invented. The proteins that make synapses, the receptors and the ion channels that do the physical work of an action potential are all present in an animal with no neurons to put them in, so the pieces were already lying around. What had not happened was the arrangement: cells specialized for signaling and for nothing else, connected to particular partners rather than to whichever cell they happen to touch, and carrying signals in one direction. The step to a nervous system is that arrangement rather than a new kind of chemistry.
rubric: States that the molecular parts, including synaptic proteins, receptors and ion channels, are present in sponges.
Rules out the invention of new chemistry as the step that was missing.
Names the three features of the arrangement — specialization, particular partners, one-way flow.
Concludes that the step to a nervous system is the arrangement.

items.stem: Placozoans are offered alongside sponges as a second case. What do they add?

options.text: Another group with no neurons at all coordinates its feeding with cells that release peptides onto their neighbors, and those cells look like something a neuron could be made out of.
options.why: Correct. Two independent cases make the point harder to dismiss as a peculiarity of sponges.

options.text: Another group with no neurons coordinates its feeding mechanically rather than chemically, which shows that cell-to-cell chemistry was not the only route available to an animal of that kind.
options.why: The peptide release is chemical, and it is the resemblance to a neuron's signaling that makes the case.

options.text: Another group has neurons of a very simple kind, which places them between sponges and cnidarians on the walk through the tree.
options.why: Placozoans are named precisely as a group with no neurons at all, and the chapter is not arranging groups on a line.

options.text: Another group lost its neurons after having them, which shows that a nervous system can be given up when it stops paying.
options.why: Loss is discussed later in the chapter for a different animal, and it is not what placozoans are brought in for.

items.stem: How does the chapter present the two dates it gives for sponges?

options.text: Around 580 million years for the oldest widely accepted fossils, and possibly 635 million from chemical traces in older rock, with the source of those traces disputed.
options.why: Correct. The hedge belongs to the claim: the older figure is attached to traces whose source is unsettled.

options.text: Around 580 million years from chemical traces in ancient rock, and 635 million from body fossils, which are much the more reliable of the two lines of evidence about sponges.
options.why: The two kinds of evidence are the other way round, and it is the trace-based figure that carries the dispute.

options.text: Around 635 million years, with 580 million given as a conservative lower bound that most researchers now consider superseded.
options.why: Neither figure is described as superseded; the older one is the disputed one.

options.text: Around 580 million years, with the older figure omitted because the chapter does not rely on contested evidence.
options.why: The older figure is given rather than omitted, with its dispute stated alongside it.

items.stem: The lecture draws the same-cell-opposite-behavior case as two panels and then says why the rest of the module looks where it looks. What is that argument?

options.text: If value lived in the molecule, chemistry would be the place to study it; if it lived in the sensory cell, the previous module would already have found it — so it lives in the wiring.
options.why: Correct. The elimination is what licenses spending the next two lectures on arrangements of neurons rather than on cells or chemicals.

options.text: If value lived in the molecule, animals would agree about which chemicals are worth approaching; they disagree, so each species builds its own verdicts out of the same chemistry.
options.why: Cross-species disagreement is not the argument used, and the lecture's elimination runs through where value could be located rather than through who agrees.

options.text: If value lived in the sensory cell, recording from that cell would reveal it; a recording shows a rate and nothing more, so value is spread across many cells instead.
options.why: Measurability is not the criterion offered, and the conclusion the lecture reaches is about wiring rather than about number.

options.text: If value lived in the wiring, an animal's verdicts would be fixed for life; animals change their minds, so value lives in something adjustable, which is what the module's later sections take up.
options.why: Changeable value is what modulation and learning address later, and it is not how the lecture places value in the wiring in the first place.

items.stem: In the lecture's two panels, what exactly is held constant and what differs?

options.text: The same animal, the same sensory cell, the same chemical and the same firing rate; what differs is which muscles the cell is wired to.
options.why: Correct. On one side the cell drives the muscles on the far side of the body and the animal turns toward the chemical; on the other it drives the near side and the animal turns away.

options.text: The same animal and the same wiring throughout; what differs is the concentration of the chemical, and with it the rate at which the sensory cell fires.
options.why: Varying the stimulus is the obvious experiment and it is not this one. Holding the rate fixed is what makes the wiring the only candidate.

options.text: The same wiring and the same chemical; what differs is which sensory cell detects it, one on each side of the head.
options.why: Two sensors on two sides is a different mechanism, and the chapter is careful that this animal does not compare left against right.

options.text: The same sensory cell and the same muscles; what differs is the strength of the connection between them.
options.why: Connection strength changes how much the animal turns rather than which way, so it could not produce approach in one panel and avoidance in the other.

items.stem: The lecture says that for one of its dates the width of the band is itself the finding. Which date, and why?

options.text: The origin of animals, which comes from molecular clocks rather than fossils and spans about 185 million years — so no single number inside it is the age of animals.
options.why: Correct. Drawing it as a band rather than a mark is what keeps the estimate from being read as a date.

options.text: The oldest bilaterian body fossil, whose age depends on which of several disputed specimens is accepted, so the band drawn for it covers the disagreement between them.
options.why: That date is given as a single figure of about 555 million years, with the care falling on the phrase body fossil.

options.text: The sponge date, whose band covers the whole gap between the widely accepted fossils and the much older chemical traces that are in dispute.
options.why: Those two figures are given separately, with the dispute attached to the older one rather than absorbed into a band.

options.text: The cnidarian date, whose band reflects how hard it is to fossilize a soft-bodied animal of that kind at all.
options.why: Preservation is not the reason given, and the band whose width carries the finding is the molecular-clock one.

items.stem: The lecture is careful to say that the oldest widely accepted bilaterian fossil at about 555 million years is a body fossil. Why does that word matter?

options.text: Because older trace fossils exist — burrows and tracks — and they are a different kind of evidence about when bilaterians appeared.
options.why: Correct. A track records that something moved through sediment; a body fossil records the animal itself, and the two can disagree.

options.text: Because a body fossil can be dated directly, where a trace fossil can only be dated from the rock around it, which is about 555 million years old here.
options.why: Both are dated by their surrounding rock, and the distinction drawn is about what each kind of fossil is evidence of.

options.text: Because a body fossil of a bilaterian shows the bilateral symmetry directly, where a trace fossil could have been left by a cnidarian.
options.why: Who left a given trace is genuinely uncertain, and the reason the lecture gives is that older traces exist at all.

options.text: Because body fossils are rarer, so the 555-million-year figure is likely to be revised downward as more are found.
options.why: Rarity would push the accepted date later rather than earlier, and no revision is predicted.

items.stem: The lecture says this is the second module built one capacity, three questions, and that the rhythm now holds to the end of the course. Which capacity does this module run through all three levels?

options.text: The steering circuit — aiming a body at something, and away from something else.
options.why: Correct. Steering at the computational level; weights, thresholds and the valence–arousal pair at the algorithmic; nerve nets, a mapped worm and neuromodulators at the implementational.

options.text: The neuron — a cell that converts an event into a fast, aimed, undiminished signal.
options.why: That was the previous module's example, and this module takes the cell as given.

options.text: The nerve net — the first arrangement of neurons that coordinates a whole body.
options.why: The nerve net is one implementational-level entry in the last column rather than the example the whole table runs on.

options.text: The sponge's sneeze — a whole-body response produced without any nervous system at all.
options.why: The sneeze is the case that opens the first section, and it is not what the three levels are being run on.

items.stem: The chapter recaps where the previous module's story ran to. What was that story, in order?

options.text: Energy became abundant enough for elaborate cells, bodies became multicellular, specialization created the problem of moving information across a body, and the neuron answered it.
options.why: Correct. It stopped there, at a cell type, with no animal named and no body described.

options.text: Bodies became multicellular, cells specialized, neurons appeared, and the animals carrying them then spread into every habitat available to them.
options.why: Where animals went afterward is not part of the recap, and the energy revolution is what starts it.

options.text: Chemical signaling proved too slow, so neurons evolved, and multicellular bodies then became possible for the first time.
options.why: Multicellularity came first and is what created the problem neurons solve.

options.text: An energy revolution made elaborate cells affordable, and those cells became neurons directly, without any intervening stage.
options.why: Multicellularity and specialization are the intervening stages, and they are what make coordination a problem at all.

items.stem: The chapter names one thing it leaves out on purpose. What is it, and how is the omission justified?

options.text: Every circuit in the chapter has weights that hold still, and real animals do learn — a circuit is far easier to follow while its numbers are not moving.
options.why: Correct. How a weight comes to change within an animal's lifetime is handed to a later module rather than denied here.

options.text: Every circuit in the chapter has weights that hold still, because the animals it describes are small enough that their connections genuinely do not change at all.
options.why: Size is not the reason, and the chapter says plainly that real animals learn — the small ones in it included.

options.text: The chapter leaves out the chemistry that retunes a circuit, because chemistry belongs to the implementational level rather than to the algorithmic one.
options.why: Neuromodulation is covered at length in the chapter's third section rather than being left out of it.

options.text: The chapter leaves out how a nervous system develops, because an account of development would need the genetics this course has not yet given.
options.why: Development is not what is set aside here, and no appeal to genetics is made anywhere in the chapter.

pools.title: Nerve Nets, and Coordination Without Aim
pools.covers: reading §4.1.3, §4.1.4, §4.1.5 · lecture 4.1 slides a_mouth_to_operate, the_bell_contracts_as_one, which_way

items.stem: What is a nerve net?

options.text: Neurons distributed through the body wall, each connected to its neighbors, spread through the animal rather than gathered anywhere in particular.
options.why: Correct. It was the earliest arrangement that moved information across a body faster than diffusing chemicals could manage.

options.text: Neurons gathered into a dense cluster near the mouth, from which fibers run outward to every other part of the body wall.
options.why: A concentration of cells at one end is what cephalization produces much later, and it is what a net conspicuously lacks.

options.text: Neurons arranged in a ring around the rim of the bell, so that a signal starting anywhere travels the whole way around it.
options.why: A ring is one shape a net can take in a particular animal, rather than what the arrangement is in general.

options.text: Neurons linked directly to every other neuron in the animal, so that a signal starting anywhere reaches the entire body at the same instant, with no delay along the way.
options.why: All-to-all connection is not what a net is; each cell connects to its neighbors, and a signal spreads from there.

items.stem: Which term names neurons spread through the body wall, each connected to its neighbors, with nothing gathered anywhere in particular?

options.text: nerve net
options.why: Correct. Cnidarians — jellyfish, sea anemones, corals and the freshwater hydra — still run on one.

options.text: nerve ring
options.why: A nerve ring is a dense band of tissue found in a very different animal later in the chapter, and it is a concentration rather than a spread.

options.text: ganglion
options.why: A ganglion is a cluster of neurons, which is the opposite of what a net is built from.

options.text: connectome
options.why: A connectome is a complete map of an animal's connections rather than a kind of arrangement.

items.stem: What does catching prey demand that filtering does not?

options.text: Prey has to be struck, held, carried to the opening and admitted, and the opening has to close behind it, all in different parts of the body and in order.
options.why: Correct. Filtering asks for no coordination beyond keeping the water moving, which is why a sponge can manage it with no neurons at all.

options.text: Prey has to be detected at a distance before it can be reached, which a filter feeder never needs to do because its food arrives with the current anyway, without anything having to be approached.
options.why: Detection at a distance is genuinely harder for a filter feeder to need, and the demand named here is about coordinating the catch itself.

options.text: Prey has to be digested in a cavity rather than by individual cells, which requires a tissue specialized for breaking food down.
options.why: Digestion in a cavity is part of what a mouth brings, and the coordination problem named is about the catching rather than the digesting.

options.text: Prey has to be chosen from among several possibilities, which means the animal has to compare what is available before acting.
options.why: Choosing between options arrives much later in the chapter, with circuits that can commit to one of two things.

items.stem: The chapter draws an inference from which animals run on nerve nets today. What is the observation, and what does it suggest?

options.text: Several cnidarians never travel at all — an anemone is fixed to rock, corals and hydra stay put — which suggests the first nervous systems were probably not for getting anywhere.
options.why: Correct. The earliest nerve nets we can reconstruct were running in animals that stayed where they were.

options.text: Every cnidarian that runs on a nerve net can swim under its own power, which suggests that the first nervous systems were for locomotion from the very beginning rather than for staying put.
options.why: Anemones, corals and hydra are the counterexamples, and free-swimming jellyfish arrived later in one branch of the group.

options.text: Cnidarians with nerve nets are all marine, which suggests that the first nervous systems arose to handle the demands of moving water.
options.why: The freshwater hydra is named among them, and water movement is not the pressure the chapter identifies.

options.text: Cnidarians run on nerve nets and bilaterians do not, which suggests the net was replaced as soon as something better became available.
options.why: The chapter treats the net as a working solution rather than as a stage that got superseded once a better one appeared.

items.stem: What does an animal anchored to a rock still have to coordinate?

options.text: Tentacles that have to fire together, a body wall that has to contract as one, and a mouth that has to open at the right moment and close afterward.
options.why: Correct. All of it is whole-body coordination in the service of eating, and none of it involves travel at all.

options.text: Its position relative to the current, so that the animal stays oriented toward whichever part of the water happens to be carrying the most food past it.
options.why: Reorienting is a form of aiming, which is exactly the capacity these animals are described as lacking.

options.text: The timing of its growth, so that new tentacles appear in proportion to how much the animal is managing to eat.
options.why: Growth is not what the passage is about, and the coordination named is on the timescale of a catch.

options.text: The chemistry of its digestion, so that enzymes are released only once prey has actually reached the cavity.
options.why: Digestion happens in the cavity, and the coordination listed is of tentacles, body wall and mouth rather than of enzymes.

items.stem: The chapter asks how confident we should be that this is how nervous systems first evolved, and answers "reasonably, and not more". What is the disagreement, and what remains agreed?

options.text: Researchers differ over whether the first neurons coordinated a contractile body surface or controlled the beating cilia of swimming larvae; the sequence itself is agreed.
options.why: Correct. Bodies coordinated slowly without neurons, then quickly with them, and mouths arrived somewhere during that transition.

options.text: Researchers differ over whether the very first neurons appeared in cnidarians or in sponges; that nervous systems arose for coordination of some kind is agreed by everyone working on the question.
options.why: Sponges have no neurons at all, so they are not a candidate, and the open question concerns the selective pressure rather than the group.

options.text: Researchers differ over how fast the earliest nerve nets conducted signals; that they beat diffusion is agreed.
options.why: Conduction speed is not the contested point, and the disagreement named is about what the first neurons were selected for.

options.text: Researchers differ over whether nerve nets are still found in living animals; that they existed in the Ediacaran is agreed.
options.why: Living cnidarians run on nerve nets, which the chapter states plainly, so there is nothing contested there.

items.stem: Why is it a live question whether nerve nets evolved once or twice?

options.text: Comb jellies have one built differently enough that it may be an independent invention rather than an inheritance from the same origin.
options.why: Correct. The chapter names the possibility and leaves it open rather than settling it either way.

options.text: Cnidarian nerve nets are not perfectly uniform, which raises the possibility that different cnidarian groups arrived at them separately.
options.why: Non-uniformity is conceded in passing about cnidarians, and it is not the basis for the once-or-twice question.

options.text: The fossil record preserves nerve tissue too rarely for the origin of any nervous system to be dated with confidence.
options.why: Preservation is a genuine difficulty for dating, and the open question here rests on a living group's anatomy instead.

options.text: Sponges carry the molecular parts of neurons, which suggests neurons could have been assembled more than once from the same components.
options.why: The sponge evidence bears on where the parts came from rather than on how many times the net arose.

items.stem: Why do the muscles around the whole rim of a moon jelly's bell have to shorten at the same time?

options.text: A contraction that traveled around the bell in sequence would waste most of its force rather than pushing the animal through the water.
options.why: Correct. Simultaneity is a mechanical requirement here, not an elegance, which is what makes the bell contraction a real solution to the coordination problem.

options.text: A contraction that traveled around the bell in sequence would tear the tissue, since one part would be pulling against another that had not yet moved.
options.why: No damage to the animal is described; what a sequential squeeze costs is force rather than tissue.

options.text: A contraction that began in one place would leave that part of the rim unable to contract again on the next pulse.
options.why: A refractory pause belongs to the previous module's account of a single cell, and it is not what the simultaneity requirement rests on.

options.text: A contraction that traveled around the bell would be too slow to escape a predator, which is what the pulse is mainly for.
options.why: Escape is not what the passage attributes the pulse to, and the argument is about where the force goes.

items.stem: How does a nerve net produce a contraction that happens all at once?

options.text: A wave of activity crossing the net reaches every part of the ring within a few thousandths of a second, so the bell squeezes as one thing.
options.why: Correct. Fast enough is what the net buys; nothing in the arrangement issues an instruction to the whole rim at the same instant.

options.text: A single pacemaker cell fires and every muscle in the rim responds to it directly, so all of them receive the signal simultaneously.
options.why: A pacemaker would be a center of exactly the kind the chapter says a net does not have.

options.text: The muscles of the rim are electrically coupled to one another, so a contraction anywhere spreads mechanically without any neurons involved.
options.why: The coordination described runs through the net rather than through the muscle, which is what makes it a nervous-system solution.

options.text: The net conducts in one direction around the ring, so the wave returns to where it started and the whole rim is caught by it.
options.why: A circulating wave would still arrive at different parts of the rim at different times, which is the outcome to be avoided.

items.stem: The bell contraction lets the chapter pull apart three things that are easy to run together. What are they?

options.text: Having a nervous system, having a brain, and making a decision — the jelly has the first, lacks the second, and needs none of the third.
options.why: Correct. A net can coordinate a whole body with nothing in it that resembles a center, and the nervous system is the arrangement itself.

options.text: Sensing the world, integrating what is sensed, and acting on it — the jelly manages the first and the third without ever doing the second one at all.
options.why: Those three verbs are the previous module's, and the jelly does integrate; the distinction drawn here is about centers and decisions.

options.text: Having neurons, having muscles, and having a body plan that lets the two work together as a single system.
options.why: Each of those is present in the animal, so pulling them apart would not do the work the passage needs.

options.text: Coordinating a body, moving through the world, and choosing where in that world to go — the jelly manages only the first of the three.
options.why: That is the distinction the next section draws, and it is about steering rather than about brains and decisions.

items.stem: A student says the jellyfish's bell contraction must be organized from somewhere, even if we have not found the place yet. What does the chapter say?

options.text: There is no one place where a decision is made or from which orders are sent; the nervous system is the arrangement itself, spread through the tissue it moves.
options.why: Correct. Cnidarian nerve nets are not perfectly uniform, but nothing in one resembles a center in the sense the student means.

options.text: There is a diffuse control region near the rim of the bell, which acts as a center of sorts even though it is not gathered into any visible structure of its own.
options.why: That would concede exactly the point the passage denies, and no such region is described.

options.text: There is no center in a moon jelly, though other cnidarians such as anemones do have one, which is why they can aim their tentacles.
options.why: Anemones are named among the animals running on nets, and aiming is not credited to any cnidarian.

options.text: There is a place of that kind in every nervous system by definition, so the jellyfish's is simply too small to have been found so far.
options.why: The chapter's point is that having a nervous system is not the same as having a brain, so no such definition holds.

items.stem: What is radial symmetry?

options.text: A body plan built around a central axis and much the same all the way around, so that turning the animal a few degrees changes nothing about it.
options.why: Correct. The consequence the chapter draws from it is geometric: no part of such an animal ever arrives anywhere first.

options.text: A body plan in which the left and right halves mirror one another exactly, so that the animal looks much the same from either side of it, with no end distinguished from the other.
options.why: Mirrored halves are what bilateral symmetry gives, and that plan does have a front and a back.

options.text: A body plan in which the same structures are repeated along the length of the body, as segments one after another.
options.why: Repetition along a length is segmentation, which is a different kind of regularity altogether.

options.text: A body plan organized around a mouth at one end and an opening at the other, with the gut running between them.
options.why: A through-gut describes a route through the body rather than the symmetry of the body's shape.

items.stem: Which term names a body plan built around a central axis, much the same all the way around, with no side that is different from any other?

options.text: radial symmetry
options.why: Correct. A moon jelly is built this way, which is why it has no front and no privileged place to put sensors.

options.text: bilateral symmetry
options.why: Bilateral symmetry gives an animal a left and a right, and with them a front and a back.

options.text: cephalization
options.why: Cephalization is the gathering of neurons and sensors toward one end, which a radial animal has no end to do it at.

options.text: steering
options.why: Steering is what an animal does with a body plan rather than a description of the plan itself.

items.stem: Why does a radially symmetric animal have no privileged place for its sensors to gather?

options.text: Because no part of such an animal always arrives anywhere first, so there is no best place to put them.
options.why: Correct. The argument is geometric rather than neural: it is about the shape of the body rather than about what its nerves can manage.

options.text: Because a nerve net conducts equally well in every direction, so gathering sensors anywhere would confer no advantage on the animal.
options.why: Conduction is a fact about the net; the reason given here is about the body plan, and it would hold whatever the net could do.

options.text: Because the animal's nervous system is too simple to make use of information gathered in one place rather than spread out.
options.why: This mis-sources the argument. It is not a limitation of the nerves, and the chapter is careful that these are not deficient animals.

options.text: Because sensors spread evenly cover more of the water around the animal, which matters more than knowing which direction a signal came from.
options.why: Coverage is a real benefit of the arrangement, and it is a consequence of the geometry rather than the reason the chapter gives.

items.stem: What can a jellyfish do, and what can it not do?

options.text: It can rise, sink, sense light, gravity and chemistry, and pulse more or less often in response; what it cannot do is answer the question which way.
options.why: Correct. It goes somewhere. It does not go somewhere in particular, which is the gap the rest of the section is built on.

options.text: It can sense light and chemistry but cannot act on either, so its behavior is limited to pulsing at one constant rate whatever it happens to detect around it.
options.why: It can pulse more often or less often in response to what it senses, so it does act on what it detects.

options.text: It can move toward food but not away from danger, since the net supports approach and has no mechanism for avoidance.
options.why: Neither approach nor avoidance is available to it, because both require aiming the body somewhere in particular.

options.text: It can steer while swimming but cannot hold a direction for long, since it has no way to keep track of where it has been.
options.why: Holding a course is not the limitation; the animal has no way to pick a direction in the first place.

items.stem: The chapter sums up the jellyfish's position in one phrase. What is it?

options.text: Coordination in time without direction in space.
options.why: Correct. Every part of the bell acts at the same moment, and no part of the animal is aimed at anything in particular.

options.text: Direction in space without coordination in time.
options.why: That is the reverse of the animal's situation, and it describes nothing the chapter discusses.

options.text: Coordination in space without direction in time.
options.why: The phrase is built on the contrast between when the body acts and where it goes, and this inverts both halves.

options.text: Sensation without any corresponding capacity for action.
options.why: The animal does act on what it senses, so its limitation is not on the action side at all.

items.stem: How does the chapter characterize whole-body coordination without steering?

options.text: As a successful strategy rather than a failure or a small way to live, since cnidarians have been doing it for six hundred million years in every ocean.
options.why: Correct. Blocking the ladder reading matters most here, because this is the point at which it bites hardest.

options.text: As a workable arrangement for a small animal, though one that sets a firm limit on how large a body can become.
options.why: Body size is not what the passage makes of it, and the moon jelly is not presented as constrained by its dimensions.

options.text: As an early stage that persisted only in those lineages that never faced predators moving fast enough to make aiming worth what it would have cost them.
options.why: Calling it an early stage is precisely the ladder reading, and no claim about predator speed is made.

options.text: As a compromise that trades the ability to aim for the ability to coordinate, since no nervous system can do both.
options.why: Bilaterians do both, which is what the rest of the section goes on to describe.

items.stem: Explain, step by step, why a radially symmetric body plan leaves an animal unable to answer the question which way.
items.answer: Radial symmetry means the body is built around a central axis and is much the same all the way around, so turning the animal a few degrees changes nothing about it. An animal built that way has no front, no back, and no left or right, which means no part of it always arrives anywhere first. Because no part arrives first, there is no privileged place for sensors to gather, since there is no best place to put them. And without sensors concentrated at a leading end, there is nothing to tell the animal that one direction differs from another. So it can rise, sink, and pulse more or less often in response to what it senses — it goes somewhere, but it does not go somewhere in particular.
rubric: Defines radial symmetry as built around a central axis and much the same all the way around.
Draws the consequence that the animal has no front, back, left or right, so nothing arrives first.
Concludes that there is therefore no privileged place for sensors to gather.
Distinguishes going somewhere from going somewhere in particular.

items.stem: How settled is the date for the oldest fossils widely accepted as cnidarians?

options.text: Less settled than it sounds: several Ediacaran identifications are argued about, and the most securely identified early cnidarian is some twenty million years younger.
options.why: Correct. Either way the date lands close enough to the oldest accepted sponges that the fossil record cannot order the two groups.

options.text: Well settled at around 580 million years, since cnidarian fossils preserve unusually clearly when set beside those of the other soft-bodied animals of the period.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite about how firm the figure is, and soft-bodied preservation is not offered as a reason for confidence.

options.text: Unsettled, because the earliest cnidarian fossils cannot be distinguished from the earliest bilaterian ones on the evidence available.
options.why: The comparison the chapter draws is with sponges rather than bilaterians, whose oldest body fossil is younger.

options.text: Settled enough to establish that cnidarians appeared before sponges, which is what makes the nerve net the earlier arrangement.
options.why: The chapter says explicitly that the record cannot settle which of the two came first.

items.stem: Where do free-swimming jellyfish fall in the history of the cnidarian group?

options.text: They arrived later, in one branch of the group, rather than being the shape the first cnidarians had.
options.why: Correct. That is why the earliest nerve nets we can reconstruct were running in animals that stayed put.

options.text: They were the earliest form, with anchored anemones and corals appearing afterward as some lineages settled down.
options.why: This reverses the order, and it would undercut the inference the chapter draws about what the first nets were for.

options.text: They arose separately from the rest of the group, which is part of why it is a live question whether nerve nets evolved twice.
options.why: The twice question concerns comb jellies rather than the swimming forms within the cnidarian group.

options.text: They appeared at the same time as anchored forms, which is why the fossil record cannot order the two.
options.why: The ordering problem the chapter describes is between sponges and cnidarians rather than within the cnidarians.

items.stem: What is a mouth, in the simple form the chapter describes?

options.text: A single opening leading into a cavity where food is broken down, with cells near it specializing for opening and closing and cells deeper along it for digestion.
options.why: Correct. That division of labor is what can eventually lead to very specialized tissues and organs.

options.text: A single opening through which water is drawn in and food is then captured by the individual cells that line the passage, one particle at a time, with nothing swallowed.
options.why: That describes the sponge's arrangement, which the chapter contrasts with having a mouth at all.

options.text: An opening surrounded by a ring of tentacles carrying stinging cells, which is what allows prey to be struck and held.
options.why: The ring of tentacles is what some of the earliest animals with mouths added, rather than part of what a mouth is.

options.text: A pair of openings connected by a gut, so that food travels in one direction through the body and waste leaves at the far end.
options.why: A through-gut is a later arrangement, and the mouth described here leads into a cavity rather than a passage.

items.stem: The chapter makes a one-clause concession about cnidarian nerve nets. What is it, and how far does it go?

options.text: They are not perfectly uniform — a concession made in passing and not developed, and not enough to give any cnidarian something resembling a center.
options.why: Correct. What matters for the argument is that a net can coordinate a whole body with nothing in it that resembles a center.

options.text: They are not perfectly uniform, which is why some regions of the bell contract before others during a pulse.
options.why: Sequential contraction is exactly what the arrangement has to avoid, so the concession cannot be doing that work.

options.text: They are not found in every cnidarian, since some members of the group have lost their nervous systems entirely.
options.why: No cnidarian is described as having lost its nervous system; loss appears later in the chapter for a different animal.

options.text: They are not the only arrangement cnidarians use, and the concession is that the swimming forms supplement the net with a ring of specialized fibers of their own.
options.why: No supplementary arrangement is described, and the bell contraction is credited to the net itself.

items.stem: The lecture counts out what catching prey demands, in a way the chapter states more briefly. What is the count, and why does it matter?

options.text: Five things, in order, in different parts of the body, and fast enough that the prey does not get away.
options.why: Correct. Counting them makes the coordination problem concrete: it is the ordering and the speed together that diffusion cannot deliver.

options.text: Three things, at the same moment, in the same part of the body, and repeated until the prey stops struggling.
options.why: Simultaneity in one place is the jellyfish's problem rather than the anemone's, and the lecture's list runs in sequence.

options.text: Five things, in any order, spread across the body, with the opening closing whenever the prey has finally been admitted.
options.why: Order is precisely what the lecture stresses; the prey has to be struck before it can be held or carried.

options.text: Four things, in order, followed by a period in which the tentacles cannot fire again until they have recovered.
options.why: No recovery period is part of the lecture's account of catching.

items.stem: The lecture says the simultaneity of the bell contraction is a mechanical requirement rather than an elegance, and says where the force would go otherwise. Where?

options.text: A contraction traveling round the bell in sequence would squeeze water sideways instead of pushing it down.
options.why: Correct. Naming where the wasted force goes is what turns a stated requirement into something a student can see for themselves.

options.text: A contraction traveling round the bell would push the animal in a circle, so the jelly would turn rather than rise.
options.why: Turning would be a kind of steering, which is the one thing this animal is described as unable to do.

options.text: A contraction traveling round the bell would be absorbed by the tissue itself, warming the animal rather than moving it.
options.why: Heat is not where the lecture says the force goes, and no thermal cost is discussed.

options.text: A contraction traveling round the bell would arrive back where it started and cancel the next pulse out.
options.why: Nothing about cancellation is described, and the loss named is in the direction the water is pushed.

items.stem: The lecture says it is blocking the ladder reading "one more time" at this point, and gives a reason for choosing this point. What is the reason?

options.text: This is where the ladder reading bites hardest, because an animal that cannot steer looks most like an unfinished version of one that can.
options.why: Correct. The lecture answers it with six hundred million years in every ocean and at every depth, which is a record of success rather than of falling short.

options.text: This is where the chapter first compares a cnidarian with a bilaterian, and a direct comparison is what invites the ladder reading.
options.why: No bilaterian has appeared yet at this point in the lecture, which comes to them only afterward.

options.text: This is where the lecture stops describing anatomy and starts describing behavior, and behavior is easier to rank than structure.
options.why: The lecture does not draw that distinction, and it has been describing behavior since the sponge's sneeze.

options.text: This is the last opportunity before the argument moves on, since the ladder warning cannot usefully be repeated once the bilaterians have been introduced.
options.why: The warning is repeated as needed rather than spent, and no such constraint is stated.

items.stem: "The first thing a nervous system was ever for" is not getting anywhere. Explain what the chapter thinks it was for, and what evidence points that way.
items.answer: It was for getting a body to act as one body, quickly. The evidence is which animals run on nerve nets: several cnidarians never travel at all, since an anemone is fixed to rock and corals and hydra stay in one place for most or all of their lives, and free-swimming jellyfish arrived later in one branch of the group. So the earliest nerve nets we can reconstruct were running in animals that stayed put. An anchored animal still has a great deal to coordinate — tentacles that have to fire together, a body wall that has to contract as one, a mouth that has to open at the right moment and close afterward — and all of that is whole-body coordination in the service of eating, with no travel involved.
rubric: States the purpose as getting a body to act as one body, quickly.
Gives the evidence: the animals running on nets are largely anchored ones.
Notes that free-swimming forms arrived later rather than first.
Lists what an anchored animal still has to coordinate, and that none of it involves travel.

items.stem: What did some of the earliest animals with mouths have around the opening?

options.text: A ring of tentacles carrying stinging cells, as in the first corals and sea anemones.
options.why: Correct. That arrangement is what changes the demands on a body, since prey now has to be caught rather than filtered.

options.text: A ring of cilia that drew water inward, which is how food was brought to the opening without being caught.
options.why: Drawing water in is closer to how a sponge feeds, and it needs no catching at all.

options.text: A ring of muscle that closed the opening, with no structure outside it for capturing anything.
options.why: Cells near the mouth do specialize for opening and closing, and the tentacles are what sit outside.

options.text: A ring of sensory cells that detected food, with the tentacles developing much later in the lineage.
options.why: No such sequence is described; the tentacles with their stinging cells are part of the early arrangement.

pools.title: Bilaterians, Steering, and the Birth of Good and Bad
pools.covers: reading §4.1.6, §4.1.7, §4.1.8 · lecture 4.1 slides a_front_and_what_it_costs, what_steering_demands, evaluate

items.stem: What is bilateral symmetry?

options.text: A body plan with a left and a right side that mirror one another and, far more consequentially, a front and a back.
options.why: Correct. The chapter is explicit that the front is the half of the definition that does the work in this module.

options.text: A body plan with a left and a right side that mirror one another, and with no distinguished end along its length.
options.why: Mirrored halves alone would leave the animal in the jellyfish's position, unable to say which way is forward.

options.text: A body plan built around a central axis, so that the two halves on either side of that axis are much the same.
options.why: An axis with sameness all the way around it is radial symmetry, which is the plan this one gave way from.

options.text: A body plan in which the nervous system runs along one side of the body rather than being spread through the body wall.
options.why: Where the nerve cord runs is a fact about the nervous system rather than about the symmetry of the body.

items.stem: Which term names the body plan shared by worms, insects, snails, fish, birds and human beings?

options.text: bilateral symmetry
options.why: Correct. Nearly every animal most people could name is built this way, with a mirrored left and right and a front and a back.

options.text: radial symmetry, the plan of a moon jelly
options.why: Radial symmetry belongs to the moon jelly and its relatives, and it is what this plan replaced in one group.

options.text: cephalization
options.why: Cephalization is what happens at the front once an animal has one, rather than the plan that gives it a front.

options.text: segmentation
options.why: Segmentation is repetition along the body's length, which some bilaterians have and which is not what defines the plan.

items.stem: Why is the front of a bilaterian the useful place to put sensors and the neurons they report to?

options.text: The front is the end that arrives first, so news of the world shows up there earliest, and a verdict reached near the sensors is a verdict reached sooner.
options.why: Correct. Both halves of that are about time, which is what makes them the right reasons rather than reasons about anatomy.

options.text: The front is the widest part of most bilaterian bodies, so more sensors fit there than in any other part of the animal.
options.why: Body width is not the consideration, and a worm's front is not notably wider than the rest of it.

options.text: The front is protected by the animal's forward motion, so delicate sensory tissue is less likely to be damaged there.
options.why: Nothing about protection is claimed, and a leading end is if anything the more exposed one.

options.text: The front is where the mouth already sits, so a verdict about food can be acted on without the signal having to travel far to reach the muscles.
options.why: The mouth's position matters to catching rather than to steering, and the argument given is about arrival and about time.

items.stem: What is steering, as this chapter defines it?

options.text: Moving forward, turning, and letting what the front end detects decide which way the turn goes.
options.why: Correct. An animal that steers does not merely move; it moves toward some things and away from others.

options.text: Moving forward and turning at intervals, so that the whole of the surrounding area is covered over time.
options.why: Systematic search does not require anything detected to decide the turn, which is the component that matters here.

options.text: Moving in whatever direction the strongest signal arrives from, without any turning being involved.
options.why: Turning is part of the definition, and forward-plus-turn is what the chapter calls a simple and general arrangement.

options.text: Moving toward food and away from danger by changing how often the body contracts overall.
options.why: Changing the rate of contraction is what a jellyfish does, and it produces no direction in space.

items.stem: The chapter calls steering this module's evolutionary addition. What does that phrase mean here?

options.text: A capacity that solved a problem, and that everything downstream is built on top of.
options.why: Correct. The four demands of the rest of the chapter are all demands steering makes, which is what downstream means in practice.

options.text: A capacity that appeared in one lineage and then spread to others that faced the same problem independently.
options.why: Independent arrival at the same solution is convergence, which is a different relationship between lineages.

options.text: A capacity that replaced an earlier one, so that the animals with it no longer need what came before.
options.why: Nerve nets are not superseded by steering; anchored animals go on using them successfully.

options.text: A capacity that arrived before the problem it solves, and found a use only once conditions changed.
options.why: Nothing waits for a use in the chapter's account, and the ordering it describes runs the other way.

items.stem: The sea squirt is offered as a case that makes the cost of steering visible. How does it do that?

options.text: It begins as a swimming larva that steers with a nerve cord and a small brain, then attaches head-first and breaks down its tail and its brain, keeping a much reduced ganglion.
options.why: Correct. An animal that stops steering does not need to go on paying for the machinery that steers.

options.text: It begins life as a filter feeder and later develops a brain once it starts to move about, which shows what the machinery is bought for.
options.why: The sequence runs the other way: it steers first and gives the machinery up afterward.

options.text: It keeps its brain after settling but stops using it, which shows that the cost of the machinery is all in the building of it rather than in the running of it.
options.why: The brain is broken down into molecules useful for other purposes, so it is not kept unused.

options.text: It grows a larger brain when food is scarce and a smaller one when food is plentiful, which prices the machinery directly.
options.why: No reversible adjustment is described, and the change the chapter reports happens once, at settlement.

items.stem: Why does the chapter insist that sea squirts are chordates rather than early animals?

options.text: To block the misreading that this is an early animal losing a brain it never fully had; it is a late animal giving up a brain it has.
options.why: Correct. The case only prices steering if the animal genuinely had the machinery before it discarded it.

options.text: To establish that an animal losing its brain has happened only once, in a group closely related to the vertebrates.
options.why: No claim about how often brain loss has occurred is made, and the point is about how to read this case.

options.text: To show that giving up a brain happened early rather than late, which makes it better evidence than anything from the Ediacaran.
options.why: Recency is not the argument, and the chapter's concern is with what the animal is rather than with when it lived.

options.text: To explain why the remaining ganglion is large enough to run the siphons and the gut rather than being broken down and disappearing entirely.
options.why: What the ganglion still does follows from what the settled animal still needs, not from the group it belongs to.

items.stem: Why does the chapter point out that cars, boats, aircraft and submarines are bilaterally symmetric with a designated front?

options.text: Because human beings keep arriving at the same design, which suggests forward-plus-turn is a simple and general arrangement for getting somewhere.
options.why: Correct. It is a check on the claim from the artificial side rather than an additional biological case.

options.text: Because the engineers who designed them were copying animal body plans, which makes it the clearest case of biological inspiration anywhere in the chapter.
options.why: No borrowing is claimed; the point is that the same arrangement was arrived at independently.

options.text: Because vehicles have to satisfy the same four demands steering makes of a nervous system, which the chapter goes on to show.
options.why: The four demands are about information processing, and the vehicles are offered for their shape rather than their computing.

options.text: Because a designed object can have a front for reasons of appearance, which shows that having one is not always functional.
options.why: The chapter's reading is the opposite: the shape recurs because it works.

items.stem: What four abilities does steering demand of a nervous system?

options.text: Evaluate what is sensed, combine signals that disagree, sharpen and commit, and let the animal's own condition modulate every one of those judgments.
options.why: Correct. Those four are the chapter's index: each is stated here, built as an arrangement later, and found in tissue later still.

options.text: Detect, transmit, integrate and act, which are the four jobs the previous module handed to a single neuron working entirely on its own.
options.why: Those are the roles inside one cell, and this list is about what an arrangement of them has to accomplish.

options.text: Sense the world, remember what happened, predict what comes next, and select an action on the basis of the prediction.
options.why: Memory and prediction belong to later modules, and neither appears among the demands named here.

options.text: Evaluate what is sensed, decide where to go, move the body, and correct the course when the target moves.
options.why: Course correction is not one of the four, and moving the body is what the demands are in service of rather than one of them.

items.stem: What does it mean to sharpen and commit?

options.text: To turn a near-tie into a clear difference, and then collapse the result into a single action.
options.why: Correct. Both halves are needed: without sharpening the difference stays small, and without committing the animal does two things at once.

options.text: To increase the strength of the winning signal until it is strong enough to drive the muscles directly.
options.why: Amplification alone would leave a near-tie a near-tie, since both signals would grow together.

options.text: To hold several possible actions in reserve until the evidence for one of them becomes overwhelming.
options.why: Waiting for certainty is not what is described, and the point of sharpening is to act on a small difference.

options.text: To repeat a judgment until it comes out the same way twice, which is what makes the resulting action reliable.
options.why: No repetition is involved, and the operation is described as working on one near-tie at a time.

items.stem: What does the demand to evaluate require, and why?

options.text: Sorting what is sensed into good, bad and neither, since no direction can be preferred without a reason to prefer it.
options.why: Correct. It is the demand that makes the other three worth having, because nothing can be combined or committed to without verdicts to work on.

options.text: Measuring how strong each signal is, since a stronger signal is more likely to be worth acting on than a weak one.
options.why: Strength is what the combining demand weighs, and strength on its own carries no verdict about good or bad.
