options.text: Identifying which chemical is present, since an animal cannot respond appropriately without knowing what it has detected.
options.why: Identification is not enough, because nothing about the identity of a compound settles whether it is worth approaching.

options.text: Comparing what is sensed now against what was sensed a moment ago, since a change is more informative than a level.
options.why: Comparison across time is how one animal steers later in the chapter, rather than what evaluating requires in general.

items.stem: How do the demands to combine and to modulate differ?

options.text: Combining weighs several cues at once, by strength and by which combination is present; modulating lets the animal's own state change the verdict and outlast the event that caused it.
options.why: Correct. One is about the signals arriving from outside, and the other is about the condition of the animal receiving them.

options.text: Combining works on signals that agree with one another, while modulating works on those signals that disagree with one another and therefore have to be reconciled somehow.
options.why: Disagreement is exactly what combining handles, which is why the chapter describes it as weighing cues that conflict.

options.text: Combining happens before a verdict is reached, while modulating happens afterward, adjusting how strongly the action is carried out.
options.why: Modulation changes the verdict itself rather than only the vigor of what follows from it.

options.text: Combining is what a single neuron already does, while modulating is the first demand that requires more than one cell.
options.why: A single cell can be modulated too, and the chapter does not divide the demands by how many cells each needs.

items.stem: The chapter says what each of its three sections does with the four demands. What is the division?

options.text: The demands are stated here, showing what has to be computed; the arrangements that compute them are built next; those arrangements are then found in real tissue and chemistry.
options.why: Correct. Naming a demand is not meeting it, which is why this section ends with four demands and no mechanisms at all.

options.text: The demands are stated here and met here as well, with the later sections supplying the evidence that real animals do go about meeting them in the same way.
options.why: Nothing here supplies a mechanism, and the later sections build rather than corroborate.

options.text: The demands are stated here in their biological form, then generalized to artificial systems, then compared across the two.
options.why: The comparison with artificial systems runs throughout the chapter rather than occupying a section of its own.

options.text: The demands are stated here, ranked by difficulty next, and then traced through the animal groups in order of appearance.
options.why: No ranking by difficulty is offered, and the walk through animal groups happens before the demands are named.

items.stem: What does the chapter mean by saying steering is not free?

options.text: The rest of the chapter describes what steering costs in information processing, which a jellyfish drifting on a current never has to pay.
options.why: Correct. The cost being priced is computational rather than metabolic, and the four demands are the bill.

options.text: Steering costs an animal energy that the chapter says it would otherwise spend on growth, which is why the animals that steer tend to be a good deal smaller than the ones that do not.
options.why: Body size is not connected to the cost here, and the cost named is in information processing.

options.text: Steering requires a brain, which is the most expensive tissue an animal can build and maintain.
options.why: What the tissue costs belongs to the previous module's accounting, and this section is at the computational level.

options.text: Steering slows an animal down, since evaluating what is sensed takes time that a drifting animal does not spend.
options.why: No speed penalty is described, and drifting is contrasted for what it does not have to compute.

items.stem: A chemical drifts past a worm's head. What does the chapter say settles whether it is good or bad?

options.text: Nothing about the molecule itself does: not its shape, not its concentration, and not the receptor it happens to fit.
options.why: Correct. Whether it is worth approaching depends on what the animal is, on what it eats, and on what eats it.

options.text: Its concentration does, since a compound harmless in small amounts becomes damaging as the amount increases.
options.why: Concentration is named among the things that do not settle it, though quantity does matter to an animal in other ways.

options.text: The receptor it fits does, since an animal builds receptors only for those compounds that already matter to its way of life.
options.why: Having a receptor shows that the compound is detectable rather than that it carries a verdict.

options.text: Its shape does, since the molecules animals treat as food share structural features that damaging ones lack.
options.why: No structural signature of good compounds is claimed, and a compound meaning food to one species can mean danger to another.

items.stem: What is valence?

options.text: The tag a nervous system attaches to what it senses, marking a thing as worth moving toward or away from.
options.why: Correct. It is the first thing steering requires, because no direction can be preferred without a reason to prefer it.

options.text: The strength of an animal's response to what it senses, which determines how vigorously it approaches or avoids.
options.why: Vigor is closer to the other of the two numbers the chapter introduces later, and it carries no good-or-bad judgment.

options.text: The property of a compound that makes it nutritious or damaging to the animal that encounters it.
options.why: Locating it in the compound is exactly what the chapter denies; good and bad are assigned rather than found.

options.text: The rate at which a sensory neuron fires in response to a chemical it has receptors for.
options.why: A rate is only a rate, and the chapter is explicit that there is no goodness in the sensory cell either.

items.stem: Which term names the tag that marks something as worth moving toward or away from, and so supplies approach and avoidance?

options.text: valence
options.why: Correct. Those two directions are the only ones a steering animal can take with respect to anything it detects.

options.text: arousal
options.why: Arousal is the other of the two numbers the chapter uses for affect, and it is about intensity rather than about sign.

options.text: internal state
options.why: An internal state is a condition of the animal that changes its verdicts, rather than the verdict itself.

options.text: steering
options.why: Steering is what an animal does once it has a verdict, and valence is what the verdict is called.

items.stem: The chapter states where value comes into existence, and is deliberately careful about it. Where does it say value arises?

options.text: Somewhere in the arrangement of cells between the sensor and the animal's actuators — not in the molecule, and not in the sensory cell either.
options.why: Correct. That is the computational-level statement, and the chapter localizes it further only in its later sections.

options.text: In the sensory cell, which is where the world first makes contact with the nervous system and so where the verdict begins.
options.why: The chapter rules the sensory cell out by name, which is the sharper half of the claim.

options.text: In the receptor the compound fits, since which receptor is engaged is what tells the animal what kind of thing has just arrived.
options.why: Placing value in the receptor is the reading the passage was written to block.

options.text: In the muscles the signal eventually reaches, since a verdict is only a verdict once it has produced approach or avoidance.
options.why: Behavior is the consequence of the verdict rather than where the verdict is formed.

items.stem: What follows from the fact that a compound meaning food to one species could mean danger to another?

options.text: Whether something is worth approaching depends on what the animal is, on what it eats, and on what eats it, so the verdict belongs to the animal.
options.why: Correct. Both verdicts are correct for the animal holding them, which is what makes assignment rather than discovery the right description.

options.text: Animals with overlapping diets will assign the same valence to the same compounds, which is part of how an ecological community of related species stays stable over time.
options.why: Nothing about shared diets or community stability is claimed anywhere in the passage.

options.text: A compound's valence changes over evolutionary time, so what is good for a species now may not have been good before.
options.why: Change over time is not the point being made; the contrast drawn is between species at the same moment.

options.text: Valence must be learned rather than inherited, since no animal could be born knowing which compounds its own species should avoid.
options.why: How a verdict comes to be set is not settled here, and learning is deferred to a later module entirely.

items.stem: "Good and bad are not inherent in the world. They are assigned." Explain what the chapter means, and how far it pushes the claim.
items.answer: Nothing about a chemical's shape, its concentration, or the receptor it happens to fit makes it inherently good or bad. Whether it is worth approaching depends on what the animal is, on what it eats, and on what eats it, so the same compound can mean food to one species and danger to another. Valence is the name for the tag a nervous system attaches, marking a thing as worth moving toward or away from, and an animal acts on a verdict it assigned rather than on a property it found. The chapter pushes the claim as far as the sensory cell: there is no goodness in the molecule and none in the cell that detects it either, so value comes into existence somewhere in the arrangement of cells between the sensor and the animal's actuators.
rubric: States that nothing about the compound itself carries the verdict.
Explains that the verdict depends on the animal — what it is, what it eats, what eats it.
Names valence as the tag, and approach and avoidance as what it supplies.
Pushes the claim past the sensory cell to the arrangement between sensor and actuator.

items.stem: The lecture tells the room to read the last two columns of the steering-demands table as a promise rather than as content. Why?

options.text: Everything in this lecture states what has to be computed and not one word says how; the arrangements and the tissue belong to the two lectures after it.
options.why: Correct. By the end of the lecture there are four named demands and no mechanisms at all, which the lecture calls the correct state to be in.

options.text: The arrangements the lecture names there are provisional, and the later meetings may well replace them with better ones.
options.why: Nothing is described as provisional; what is deferred is the explanation rather than the choice of mechanism.

options.text: The columns name where each demand is met in the reading, and a student is better off checking the chapter itself than relying on a summary of it.
options.why: The columns point forward to the later lectures as well, and the lecture does not send anyone off to verify them.

options.text: The demands are ordered by how well understood they are, so the last two columns are fuller for some rows than others.
options.why: Every row carries entries in both columns, and no ranking by understanding is offered.

items.stem: The lecture names the most common way to go wrong with Marr's levels, and says which direction the mistake runs in. What is it?

options.text: Naming a demand is not meeting it, and the mistake runs toward feeling that something has been understood when it has not.
options.why: Correct. The lecture makes the boundary explicit precisely because the feeling of understanding arrives before the mechanism does.

options.text: Treating the levels as a sequence, and the mistake runs toward believing that the implementational level must come last.
options.why: Order of presentation is a choice the course makes rather than an error it warns against here.

options.text: Mixing the vocabulary of two levels in one sentence, and the mistake runs toward describing a cell where a unit was meant.
options.why: That is a real constraint later in the module, and it is not the error named on this slide.

options.text: Assuming every level has an answer, and the mistake runs toward inventing a mechanism where none is known.
options.why: The lecture's concern is with stopping at the name rather than with fabricating what comes after it.

items.stem: The lecture says the sea squirt is the better of its two checks on the steering claim, and gives a reason. What is it?

options.text: It runs the story backward: instead of showing what having a front buys, it shows what an animal stops paying for when it stops steering.
options.why: Correct. The machinery is broken down into molecules useful for other purposes, which prices it in the plainest way available.

options.text: It is a living animal rather than a designed object, so the evidence it offers about steering is biological rather than drawn from engineering.
options.why: Both checks concern living arrangements and designed ones respectively, and the lecture's reason is about direction rather than kind.

options.text: It is a chordate, so the case bears directly on the vertebrate lineage rather than on a distantly related group.
options.why: The chordate point is raised to block a misreading rather than to strengthen the evidence.

options.text: It shows the machinery being built rather than assumed, which is what the first check could only take for granted.
options.why: The larva arrives with the machinery already in place, and what the case shows is its removal.

items.stem: Before giving the chapter's answer, the lecture asks the room to try something first. What, and why does it say the exercise is worth doing?

options.text: To decide for oneself whether anything about a compound could settle whether it is good or bad — because people do not always agree, and the disagreement is the interesting part.
options.why: Correct. Holding the question open for a moment is what makes the answer land as an argument rather than as a definition.

options.text: To name a compound that is good for one species and bad for another — because a worked example of that kind is easier to remember than a principle stated on its own.
options.why: The worked example arrives afterward, and the exercise the lecture sets is about the principle instead.

options.text: To predict which of the four demands will turn out to be hardest — because the ordering of the demands is not obvious in advance.
options.why: No prediction about difficulty is invited, and the demands are not ranked.

options.text: To recall where the previous module located value — because the answer here is a correction of what was said there.
options.why: Nothing here corrects the earlier module, which reached the same conclusion about where value is not.

items.stem: A front is worth having, on the chapter's argument, for two reasons that are both about time. Give both, and say what having a front makes possible.
items.answer: The first is that an animal with a front has an end that arrives first, so that end is the useful place to put sensors: news of the world shows up there earliest. The second is that the front is also the useful place to put the neurons those sensors report to, because a verdict reached near the sensors is a verdict reached sooner. What the arrangement makes possible is steering — moving forward, turning, and letting what the front end detects decide which way the turn goes. An animal that steers does not merely move; it moves toward some things and away from others.
rubric: Gives the sensor reason: the end that arrives first is where the world shows up earliest.
Gives the second reason: a verdict reached near the sensors is reached sooner.
Defines steering as forward motion plus turning, with the front end deciding the turn.
Notes that steering means moving toward some things and away from others rather than merely moving.

items.stem: Name the four demands steering makes of a nervous system, and give one sentence on what each requires.
items.answer: Evaluate: sort what is sensed into good, bad and neither, since no direction can be preferred without a reason to prefer it. Combine: weigh several cues at once, both by how strong each one is and by which combination of them is present. Sharpen and commit: turn a near-tie into a clear difference, and then collapse the result into a single action. Modulate: let the animal's own condition change every one of those judgments, and let a state outlast the event that caused it.
rubric: Names evaluating, and ties it to needing a reason to prefer one direction.
Names combining, and includes both strength and which combination is present.
Names sharpening and committing, with both the near-tie and the single action.
Names modulating, including that a state can outlast its cause.

items.stem: Where does valence sit among the demands steering makes?

options.text: It is the first thing steering requires, because no direction can be preferred without a reason to prefer it.
options.why: Correct. It is what makes the other three demands worth having at all.

options.text: It is the last thing steering requires, since a verdict can only be reached once the cues have been combined.
options.why: Combining works on verdicts that have already been assigned, so evaluating comes first.

options.text: It sits alongside committing, since both concern how a decision is finally settled.
options.why: Committing collapses the result into one action, and valence supplies the material for that result.

options.text: It is not one of the demands at all, since valence is a property of the world rather than something computed.
options.why: Valence is assigned rather than found, which is the chapter's central claim about it.

pools.title: Combine, Sharpen, Modulate, and a Machine That Steers
pools.covers: reading §4.1.9, §4.1.10, §4.1.11, §4.1.12 · lecture 4.1 slides combine, sharpen_and_commit, modulate, a_machine_that_steers

items.stem: The chapter says combination has two aspects worth keeping separate. What are they?

options.text: A quantitative aspect, in which cues of different strengths are weighed against one another, and a relational one, in which what matters is which combination of cues is present.
options.why: Correct. The two are kept apart because the next section builds different machinery for each — weights for the first, thresholds and logic units for the second.

options.text: A spatial aspect, in which cues arriving on different sides are compared, and a temporal one, in which the combination arriving now is compared with the one arriving a moment later.
options.why: Comparing places against moments is how two particular animals steer later in the chapter, rather than how combination divides in general.

options.text: A sensory aspect, in which cues of different kinds are converted to a common currency, and a motor one, in which the result is turned into a movement.
options.why: Conversion and output are stages of the whole process rather than the two aspects of combining named here.

options.text: An immediate aspect, in which cues present now are added together, and a remembered one, in which cues from earlier are given less weight than recent ones.
options.why: Nothing about memory or decay enters the account of combining, and learning is deferred to a later module entirely.

items.stem: What is a cue, as the chapter uses the word?

options.text: Something an animal can sense that carries information about what is out there.
options.why: Correct. Out in the world several arrive at once, and they often imply different things, which is what makes combining them a demand.

options.text: Something an animal can sense that has already been tagged as good or bad by its nervous system.
options.why: The tag is valence, which is applied to a cue rather than being part of what makes something a cue.

options.text: Something in the world that reliably predicts a reward, so that an animal can learn to act on it.
options.why: Prediction and reward belong to a later module, and the chapter's sense here is simply informational.

options.text: Something an animal can sense strongly enough to act on without needing to combine it with anything else.
options.why: A cue strong enough to act on alone would remove the very problem this section is about.

items.stem: What does the copper-barrier experiment with C. elegans show about how the worm combines cues?

options.text: Whether it crosses depends on how strong the food odor is set against how forbidding the barrier is: more attractant and more worms cross, more copper and fewer do.
options.why: Correct. Nothing here is a yes-or-no rule; two graded quantities are set against each other and the behavior follows whichever wins.

options.text: Whether it crosses depends on whether the food odor is present at all, since the barrier is avoided outright unless something on the far side of it is worth having the trouble.
options.why: A presence-or-absence rule is the relational aspect of combining, and this case is chosen to illustrate the quantitative one.

options.text: Whether it crosses depends on how long the worm has been in contact with the copper, since the avoidance response weakens with exposure.
options.why: Habituation to the barrier is not described, and the variables the experiment moves are the two concentrations.

options.text: Whether it crosses depends on which side of its head detects the copper first, since the worm turns away from whichever side is affected.
options.why: Left-against-right comparison is a mechanism the chapter is careful the worm does not use.

items.stem: What is a truth table?

options.text: A listing of every combination of the conditions with, beside each combination, what the outcome should be.
options.why: Correct. It beats a sentence describing the relationship because it says what happens in every case, including the cases nobody thought to mention.

options.text: A listing of the conditions an animal can detect, ranked by how reliably each predicts what the animal should do next.
options.why: Nothing in a truth table is ranked, and reliability is not among the things it records.

options.text: A listing of the steps a circuit goes through as it turns a set of inputs into a single action.
options.why: Steps would be a mechanism, and a truth table is deliberately silent about how anything is computed.

options.text: A listing of which cues an animal treats as good and which as bad, with the strength of each verdict beside it.
options.why: Assigning valence is the first demand rather than what a truth table records, and no strengths appear in one.

items.stem: Which term names a piece of a nervous system that computes AND, OR or NOT?

options.text: logic gate
options.why: Correct. Those three relations are primitive operators in symbolic logic, and long before that they arrived as demands on behavior.

options.text: truth table
options.why: A truth table is the written specification of what such a piece has to do rather than the piece itself.

options.text: target function
options.why: A target function is the mapping from conditions to action, which is again the specification rather than the machinery.

options.text: circuit motif
options.why: A circuit motif is a recurring wiring pattern introduced later, and not every motif computes a logical relation.

items.stem: What is a target function?

options.text: The mapping from conditions to action — what a piece of a nervous system must do, stated without any claim about how it does it.
options.why: Correct. That what-versus-how separation is the firewall for the whole computational level.

options.text: The action a circuit produces most often, which is the behavior any account of that circuit will have to explain before it explains anything else.
options.why: Frequency of a behavior is not what the term picks out, and a target function covers every combination rather than the common one.

options.text: The arrangement of weights and thresholds that produces the behavior a truth table specifies.
options.why: Weights and thresholds are the mechanism built in the next section, which a target function deliberately says nothing about.

options.text: The goal an animal is pursuing, expressed as the state of the world it is trying to bring about by acting.
options.why: Goals in that sense are not what the term names; it is a mapping from conditions to action rather than a desired outcome.

items.stem: A student says a truth table explains how a circuit works. What is wrong with that?

options.text: A truth table states what a piece of a nervous system does and says nothing whatever about how, which is what makes it a specification rather than an explanation.
options.why: Correct. Naming the target before knowing the mechanism is ordinary business at the computational level, and the previous module did the same.

options.text: A truth table only covers the combinations that actually occur, so it cannot explain what a circuit would do in any case that has not actually arisen for the animal.
options.why: A truth table covers every combination, including the ones nobody thought to mention, which is precisely its advantage.

options.text: A truth table describes behavior rather than computation, so it belongs to ethology rather than to any of Marr's three levels.
options.why: It belongs squarely to the computational level, which is one of the three, and it describes a computation rather than behavior.

options.text: A truth table works only for two cues at a time, so it cannot explain a circuit that has to combine more than two.
options.why: No limit of two is stated, and the objection would be about scope rather than about what kind of thing a truth table is.

items.stem: The chapter gives three relational demands as things an animal might need to do. Which pairing is right?

options.text: Feed only when there is food odor AND the water is not too warm; flee when there is a shadow OR a vibration; advance when there is food odor AND NOT the scent of a predator.
options.why: Correct. Either the shadow or the vibration is sufficient on its own, which is what makes the middle case an OR.

options.text: Feed when there is food odor OR the water is not too warm; flee only when there is a shadow AND a vibration; advance when there is food odor AND NOT the scent of a predator.
options.why: Requiring both a shadow and a vibration before fleeing would leave an animal standing still through half the threats it meets.

options.text: Feed only when there is food odor AND NOT warm water; flee when there is a shadow AND a vibration; advance whenever there is food odor OR no predator scent.
options.why: Advancing on either condition alone would send the animal forward when a predator's scent was the only thing in the air.

options.text: Feed when there is food odor AND warm water; flee when there is a shadow AND NOT a vibration; advance only when there is food odor AND a predator scent.
options.why: Advancing only when a predator is detected inverts the demand, and warm water is the condition the feeding case rules out.

items.stem: Two cues arrive nearly equal. What does sharpening do about it, and why is it worth doing?

options.text: It takes a shallow gap in the input and produces a steep one in the output, so the marginally better direction becomes plainly the better one.
options.why: Correct. An animal that exaggerates a difference that way can act more decisively, and sooner, than one that does not.

options.text: It waits until one of the two cues grows stronger, so that the decision is made on evidence rather than on an exaggeration.
options.why: Waiting is exactly what the demand exists to avoid, since a near-tie can persist for as long as the animal can afford to stand still.

options.text: It discards the weaker of the two cues entirely, so that only one signal reaches the muscles and no conflict remains.
options.why: Discarding is closer to what committing does with alternatives, and sharpening works on the size of the difference itself.

options.text: It reports the difference faithfully but amplifies both signals, so that the muscles receive an instruction that is at least strong enough to be acted on decisively.
options.why: Amplifying both together would leave the gap between them as shallow as it was.

items.stem: The chapter says committing follows from a fact about bodies rather than a fact about information. What is that fact?

options.text: A worm has one body and the body can go in one direction, so however many cues were weighed, the result has to be a single action.
options.why: Correct. The argument is anatomical, which is why it would still hold for an animal with unlimited capacity to process what it senses.

options.text: A body can only act as fast as its slowest muscle, so a decision has to be reached and settled before the muscles are ever asked to move at all.
options.why: Timing is not the constraint; the constraint is that there is one body to send in one direction.

options.text: A nervous system has limited capacity, so it cannot hold two candidate actions ready at the same time.
options.why: Justifying commitment by limited capacity is precisely the informational argument the chapter does not use.

options.text: A body's sensors report continuously, so a decision left open would be revised before it could ever be acted on.
options.why: Continuous revision is not raised, and the reason given is about how many directions a body can travel in.

items.stem: What is wrong with a nervous system that averages its options?

options.text: It walks between two doors into the wall: half a turn left with half a turn right carries the animal somewhere neither cue recommended.
options.why: Correct. The result of combining has to be exactly one action rather than a blend of two.

options.text: It reaches a decision more slowly than one that commits, since averaging requires every one of the options to be weighed to the very same precision first.
options.why: Speed is what sharpening buys; the objection to averaging is that its output is an action nothing recommended.

options.text: It produces an action that is right on average but wrong on any particular occasion, which is worse than being consistently wrong.
options.why: Being right on average is too generous a description of walking into a wall, and the chapter's objection is sharper.

options.text: It cannot represent a case in which two cues genuinely deserve equal weight, so it fails exactly when the decision matters most.
options.why: Equal weight is the situation to be resolved rather than something the system fails to represent.

items.stem: The chapter warns that some arrangements in the next section look strange on first meeting. Which, and why are they there?

options.text: Neurons whose main job is to quiet other neurons — machinery of exactly the kind a body needs when it must make a choice and suppress the alternatives.
options.why: Correct. Spending cells on shutting cells up looks wasteful until commitment is understood as a demand.

options.text: Neurons that fire steadily whether or not anything is detected — machinery a body needs in order to have a steady baseline to vary upward and downward around.
options.why: A resting baseline is discussed later as part of how a unit computes, and it is not what this warning points at.

options.text: Neurons that connect to themselves — machinery a body needs in order to keep a state going after its cause has gone.
options.why: Self-connection does appear later and serves persistence, but the warning here is specifically about suppression.

options.text: Neurons that respond to several kinds of cue at once — machinery a body needs in order to combine what it senses.
options.why: Convergence of several inputs onto one cell is not strange on first meeting, and it is not what the warning names.

items.stem: What assumption do the first three demands make, and why does the chapter say it will not hold?

options.text: They treat an animal's verdicts as fixed, and few verdicts are: valence depends on the animal's own condition as well as on the world.
options.why: Correct. A worm that has just eaten gains little by crossing a strip of copper, and an odor worth a burn an hour ago is not worth one now.

options.text: They treat an animal's senses as accurate, and few are: what reaches the nervous system is always a noisy version of whatever is actually out there.
options.why: Noise is not the complication introduced here, and the chapter's fourth demand concerns the animal's condition instead.

options.text: They treat cues as arriving one at a time, and few do: several arrive together and have to be weighed against one another.
options.why: That is the second demand rather than an assumption the first three make, and combining is already among them.

options.text: They treat every animal as facing the same problem, and few do: what counts as a good direction depends on the species.
options.why: Species differences are raised when valence is introduced rather than as the assumption modulation corrects.

items.stem: What is an internal state, and what does the fourth demand ask of it?

options.text: The animal's own condition — hunger, injury, fatigue, whatever it was doing a moment ago — and the demand is that it reach into the evaluation and change the verdict.
options.why: Correct. It is the condition of the animal rather than anything about the world the animal is sensing.

options.text: The animal's current position in the world, which the fourth demand asks be taken into account when a direction is chosen.
options.why: Position is information about the world rather than a condition of the animal, and it is not what the term names.

options.text: The pattern of activity in the animal's circuits at a given instant, which the fourth demand asks be held steady for as long as a decision is being made.
options.why: Holding activity steady is close to committing, and an internal state is a condition rather than a snapshot to be protected.

options.text: The set of verdicts the animal has already assigned, which the fourth demand asks be revised whenever new evidence arrives.
options.why: Revision in the light of evidence is not the demand; the demand is that the animal's own condition change the verdict.

items.stem: What does the carbon-dioxide case show about C. elegans?

options.text: A cue the worm normally avoids is avoided far less after some hours without food, and under some conditions the worm is drawn toward it instead.
options.why: Correct. Same animal, same molecule, opposite behavior — and carbon dioxide can mark decaying material that other worthwhile things gather around.

options.text: A cue the worm normally approaches becomes aversive once it has eaten, which shows that an animal with a full gut has fewer reasons to move anywhere at all.
options.why: The direction of the effect runs the other way: the cue is normally avoided, and hunger weakens the avoidance.

options.text: A cue the worm cannot normally detect becomes detectable when it is hungry, which shows that internal state changes what is sensed.
options.why: Detection is not what changes; the chapter's point is that the verdict changes while the sensing stays the same.

options.text: A cue the worm avoids is avoided more strongly when it is hungry, which shows that a hungry animal is more cautious about risk.
options.why: Increased caution would be the opposite result, and it would leave the hungry worm less able to find food.

items.stem: The demand to modulate hides a second, subtler requirement. What is it, and what problem does it solve?

options.text: That a state outlast the event which caused it, because sensory evidence is fleeting and an animal tracking only this instant would stop fleeing the moment the smell thinned.
options.why: Correct. It would also stop searching the moment the last morsel was gone, which is why persistence is worth having.

options.text: That a state be revisable, because an animal locked into a state would go on fleeing long after the danger had actually passed.
options.why: Revisability is a real concern, and it is not what the chapter identifies as hidden inside the demand to modulate.

options.text: That a state be shared across the animal, because a verdict held in one part of a nervous system is of no use at all to muscles somewhere else in the body.
options.why: Distribution of a signal is the previous module's problem and is not what this requirement is about.

options.text: That a state be graded, because an animal that was either hungry or not could not weigh food against a barrier.
options.why: Grading matters to combining, and the subtler requirement identified here is about persistence over time.

items.stem: What is affect, in the chapter's sense?

options.text: An internal state that outlasts its cause and biases what an animal does over a stretch of time rather than at a single instant.
options.why: Correct. The definition is deliberately mechanical and says nothing about feeling, so that a worm can have one.

options.text: A conscious feeling that accompanies an animal's verdict about something it has just sensed somewhere in its surroundings.
options.why: Equating affect with conscious feeling goes well past what the chapter claims, and it would exclude the worm.

options.text: The strength of an animal's response to a cue, which determines how vigorously it approaches or avoids.
options.why: Vigor is closer to arousal, which is one of the two quantities used to describe affect rather than affect itself.

options.text: The verdict an animal assigns to a cue, marking it as worth approaching or worth moving away from.
options.why: That verdict is valence, which is one coordinate of an affective state rather than the state as a whole.

items.stem: What is arousal?

options.text: How activated an animal is — how vigorously and how readily it will react to anything at all.
options.why: Correct. It is deliberately not about any particular cue, which is what makes it independent of valence.

options.text: How strongly an animal prefers one direction over another once it has weighed the cues available.
options.why: Preference between directions is the outcome of combining and sharpening rather than a measure of activation.

options.text: How quickly an animal's internal state returns to normal after the event that changed it has passed.
options.why: The rate at which a state decays is not what the term measures, though persistence is discussed alongside it.

options.text: How good or bad an animal currently judges its situation to be, on a scale running from one to the other.
options.why: Good or bad is valence, which is the other axis of the two-dimensional space.

items.stem: Which pairing separates valence from arousal most cleanly, on the chapter's own examples?

options.text: Panic and excitement, which sit at much the same arousal and differ in nothing but whether things are going well.
options.why: Correct. Because the two are identical in arousal and opposite in valence, the pair also shows that high arousal is not in itself a bad sign.

options.text: Panic and gloom, which share a negative valence and differ in arousal rather than in how things are going.
options.why: That pair holds valence constant and varies arousal, which separates the axes in the other direction.

options.text: Contentment and boredom, which sit at much the same arousal and differ in valence about how things are going.
options.why: That pair does separate the axes, and the chapter draws the sharpest version of the contrast from panic and excitement.

options.text: Gloom and boredom, which sit at much the same arousal and differ only in how negative the situation is being judged to be.
options.why: Both are low-arousal states, and the chapter does not use them as its cleanest separation of the two quantities.

items.stem: A student writes that valence and arousal are a complete account of affect. Where does that overstate the chapter?

options.text: The chapter says two quantities describe a surprising amount of affect, which is a claim about how much they capture rather than about capturing all of it.
options.why: Correct. An affective state is a position in the space those two define, and the chapter does not claim the space has only two dimensions' worth of content.

options.text: The chapter says the two quantities apply to human affect but not to a worm's, so a complete account would need a third for invertebrates.
options.why: The definition is deliberately species-neutral, and the chapter's whole point is that a worm can have a version of it.

options.text: The chapter says the two quantities describe affect only while a state persists, so a complete account of it would need some third quantity for the briefer states.
options.why: Persistence is built into the definition of affect rather than being a limitation on the two quantities.

options.text: The chapter says arousal is measurable and valence is not, so a complete account would need a way of observing the second.
options.why: No asymmetry of measurability is claimed between the two.

items.stem: Define affect as the chapter does, name the two quantities used to describe it, and use one of the chapter's pairs to show that the two are independent.
items.answer: Affect is an internal state that outlasts its cause and biases what an animal does over a stretch of time rather than at a single instant. The two quantities are valence — whether things are currently good or bad — and arousal, meaning how activated the animal is, how vigorously and readily it will react to anything at all. Together they define a two-dimensional space, and an affective state is a position in it. Panic and excitement show the independence most clearly: they sit at much the same arousal and differ in nothing but whether things are going well. Panic and gloom make the point the other way round, sharing a negative valence and differing in arousal.
rubric: Defines affect as a state that outlasts its cause and biases behavior over a stretch of time.
Names valence and arousal, with a correct gloss of each.
States that the two define a space in which an affective state is a position.
Uses one of the chapter's pairs correctly to show the two quantities vary independently.

items.stem: The chapter flags one connection between persistent states and the previous module's discussion of energy. What is it?

options.text: A persistent state is partly an accounting decision: reacting hard is metabolically expensive, so staying keyed up spends energy and ceasing to respond conserves it.
options.why: Correct. The chemistry that holds a state like that is taken up in the chapter's third section.

options.text: A persistent state is cheaper than re-evaluating a cue each time it arrives, which is why animals hold on to states rather than recomputing their verdicts from scratch each time.
options.why: No comparison between holding a state and recomputing is drawn, and the accounting runs on the cost of reacting.

options.text: A persistent state costs nothing to maintain once entered, which is why it can outlast the event that caused it so easily.
options.why: Staying keyed up is described as spending energy rather than as free.

options.text: A persistent state is limited by how much energy an animal has stored, which is why hungry animals hold fewer of them.
options.why: Hunger changes verdicts in the chapter's example rather than limiting how many states an animal can hold.

items.stem: How does a robot vacuum steer, and where does it assign valence?

options.text: It has a front with a bumper and sensors, and turns on what that end detects; a wall is bad and the dock good, and neither fact is in the wall or the dock.
options.why: Correct. Both facts are in how the machine is wired to respond to them, which is the chapter's claim about value arriving in a different substrate.

options.text: Its round body lets it turn on the spot, so it has no front at all and assigns valence by how hard an obstacle resists it.
options.why: The body is round and the machine nonetheless has a front, which is the observation the passage turns on.

options.text: It follows a route planned from a stored map, and it assigns valence to the locations recorded on that map rather than to anything it senses as it goes.
options.why: Planning from a stored map is the older robotics tradition the passage says was abandoned.

options.text: It steers toward whatever its sensors report most strongly, so valence is simply the strength of the strongest signal available.
options.why: Signal strength carries no verdict, which is the same point the chapter makes about a rate being only a rate.

items.stem: Which two facts about a robot vacuum show modulation and persistence?

options.text: The dock is good only when the battery is low, and a machine that has found a dirty patch keeps working it for a while after the sensor stops reporting dirt.
options.why: Correct. The first is the machine's own state changing a verdict, and the second is a state outlasting its cause.

options.text: The machine slows down on carpet and speeds up on a hard floor, and it returns to its dock at the same time every day whatever it has found on the floor.
options.why: Neither of those changes a verdict, and a fixed schedule is not a state outlasting anything.

options.text: The machine avoids a drop-off however dirty the floor is, and it cleans the same room in the same pattern each time.
options.why: An unconditional avoidance is the opposite of a modulated verdict, and a repeated pattern is not persistence in this sense.

options.text: The machine maps the room as it goes, and it uses that map to decide where it has not yet cleaned.
options.why: Building and consulting a map is the planning approach the passage contrasts with the four demands.

items.stem: Is the robot vacuum's resemblance to a steering animal a case of convergence?

options.text: Not quite: the robotics tradition it comes from turned to animals deliberately, so the resemblance is partly borrowed rather than independently arrived at.
options.why: Correct. The borrowing is itself evidence, since the demands were legible enough in real animals for engineers to read them off and build with them.

options.text: Yes: one problem has produced much the same solution in two histories that shared nothing, which is exactly what convergence means.
options.why: That is the tempting reading, and the chapter blocks it by pointing at where the design came from.

options.text: No: the machine meets the four demands in a completely different way, so there is no resemblance of the kind convergence describes.
options.why: The resemblance is real and is worked through demand by demand; what is in question is how it arose.

options.text: Yes: the engineers arrived at the design independently and only noticed the animal parallel afterward, which is convergence in the usual sense of the word as an earlier module gave it.
options.why: The tradition turned to animals deliberately, after years of building machines that planned from stored maps.

items.stem: What does the robot vacuum establish, on the chapter's own account of it?

options.text: That the four demands belong to the problem rather than to biology: anything that has to get somewhere useful in a world it only partly senses will meet them.
options.why: Correct. The example is fair precisely because the machine is not trying to be an animal.

options.text: That the four demands can be met more efficiently in silicon than in tissue, since a machine of that kind needs no energy budget of its own to worry about.
options.why: No efficiency comparison is drawn, and the machine's power supply is not discussed.

options.text: That the four demands are the only problems a steering system has to solve, since the machine solves nothing else.
options.why: Completeness of the list is not claimed, and the vacuum does other things besides steering.

options.text: That the four demands were discovered by engineers before biologists described them in animals.
options.why: The borrowing ran the other way: engineers read the demands off real animals.

items.stem: The chapter closes its first section by saying what all four demands have in common. What is it?

options.text: Every one is a statement about what has to be computed, and none of them says what has to be represented, or by what procedure.
options.why: Correct. That is the level boundary, and it is why the next section starts over with arrangements rather than continuing the list.

options.text: Every one is a statement about what an animal must be able to sense, and none of them says what the animal must then do about whatever it has sensed.
options.why: Acting is built into several of the demands, notably committing to exactly one action.

options.text: Every one is a demand that only an animal with a front can meet, and none applies to a radially symmetric body.
options.why: A machine with no biology at all meets all four, so the demands are not tied to any body plan.

options.text: Every one is a demand the worm has been shown to meet, and none has been demonstrated in any other animal.
options.why: The demands are stated generally, and the chapter's last example is a machine rather than an animal.

items.stem: Introducing AND, OR and AND NOT, the lecture says it wants to reverse the usual order of credit. What does it mean?

options.text: These are primitive operators in symbolic logic and the basis of computers, but long before any of that they arrived as demands on behavior.
options.why: Correct. Reversing the credit puts the behavioral demand first and the formal apparatus second, which is the order the chapter's argument runs in.

options.text: These are demands on behavior that engineers later formalized, so the logic running in a computer should properly be called biological in origin.
options.why: The lecture reverses the order of credit rather than reassigning the invention, and it makes no claim about what computers should be called.

options.text: These are relations animals compute without representing, so crediting them to logic misdescribes what a nervous system does.
options.why: Whether the relation is represented is not what the remark is about, and the lecture calls a piece of nervous system a logic gate quite happily.

options.text: These are operators that appear in every nervous system, so crediting them to any one lineage would be a mistake.
options.why: Universality across nervous systems is not claimed, and the demands are given as things an animal might need to do.

items.stem: The lecture says sharpening and committing are justified in different kinds of way. How do the two justifications differ?

options.text: Sharpening is justified by what a near-tie is worth as an instruction; committing does not follow from anything about information, but from a fact about bodies.
options.why: Correct. A worm has one body and the body can go in one direction, which would hold however much the animal could compute.

options.text: Sharpening is justified by speed and committing by accuracy, so the two pull against each other and have to be balanced.
options.why: No trade-off between the two is described, and both serve the same decision.

options.text: Sharpening is justified by evidence from real animals and committing by an argument from first principles about what any nervous system must be able to do.
options.why: No evidence is offered for one and withheld from the other; the difference is in the kind of reason given.

options.text: Sharpening is justified at the computational level and committing at the implementational one, which is why the machinery arrives later.
options.why: Both demands are stated at the computational level, and the machinery for both arrives in the next section.

items.stem: The lecture draws attention to how its definition of affect is written. What does it point out?

options.text: How mechanical the definition is, and how little it says about feeling — it is meant to be something a worm can have.
options.why: Correct. Affect is defined as a state that outlasts its cause and biases behavior over a stretch of time, with no mention of experience.

options.text: How closely it follows the everyday use of the word, which is what makes it easy to apply to human beings and to animals alike.
options.why: The lecture stresses the distance from the everyday sense rather than the closeness to it.

options.text: How much it owes to the previous module's account of energy, since a state that persists is a state being paid for.
options.why: The energy connection is made at the end of the slide rather than being a feature of the definition.

options.text: How provisional it is, since a better definition will be available once the chemistry has been described.
options.why: Nothing is described as provisional, and the third lecture supplies the implementation rather than a new definition.

items.stem: Run the four demands against a robot vacuum, one at a time, and say what the exercise is meant to establish.
items.answer: It steers: the body is round but the machine has a front, with a bumper, a direction of travel and its sensors clustered at that end, and what the leading end detects settles which way it turns. It evaluates: a wall is bad and the dock is good, and neither fact is in the wall or the dock but in how the machine is wired to respond to them. It combines: dirt detected underneath is a reason to stay the course and a detected drop-off is a reason to turn away, and the two have to be settled against each other rather than obeyed in turn. And its own state modulates the verdict, with some states outlasting their causes: the dock is good only when the battery is low, and a machine that has found a dirty patch keeps working it after the sensor has stopped reporting dirt. What the exercise establishes is that the four demands belong to the problem rather than to biology.
rubric: Identifies the front, and steering as forward motion with the leading end deciding the turn.
States that the machine assigns valence, and that the verdict is in the wiring rather than in the wall or dock.
Gives the combining case with two cues that have to be settled against each other.
Gives both the modulation case and a state outlasting its cause.
Concludes that the demands belong to the problem rather than to biology.

items.stem: The lecture calls the convergence qualification an honest one, and gives a reason for making it at all. What is the reason?

options.text: The example looks like a textbook case of something it is not, and the lecture would rather say so than let the example do more work than it can.
options.why: Correct. The resemblance is partly borrowed, because the robotics tradition turned to animals deliberately rather than arriving independently.

options.text: The qualification matters for the exam, since convergence is a term from an earlier module that students are expected to be able to apply correctly.
options.why: Nothing about assessment is offered as the reason, and the concern stated is about what the example can support.

options.text: The robotics tradition disputes the animal parallel, so the lecture is reporting a disagreement rather than reaching a verdict.
options.why: No disagreement among engineers is described; the tradition is said to have turned to animals quite deliberately.

options.text: The machine meets only three of the four demands, so calling the resemblance convergence would overstate how complete it is.
options.why: All four demands are run against the machine and all four are met, which is what makes the example work.

items.stem: The lecture calls one feature of a truth table the firewall for the whole first lecture. What is it?

options.text: A truth table says what has to be done and says nothing whatever about how it is done.
options.why: Correct. Naming the target before knowing the mechanism is ordinary business at the computational level, and the previous module did the same.

options.text: A truth table covers every combination of the conditions, including the ones nobody thought to mention in advance.
options.why: That is what makes a truth table better than a sentence, rather than what keeps the levels apart.

options.text: A truth table is written before the animal is observed, so it cannot be adjusted to fit whatever behavior turns up.
options.why: No claim about the order of writing and observing is made anywhere on the slide.

options.text: A truth table treats each cue as present or absent, so it cannot smuggle in the graded strengths that belong to the other face of combining.
options.why: Keeping the two faces apart is a separate point, and the firewall named is about what versus how.

items.stem: Why does combining arise as a demand at all?

options.text: In a laboratory a stimulus can be presented on its own, but out in the world several arrive at once and often imply different things.
options.why: Correct. So many signals have to become one direction of travel.

options.text: In the world a stimulus is always weaker than in a laboratory, so several have to be added together before any of them is usable.
options.why: Weakness is not the problem; the problem is that the cues disagree.

options.text: In the world a stimulus changes over time, so an animal has to combine what it senses now with what it sensed before.
options.why: Comparison across time is how one animal steers later, rather than why combining is a demand.

options.text: In the world an animal has several sensory systems, so their outputs must be converted into a common form before use.
options.why: Conversion to a common form is not the difficulty named; disagreement between cues is.

items.stem: What do sharpening and committing concern, and what does sharpening buy an animal?

options.text: The quality of a decision; an animal that exaggerates a difference can act more decisively, and sooner, than one that does not.
options.why: Correct. Both halves are about how good the decision is rather than about what it is made from.

options.text: The accuracy of a measurement; an animal that exaggerates a difference reports the world more faithfully than one that does not.
options.why: Exaggeration is a departure from faithful reporting, which is exactly the trade being made.

options.text: The speed of a response; an animal that exaggerates a difference conserves energy compared with one that does not.
options.why: Energy is not what the demand is argued from, and speed is one benefit rather than the concern itself.

options.text: The range of an animal's repertoire; an animal that exaggerates a difference has more actions available than one that does not.
options.why: The number of available actions does not change; what changes is how clearly one of them wins.

items.stem: How does this chapter take the natural–artificial comparison further than the previous module did?

options.text: The previous module set one artificial neuron beside one real one; here the comparison is taken up a level, to a whole agent with a job to do.
options.why: Correct. A robot vacuum is the case, precisely because it is not trying to be an animal.

options.text: The previous module compared two whole artificial systems; here the comparison is narrowed to the single unit the two of them share.
options.why: The direction runs the other way, from a cell up to an agent.

options.text: The previous module found the two alike at every level; here the comparison is tested and found to fail.
options.why: The earlier comparison was close at the algorithmic level and nonexistent at the implementational one.

options.text: The previous module compared behavior; here the comparison is made between the materials the two are built from.
options.why: Materials were the earlier comparison's finding, and the new one is about an agent's whole problem.

pools.title: From a Unit to a Wiring Diagram
pools.covers: reading §4.2.1, §4.2.2, §4.2.3 · lecture 4.2 slides from_a_unit_to_a_diagram, convergence_and_divergence, the_floor_and_the_ceiling

items.stem: What does the algorithmic question ask?

options.text: What information a system represents, and what procedure it runs on those representations.
options.why: Correct. The first section said what had to be computed; this is where what is represented and by what procedure finally get answered.

options.text: What physical parts a system is built from, and what each of those parts contributes to the whole.
options.why: Physical parts belong to the implementational question, which the chapter's third section asks.

options.text: What problem a system is solving, and why solving that problem was worth what it cost.
options.why: That is the computational question, which the first section asked and answered.

options.text: What behavior a system produces, and how reliably it produces that behavior under natural conditions.
options.why: Observed behavior is evidence about a system rather than one of the three questions in the framework.

items.stem: What fact established in the previous module makes it possible to draw a nervous system as a diagram?

options.text: Connection is a matter of wiring rather than of being near each other, so what is joined to what is a fact independent of where the cells sit.
options.why: Correct. Two cells pressed against one another may have nothing to do with each other, while an axon may reach across a whole animal.

options.text: Neurons are arranged in regular layers, so a drawing can represent each layer as a row and every connection between them as a line.
options.why: No layered anatomy is claimed, and the point holds for a nerve net as much as for anything orderly.

options.text: Every neuron computes the same function, so one symbol can stand for any cell without losing anything that matters.
options.why: Units do share a form of computation, and what licenses the diagram is the wiring rather than the sameness.

options.text: Signals travel fast enough that the distances in a nervous system can be ignored when reasoning about what it computes.
options.why: Speed is what the previous module bought with the neuron, and it is not what makes the diagram legitimate.

items.stem: What is a neural circuit?

options.text: A set of neurons connected in a specific pattern, doing something together that no one of them does alone.
options.why: Correct. The last clause is the load-bearing one, since it is what makes the circuit worth naming as a unit of analysis.

options.text: A set of neurons that are physically adjacent to one another and therefore influence what their neighbors do.
options.why: Adjacency is exactly what the previous module ruled out as the basis of connection; that arrangement is a puddle.

options.text: A set of neurons that all respond to the same cue, so that their outputs can be averaged into one reliable signal.
options.why: Shared sensitivity is not what defines a circuit, and averaging is what committing exists to avoid.

options.text: A path along which a signal travels from a sensor to a muscle without being changed on the way.
options.why: An unchanged signal would make the intervening cells relays, and a circuit is defined by doing something together.

items.stem: What is a circuit motif?

options.text: A wiring pattern that turns up again and again, in different animals and in different parts of the same brain, because it computes something generally useful.
options.why: Correct. Motifs stand to circuits roughly as letters stand to words, and there are not many of them.

options.text: A wiring pattern that is found in one animal and used as a model for what might be happening in others.
options.why: Recurrence across animals is part of what makes a pattern a motif rather than a single case to generalize from.

options.text: A wiring pattern that an animal is born with rather than one that develops through its experience of the world.
options.why: How a pattern comes to be there is not what the term picks out, and development is not discussed here.

options.text: A wiring pattern that produces much the same behavior whatever inputs happen to reach it, which is what makes it recognizable wherever it turns up.
options.why: A pattern indifferent to its inputs would compute nothing, and motifs are named for computing something useful.

items.stem: Which term names a recurring wiring pattern that stands to a circuit roughly as a letter stands to a word?

options.text: circuit motif
options.why: Correct. There are not many of them, and almost everything in this section of the chapter is built from five.

options.text: neural circuit
options.why: A circuit is the larger thing built out of motifs, which is the word side of the same analogy.

options.text: connectome
options.why: A connectome is a complete map of one animal's connections rather than a pattern that recurs across animals.

options.text: activation function
options.why: An activation function is the step a single unit applies to its own total, and it is not a wiring pattern at all.

items.stem: What does the chapter say its answers to the four demands add up to?

options.text: That a small number of wiring patterns do nearly all of the work, and almost everything in the section is built from five motifs.
options.why: Correct. Presenting the whole vocabulary at once is deliberate, so each motif arrives as a member of a set.

options.text: That each demand requires its own dedicated arrangement, so the number of patterns grows with the number of demands.
options.why: The chapter's claim runs the other way, since several demands are met by re-using the same few patterns.

options.text: That the arrangements meeting the four demands are found only in animals that steer, which is what makes steering the module's spine.
options.why: One of the chapter's own examples is a machine, and the motifs are not restricted to steering animals.

options.text: That the four demands cannot be met separately, so a single arrangement has to satisfy all of them at once.
options.why: The section takes the demands in order and meets them with different motifs, so they are not met all at once.

items.stem: What is convergence, as a circuit motif?

options.text: Many cells projecting onto one cell.
options.why: Correct. It is what makes the second demand, combination, possible, because a cell can only weigh what actually arrives at it.

options.text: One cell projecting onto many cells.
options.why: That is divergence, which serves coordination rather than combination.

options.text: Two cells each projecting onto the other, so that activity in one raises activity in the other.
options.why: Mutual connection of that kind is a different motif, and the chapter uses it to force a choice rather than to combine.

options.text: A cell projecting back onto itself, so that activity continues after the input has stopped.
options.why: Self-connection is a feedback loop, which serves persistence rather than combination.

items.stem: Why is convergence what makes combining possible?

options.text: A cell can only weigh and combine information that actually arrives at that cell, so something has to bring the cues together first.
options.why: Correct. The previous module described a neuron summing whatever reached it; convergence is the question of what should be arranged to reach it.

options.text: A cell can combine only two inputs at a time, so cues have to be brought together in stages before a verdict is possible.
options.why: No limit of two is stated anywhere, and convergence is described as many cells onto one.

options.text: A cell weighs its inputs more heavily when more of them arrive at once, so convergence is what gives a combined signal its strength.
options.why: Weight is a property of a connection rather than something that grows with how many inputs arrive.

options.text: A cell can only combine cues of the same kind, so convergence is what converts different sorts of signal into a common form.
options.why: Conversion to a common form is not attributed to the motif, and units receive rates whatever the cue was.

items.stem: What is divergence, and what does it make possible?

options.text: One cell projecting onto many, which is how a single verdict reaches muscle all over the body at once.
options.why: Correct. It is what makes an action a whole-body commitment rather than a local twitch.

options.text: Many cells projecting onto one, which is how several cues can be weighed against each other in one place.
options.why: That is convergence, and it serves combination rather than coordination.

options.text: One cell projecting onto many, which is how a verdict can be checked against several independent copies of itself.
options.why: Redundancy and error-checking are not what the motif is credited with here.

options.text: One cell projecting onto many, which is how an animal can pursue several actions at once when the cues do not conflict.
options.why: Pursuing several actions at once is precisely what committing rules out.

items.stem: How does the worm's reversal illustrate divergence?

options.text: A worm that reverses does not reverse in one segment; it coordinates its whole body to do so at the same time.
options.why: Correct. Divergence is how one decision gets everywhere in the body that it needs to be.

options.text: A worm that reverses does so a segment at a time, with each segment triggering the next along the length of the body.
options.why: A traveling sequence is what a diverging verdict avoids, and the coordination described is simultaneous.

options.text: A worm that reverses weighs food odor against the barrier before it moves, which requires many cues in one place.
options.why: Weighing cues in one place is convergence, and the reversal is used to illustrate the other motif.

options.text: A worm that reverses does so only when several sensory cells agree, so the verdict is distributed across them.
options.why: Agreement among sensors is a combining problem rather than an illustration of one verdict reaching many muscles.

items.stem: What two things does a bare weighted sum say that no real cell can do?

options.text: It can go negative when the inhibitory input is strong enough, and it has no maximum at all, where a real neuron has some maximum firing rate.
options.why: Correct. Those are two physical facts about cells rather than inconveniences of the modeling.

options.text: It can change instantaneously, and it can take any value between zero and the maximum, where a real neuron fires in discrete events separated by gaps.
options.why: Discreteness is handled by the previous module's account of the spike, and the two problems named here are the floor and the ceiling.

options.text: It can weigh an unlimited number of inputs, and it can give any of them an arbitrarily large weight.
options.why: Neither the number of inputs nor the size of a weight is raised as a problem here.

options.text: It can produce an output before its inputs have arrived, and it can hold that output indefinitely afterward.
options.why: Timing and persistence are not what the linear equation gets wrong at this point in the argument.

items.stem: What is an activation function?

options.text: A function that takes the total and squashes it into the range the cell can actually produce.
options.why: Correct. It is added as one step at the end, and nothing else about the unit changes.

options.text: A function that decides which of the unit's inputs are worth including in the total before the sum is taken.
options.why: Selecting inputs is not what the step does; every input still arrives and is still weighted.

options.text: A function that converts a firing rate into the sequence of individual spikes a real cell would produce.
options.why: Turning a rate into spikes belongs to the implementational level, and the unit here stays in rates throughout.

options.text: A function that sets how strongly each connection into the unit contributes to the weighted sum.
options.why: That is what a weight does, and weights are unchanged by the addition of this step.

items.stem: Which term names the step that gives a unit's output a floor and a ceiling?

options.text: activation function
options.why: Correct. Both of the two common ones have a floor and a ceiling, which is what solves the problems the linear equation introduced.

options.text: target function
options.why: A target function is the mapping a circuit is supposed to compute, stated without any mechanism at all.

options.text: threshold function, the hard-boundary one
options.why: A threshold function is one particular activation function rather than the general name for the step.

options.text: decision boundary
options.why: A decision boundary is the line a unit's parameters draw through the space of possible inputs.

items.stem: How do a threshold function and a sigmoid function differ?

options.text: The threshold has a hard boundary with nothing between silence and firing; the sigmoid is S-shaped, threshold-like at the extremes and graded in the middle.
options.why: Correct. Both buy the same two things, a floor and a ceiling, and what they cost differs.

options.text: The threshold has a floor and no ceiling; the sigmoid has both, which is why only the sigmoid manages to solve the problems the bare linear model introduced.
options.why: Both have a floor and a ceiling, and both therefore solve the problems the linear equation introduced.

options.text: The threshold varies from unit to unit; the sigmoid is the same curve everywhere, which makes it easier to reason about.
options.why: Nothing is said about one varying and the other being fixed across units.

options.text: The threshold operates on the inputs before they are summed; the sigmoid operates on the total after the sum is taken.
options.why: Both are applied to the total at the end, which is what makes them the same kind of step.

items.stem: Which of the two activation functions does the chapter say is better?

options.text: Neither: the smooth curve is closer to what a real neuron does, the hard step is easier to compute logic with, and which is reached for is a claim about what matters for the question.
options.why: Correct. That is the previous module's point about models arriving again — a simplification is a claim about what matters.

options.text: The sigmoid, since being closer to what a real neuron does is what makes a model of a neuron a good one.
options.why: Closeness to the biology is one virtue among others, and the chapter explicitly declines to rank the two on it.

options.text: The threshold, since the whole of the section that follows is built on computing logic with hard boundaries.
options.why: Ease of computing logic is real and it is a reason for a purpose rather than a verdict about which function is better.

options.text: The sigmoid for describing real animals and the threshold for describing artificial systems, since each of the two matches the properties of its own substrate more closely.
options.why: No such division by substrate is drawn, and artificial units use both.

items.stem: What changes about a unit when an activation function is added, and what stays the same?

options.text: Only one step is added at the end: the inputs still arrive as rates, the connections still carry weights with signs, and the weighted sum still happens.
options.why: Correct. The chapter makes a point of the reassurance, because the addition can look like a rebuild of the whole model.

options.text: The weights become positive only, since the step added at the end now supplies the floor that negative weights had been providing up to this point.
options.why: Weights keep their signs, and the floor comes from the new step rather than from any change to them.

options.text: The inputs arrive as individual spikes rather than as rates, since a floor and a ceiling are properties of discrete events.
options.why: Inputs remain rates, and the level of description does not change.

options.text: The sum is taken after the function is applied rather than before, so each input is squashed on its own.
options.why: The function is applied to the total, which is why it is described as one step at the end.

items.stem: Where do a real cell's floor and ceiling come from?

options.text: It cannot fire less often than never, and it cannot fire faster than its refractory period allows.
options.why: Correct. Both were established in the previous module, which is why the debt could be flagged there and paid here.

options.text: It cannot fire without an input arriving, and it cannot fire while its own output is still traveling down the axon.
options.why: A cell with a baseline fires without any input arriving, and nothing about the traveling signal sets the ceiling.

options.text: It cannot respond to an inhibitory input alone, and it cannot exceed the rate of the fastest input reaching it.
options.why: Neither constraint is described, and a unit's output is not bounded by its inputs' rates.

options.text: It cannot fire below its baseline rate, and it cannot fire above the rate its energy budget will pay for.
options.why: The energy budget is the previous module's subject, and the ceiling given here is the refractory period.

items.stem: The previous module left a debt that this chapter's algorithmic account pays. State the debt, and say exactly how it is paid.
items.answer: The debt is that a bare weighted sum says two impossible things. Make the inhibitory input strong enough and the sum goes negative, but no cell can fire a negative number of times per second. And a linear equation has no maximum, while any real neuron has some maximum firing rate. A real cell has a floor and a ceiling that a bare sum does not: it cannot fire less often than never, and it cannot fire faster than its refractory period allows. The debt is paid by passing the total through one more step, an activation function, which squashes it into the range the cell can actually produce. Nothing else changes — the inputs still arrive as rates, the connections still carry weights with signs, and the weighted sum still happens.
rubric: States both impossibilities: a negative rate and an unbounded maximum.
Names the floor and the ceiling as facts about real cells.
Names the activation function and says it squashes the total into the achievable range.
Notes that the addition is one step at the end and nothing else about the unit changes.

items.stem: Two neurons have their cell bodies pressed against each other. What follows about whether they are connected?

options.text: Nothing at all: they may have nothing to do with each other, while another neuron's axon may reach across a whole animal to form a connection.
options.why: Correct. Connection being a matter of wiring rather than proximity is the permission slip for reasoning about diagrams.

options.text: They are weakly connected, since chemical signals released by one will reach the other before they disperse.
