options.why: Signaling to whatever happens to be nearby is the puddle arrangement rather than a circuit.

options.text: They are connected if they respond to the same cue, since cells that fire together are wired together.
options.why: Firing together is a rule about how connections change, which belongs to a later module entirely.

options.text: They are connected, but only in those animals whose nervous systems are spread through the body wall rather than gathered at one end.
options.why: Even in a net the connections are wiring, and the chapter makes no exception of that kind.

items.stem: How does convergence change the question the previous module asked about a neuron?

options.text: That module described a neuron summing whatever reached it; convergence asks what should be arranged to reach it, which is a design question rather than an arithmetic one.
options.why: Correct. The interesting half moves from the summing to what is brought together to be summed.

options.text: That module described a neuron summing whatever reached it; convergence asks the further question of how many inputs a cell can sum before its total becomes unreliable.
options.why: No limit on the number of inputs is raised, and reliability of the sum is not discussed.

options.text: That module treated the weights as fixed; convergence asks the further question of how they come to have the values they have.
options.why: Where the weights come from is deferred to a later module rather than being what convergence asks.

options.text: That module treated each input as independent; convergence asks how inputs that carry the same information should be told apart.
options.why: Redundancy among inputs is not what the motif raises.

items.stem: The lecture shows all five motifs at once and says why it is doing so. What is the reason?

options.text: So that each motif arrives as a member of a set rather than as another thing to remember, once they are taken one at a time.
options.why: Correct. The lecture also invites the room to be skeptical of the claim for forty minutes and check it at the end.

options.text: So that students can see which motifs the lecture will skip, since not all five of them are covered in anything like the same depth.
options.why: All five are taken in turn, and nothing is flagged as being skipped.

options.text: So that the motifs can be compared against the four demands before any of them is explained in detail.
options.why: The mapping onto demands is drawn as each motif arrives rather than in advance.

options.text: So that the vocabulary is available for the reading, which introduces the five in a different order.
options.why: No difference in order between the two sources is mentioned.

items.stem: The lecture says convergence turns something from an arithmetic question into a different kind of question. Which kind, and why does it matter?

options.text: A design question: the previous module made the summing the interesting part, and here the interesting part is what should be arranged to reach the cell.
options.why: Correct. The reason convergence makes combining possible is almost too obvious to state, which is why the lecture stops to state it.

options.text: An anatomical question: what matters is how many cells can physically project onto one, which is a fact about the tissue rather than about the diagram.
options.why: Tissue is the third lecture's subject, and the shift named is about what should be arranged rather than what will fit.

options.text: An evolutionary question: what matters is why the arrangement was selected for, which belongs to the first lecture.
options.why: The lecture is careful to keep the computational and the algorithmic apart, and this shift happens inside the algorithmic level.

options.text: A statistical question: what matters is how many inputs are needed before the total becomes a reliable estimate.
options.why: Reliability and estimation are not raised, and no number of inputs is given.

items.stem: At the end of this stretch the lecture announces a change in its own vocabulary. What is it, and why does it matter?

options.text: It will say unit for the abstract computing element and save neuron for the cell, because the distinction is going to matter.
options.why: Correct. Swapping the two words moves between Marr's levels without saying so, which is what the chapter is strict about.

options.text: It will say circuit rather than arrangement, because the technical term is what will matter once wiring diagrams are in play.
options.why: Both words continue in use, and the announced change concerns the computing element rather than the assembly.

options.text: It will say weight rather than connection strength, because the equation now needs a single word for the quantity.
options.why: Weight was already the word in the previous module, and no change on that point is announced.

options.text: It will say activation function rather than threshold, because the threshold is only one of the two functions available.
options.why: The threshold function keeps its name as one particular activation function.

items.stem: The lecture insists that the two problems with a bare weighted sum are not modeling inconveniences. What does it call them instead?

options.text: Two physical facts about cells: a cell cannot fire less often than never, and it cannot fire faster than its refractory period allows.
options.why: Correct. Calling them facts rather than inconveniences is what makes the activation function a correction rather than a convenience.

options.text: Two consequences of using rates rather than spikes, which would not arise at all in a model built at the implementational level instead.
options.why: The floor and the ceiling are facts about the cell rather than artifacts of describing it in rates.

options.text: Two places where the previous module's model was wrong on purpose, in the way that all models are wrong on purpose.
options.why: Deliberate wrongness is the previous module's point about simplification, and these two are presented as genuine failures to fix.

options.text: Two limits that only matter for units wired into circuits, since a single unit is never driven that hard.
options.why: Both were demonstrated on a single unit in the previous module, with numbers worked through.

items.stem: Define the two simplest circuit motifs, and say which demand each one serves.
items.answer: Convergence is many cells projecting onto one cell. It is what makes combining possible, because a cell can only weigh and combine information that actually arrives at that cell, so something has to bring the cues together before any weighing can happen. Divergence is one cell projecting onto many. It is how a single verdict can reach muscle all over the body at once, which is what makes coordination possible and what lets an action be a whole-body commitment rather than a local twitch. A worm that reverses does not reverse in one segment; it coordinates its whole body at the same time.
rubric: Defines convergence as many cells onto one, and ties it to combining.
Gives the reason: a cell can only weigh what actually arrives at it.
Defines divergence as one cell onto many, and ties it to whole-body commitment.
Uses the worm's reversal, or an equivalent case, to show one verdict reaching the whole body.

items.stem: Compare the threshold function with the sigmoid function, and explain why the chapter refuses to call either one better.
items.answer: A threshold function has a hard boundary: below the threshold the unit is silent, at or above it the unit fires, and there is nothing in between. A sigmoid function is an S-shaped curve that behaves like a threshold at the extremes and grades smoothly in the middle. Both give the unit a floor and a ceiling, which is what solves the problems the bare linear sum introduced. What differs is the cost. The smooth curve is closer to what a real neuron does, and the hard step is easier to compute logic with. Neither is simply better, because a model's simplifications are claims about what matters or what is useful for the question being asked, so which function to reach for depends on that question.
rubric: Describes the threshold function's hard boundary with nothing in between.
Describes the sigmoid as S-shaped, threshold-like at the extremes and graded in the middle.
States that both supply a floor and a ceiling.
Explains the refusal to rank them as a point about simplifications being claims about what matters.

items.stem: In what order does the chapter's algorithmic section supply its answers?

options.text: In the order the four demands were raised at the computational level.
options.why: Correct. Each demand is met in turn by a wiring pattern, which is what keeps the two sections in step.

options.text: In order of increasing complexity, from the simplest motif to the most elaborate arrangement.
options.why: Convergence and divergence do come first as the simplest, and the organizing principle is the order of the demands.

options.text: In the order the motifs were discovered, so that the history of the field is preserved.
options.why: No history of discovery is given anywhere in the section.

options.text: In the order the animals were introduced, so that each arrangement is attached to the animal that uses it.
options.why: The animals belong to the first and third sections rather than to this one.

items.stem: What is a threshold function?

options.text: An activation function with a hard boundary: below the threshold silence, at or above it firing, and nothing in between.
options.why: Correct. It is the easier of the two common activation functions to compute logic with.

options.text: An activation function that grades smoothly in the middle while behaving like a hard boundary at the extremes.
options.why: That describes the sigmoid function, which is the softer of the two.

options.text: The level a unit's weighted total has to reach, which the activation function then compares the total against.
options.why: That level is the threshold itself rather than the function applied to the total.

options.text: A function that sets how strongly each input contributes to a unit's total before the sum is taken.
options.why: Weighting inputs is what a weight does, and it happens before the activation function is applied.

items.stem: What is a sigmoid function?

options.text: An activation function with a softer, S-shaped curve: threshold-like at the extremes, graded in the middle.
options.why: Correct. The name means nothing more than S-shaped, and the function is closer to what a real neuron does.

options.text: An activation function with a hard boundary, so that a unit is either silent or firing at its maximum.
options.why: That is the threshold function, which is the harder-edged of the two.

options.text: An activation function that rises without limit, so that a unit's output is proportional to its total input.
options.why: A function without a ceiling would reintroduce the very problem the activation step was added to fix.

options.text: An activation function whose shape is set by the unit's weights, so that each unit grades differently.
options.why: The curve's shape is a property of the function rather than something the weights determine.

items.stem: Besides keeping a unit's output inside the range a real cell can produce, what else does a bounded activation function do?

options.text: It turns the unit into a logic gate, because a unit that fires only when its weighted inputs pass a threshold answers a yes-or-no question about a combination of conditions.
options.why: Correct. That is exactly the shape of the truth tables written down at the computational level.

options.text: It makes the unit's output proportional to how far past the threshold the total has gone, which is what lets a circuit represent a quantity rather than a yes or a no.
options.why: A bounded function does the opposite at the extremes, flattening the output rather than keeping it proportional.

options.text: It allows the unit to change its own weights in response to how often it has fired, which is how a circuit comes to compute anything useful.
options.why: Weights changing with experience is deferred to a later module and is no part of what the bounded function does.

options.text: It lets the unit hold its output steady after the input has stopped, which is how a circuit keeps a state going.
options.why: Persistence comes from a feedback loop later in the section rather than from the activation function.

items.stem: A unit y has two excitatory inputs x₁ and x₂, each with a weight of 1, and a threshold of 2. What does y compute?

options.text: AND — either input alone contributes 1 and leaves y silent, while both together contribute 2 and make it fire.
options.why: Correct. The truth table written at the computational level is satisfied here by a wiring diagram and two numbers.

options.text: OR — either input alone contributes 1, which is enough to reach a threshold set anywhere at or below 2.
options.why: A threshold of 2 is not reached by a single input contributing 1, so one input alone leaves the unit silent.

options.text: NOT — the threshold of 2 means the unit is silent whenever either input is firing on its own.
options.why: Computing NOT requires an inhibitory input with a negative weight, which this unit does not have.

options.text: Nothing logical at all — with both weights equal the unit has no way to distinguish which of its two inputs is the active one.
options.why: Distinguishing which input is active is not what these functions require; all three depend only on how many are.

items.stem: Starting from that AND unit, what single change makes it compute OR?

options.text: Setting the threshold to 1 instead of 2, which leaves the wiring and the weights exactly as they were.
options.why: Correct. The chapter is heavy-handed about it because it is the whole point: nothing about the wiring changed and one number moved.

options.text: Raising both weights from 1 to 2, so that either one of the inputs on its own now reaches the threshold of 2.
options.why: That would also produce OR, and it is not the change the chapter makes, which varies the threshold alone.

options.text: Adding a standing excitation to y large enough that either input can push it over the threshold.
options.why: Standing excitation is what the NOT construction uses, and adding it here changes more than one thing.

options.text: Reversing the sign of one weight, so that the unit fires when either input is active on its own.
options.why: A negative weight would make one input inhibitory, which produces a quite different function.

items.stem: How is a unit wired so that it computes NOT?

options.text: Give it a standing excitation strong enough to fire it on its own, and one inhibitory input whose negative weight is large enough to cancel that excitation.
options.why: Correct. The unit then fires whenever the input is silent and falls quiet whenever the input is firing.

options.text: Give it one excitatory input and set the threshold above what that input can contribute, so the unit stays silent for as long as the input carries on firing.
options.why: A unit silent whether or not its input fires computes nothing; NOT has to fire when the input is absent.

options.text: Give it two inhibitory inputs and no excitation, so that the unit's output falls whenever either of them is active.
options.why: With no excitation there is nothing for inhibition to cancel, so the unit is silent in every case.

options.text: Give it one excitatory input with a negative threshold, so that the unit fires until the input pushes the total upward.
options.why: A negative threshold would leave the unit firing in every case rather than switching with the input.

items.stem: What does a unit compute when an inhibitory input is wired alongside an excitatory one?

options.text: This and not that — which is one of the demands a steering animal faces, such as advancing when there is food odor and not the scent of a predator.
options.why: Correct. The relational demand stated at the computational level is satisfied by a wiring diagram and two numbers.

options.text: Either this or that — since the excitatory input can fire the unit on its own whenever the inhibitory one is quiet.
options.why: Firing on either input alone is OR, which needs two excitatory inputs rather than one of each.

options.text: Both this and that — since the unit needs the excitatory input present as well as the absence of any inhibition before it will fire.
options.why: Requiring the absence of something is not the same as requiring a second thing present, which is what AND asks.

options.text: Nothing stable — since whether the unit fires depends on which of the two inputs arrives first.
options.why: Order of arrival plays no part in the account; the unit sums whatever is arriving.

items.stem: The chapter is careful to say what the unit y is not doing. What is the point?

options.text: The unit is not choosing anything and does not know what AND means; the logic is in the weights and the threshold and nowhere else.
options.why: Correct. Set them one way and the unit computes one function; set them another way and the same unit computes a different one.

options.text: The unit is not computing reliably, since the very same weights will produce different outputs as the condition of the cell varies.
options.why: Nothing about unreliability is claimed, and the demonstration depends on the unit behaving the same way every time.

options.text: The unit is not representing its inputs, since a rate carries no information about which cue produced it.
options.why: What a rate carries is discussed elsewhere, and the point made here is about where the logic sits.

options.text: The unit is not doing anything a single neuron could not do, since the whole arrangement is one cell with two inputs.
options.why: That a single unit suffices is true and is not the caution being given; the caution is against crediting it with understanding.

items.stem: The chapter says this stretch shows an earlier claim about Marr's levels from close up. Which claim, and how?

options.text: That the levels are separable but not independent: a truth table proposed as a computation an animal needs is the outcome an arrangement of units produces.
options.why: Correct. The same object appears once as a specification and once as a result, which is what non-independence looks like in practice.

options.text: That the levels can be studied in any order, since the algorithmic account given here was reached without any implementational detail at all.
options.why: Independence of order is not what the claim says, and the chapter's own order runs computational to implementational.

options.text: That the levels describe different systems, since a truth table describes a demand and a wiring diagram describes a circuit.
options.why: Treating them as different systems is the opposite of the point; both describe the same thing at two levels.

options.text: That the implementational level constrains the two above it, which is why a real cell's floor and ceiling had to be fixed first.
options.why: That constraint is a different lesson, drawn in the previous module rather than here.

items.stem: How does the chapter turn a two-input circuit into a picture?

options.text: The two inputs go on a pair of axes, so every combination of their values is a point on a plane, with the four corners color-coded by whether y should be firing.
options.why: Correct. Blue marks the combinations where the output should be on and orange where it should be off.

options.text: The two inputs go on one axis and the output on the other, so the circuit's behavior comes out as a curve rather than as a set of separate points.
options.why: Putting the output on an axis would not distinguish the four combinations, which is what the picture is for.

options.text: The weights go on a pair of axes, so that every setting of the circuit is a point and the correct settings form a region.
options.why: The axes carry the inputs rather than the weights, though where the boundary sits is decided by the weights.

options.text: The inputs go on a pair of axes and time runs along a third, so that the order in which cues arrive can be read off.
options.why: Timing plays no part in this picture, which shows what the circuit does for each combination.

items.stem: On that picture, how do the AND and OR colorings differ?

options.text: For AND only the (1,1) point is blue and the rest orange; for OR only the (0,0) point is orange and the rest blue.
options.why: Correct. The two agree at those two corners and disagree at the two in between, which is what the boundary has to sort out.

options.text: For AND only the (0,0) point is orange and the rest blue; for OR only the (1,1) point is blue and the rest orange.
options.why: This swaps the two functions, and it would make AND the easier of the two to satisfy.

options.text: For AND the two middle points are blue and the corners orange; for OR the reverse.
options.why: No coloring of that shape arises, and it could not be produced by a single straight boundary.

options.text: For AND all four points are orange except when both inputs are absent; for OR all four are blue.
options.why: A function that is on for every input would not need a boundary at all.

items.stem: What is a decision boundary?

options.text: The single line with which a unit using a threshold or sigmoid activation function divides the input space, saying yes on one side and no on the other.
options.why: Correct. That such a circuit divides the space with one line is a necessity rather than a feature of any particular drawing.

options.text: The level a unit's weighted total has to reach before the unit will fire at all.
options.why: That is the threshold, which is one of the things whose setting decides where the boundary sits.

options.text: The line beyond which a unit's output stops increasing, since the activation function has by then reached its ceiling and cannot rise any further.
options.why: The ceiling is a bound on the output rather than a division of the input space.

options.text: The range of input values over which a sigmoid unit's output grades smoothly rather than saturating.
options.why: The graded middle of a sigmoid is a property of the function rather than the division the unit draws.

items.stem: What decides where a circuit's decision boundary sits?

options.text: Its weights — which in the two-input case are the three numbers b₀, b₁ and b₂.
options.why: Correct. Which is why setting the weights one way and another makes the same unit compute different functions.

options.text: Its activation function, since a threshold draws the boundary in a different place than a sigmoid would.
options.why: The choice of function decides how sharply the boundary is drawn rather than where it sits.

options.text: The inputs it happens to receive, since the boundary is fitted to whichever combinations actually arrive.
options.why: Nothing fits the boundary to the data here; it is a consequence of the circuit's own parameters.

options.text: The number of input units, since each additional input adds a further line to the division of the space.
options.why: More inputs make the boundary a surface in more dimensions rather than adding lines.

items.stem: Going from the AND circuit to the OR circuit, what has to happen to the decision boundary?

options.text: It shifts in space without rotating, so that (0,1) and (1,0) change which side of it they are on.
options.why: Correct. The two functions agree at (0,0) and at (1,1), and differ only on the two combinations in between.

options.text: It rotates about the origin, so that the two middle points swap sides while the corners stay where they are.
options.why: Rotation is exactly what the change does not require, which is why the two boundaries come out parallel.

options.text: It steepens, so that the transition from no to yes happens over a narrower range of input values.
options.why: Steepness is a property of the activation function rather than of where the boundary is placed.

options.text: It splits into two lines, since OR has three points on one side and a single line cannot separate three from one.
options.why: A single line separates three corners from one perfectly well, which is what the OR boundary does.

items.stem: A shift in a line with no rotation is a change in the intercept. What does that turn out to mean for a unit?

options.text: Raising the threshold does the same work as lowering the baseline firing rate, so baseline and threshold are two knobs that slide the same line.
options.why: Correct. It is the hardest idea in the section, and it is stated nowhere else in the chapter.

options.text: Raising the threshold does the same work as raising both weights, so weight and threshold turn out to be interchangeable adjustments to the same circuit.
options.why: Changing the weights alters the slope of the boundary as well as its position, so the two are not interchangeable.

options.text: Raising the threshold does the same work as adding a further input, since both increase the total the unit has to reach.
options.why: An added input changes what the unit is responding to rather than sliding the same boundary.

options.text: Raising the threshold does the same work as steepening the activation function, since both make the unit harder to fire.
options.why: A steeper function sharpens the transition without moving where it happens.

items.stem: What limitation does the chapter attach to a single straight decision boundary?

options.text: There are computations organisms need that no single line can produce, however the weights and threshold are set.
options.why: Correct. The limit is geometric rather than a matter of not yet having found the right settings.

options.text: There are computations that no single line can produce until the activation function has been made smooth rather than hard.
options.why: Neither function changes what a single boundary can separate; both draw one line.

options.text: There are computations a single line can produce only for inputs that are either fully on or fully off.
options.why: The picture is drawn for every input, including those between the corners, and the background is colored throughout.

options.text: There are computations no single line can produce unless the inputs are first converted to a common scale.
options.why: Rescaling the inputs moves the line rather than changing what one line can do.

items.stem: What does the decision-boundary picture establish about neural circuits?

options.text: That simple straight-line boundaries are enough to show how circuits compute basic logical functions such as AND, OR and NOT on their inputs.
options.why: Correct. It is a second way of seeing what the threshold demonstration already showed, and for some readers it is the one that makes it click.

options.text: That circuits compute logical functions more accurately when their boundaries are drawn as curves rather than lines.
options.why: A unit with either activation function draws a line, and curved boundaries are not on offer here.

options.text: That the logical function a circuit computes can be read off its behavior without anyone needing to know anything at all about its weights.
options.why: The boundary's position is decided by the weights, which is what makes the picture informative about the circuit.

options.text: That basic logical functions require at least two output units, one for each side of the boundary.
options.why: One output unit is what draws the boundary, and every case in the section uses a single one.

items.stem: Show how one unit can be made to compute AND and then OR, and say where the logic actually resides.
items.answer: Give a unit y two excitatory inputs, x₁ and x₂, each with a weight of 1, and set its threshold at 2. Either input on its own contributes 1, which does not reach 2, so y stays silent; both together contribute 2, so y fires. That is AND. Now leave both weights at 1 and set the threshold to 1 instead. Either input on its own now reaches the threshold, and so do both together, so the unit computes OR. Nothing about the wiring changed and only one number moved. The unit is not choosing anything and does not know what AND means: the logic is in the weights and the threshold and nowhere else, so setting them one way makes the unit compute one function and setting them another way makes the same unit compute a different one.
rubric: Gives the AND construction with both weights at 1 and the threshold at 2.
Gives the OR construction by moving the threshold to 1, leaving the weights alone.
States explicitly that the wiring is unchanged and only one number moved.
Locates the logic in the weights and the threshold rather than in any understanding the unit has.

items.stem: Explain what a decision boundary is, and use the move from AND to OR to show why baseline and threshold are described as two knobs that slide the same line.
items.answer: Put a circuit's two inputs on a pair of axes so that every combination of their values is a point on a plane. A circuit with one output unit using a threshold or sigmoid activation function will necessarily divide that space with a single line, saying yes on one side and no on the other, and that line is the decision boundary; where it sits is decided by the weights. Going from AND to OR does not need the slope to change, because the two agree at (0,0) and (1,1) and differ only at (0,1) and (1,0) — so the line only has to shift so those two points change sides. A shift with no rotation is a change of intercept, which in the equation is the unit's baseline firing rate. So raising the threshold does the same work as lowering the baseline, and the two are knobs that slide the same line.
rubric: Defines the decision boundary as the single line a threshold or sigmoid unit divides the space with.
Notes that the weights decide where the line sits.
Explains that AND and OR differ only at the two middle points, so the line shifts without rotating.
Identifies a shift without rotation as a change of intercept, and equates raising the threshold with lowering the baseline.

items.stem: The lecture says it wants to be heavy-handed on one point in the AND-to-OR demonstration. Which point?

options.text: That nothing about the wiring changed: the units are identical, the weights are identical, and one number moved.
options.why: Correct. A demonstration that varied the weights instead would have changed the argument rather than made it.

options.text: That the threshold has to be an integer, since a unit cannot compare its total against a fraction of an input.
options.why: No constraint on what values a threshold can take is offered anywhere.

options.text: That the two inputs have to arrive at the same moment, since a unit sums only what reaches it together.
options.why: Timing is not part of the demonstration, which works entirely in rates.

options.text: That the unit has to use a threshold function rather than a sigmoid, since a graded output could not produce a clean logical answer.
options.why: Both activation functions are available throughout, and neither is required for the demonstration.

items.stem: The lecture closes off "the most natural wrong idea in this material" and connects it to an earlier lab. What is the idea, and what is the connection?

options.text: That the unit understands what it performs; the connection is the Braitenberg lab, where behavior that looked as if it needed an inner life was in the arrangement.
options.why: Correct. The logic is in the weights and the threshold, with nothing inside the unit that could be called understanding.

options.text: That the unit is too simple to compute anything interesting; the connection is that lab's demonstration that two sensors and two motors are enough on their own.
options.why: The lecture guards against crediting the unit with too much rather than too little.

options.text: That the unit's output means something on its own; the connection is the earlier claim that a rate is only a rate.
options.why: A rate being only a rate is this module's own opening claim rather than the lab's lesson.

options.text: That the unit must be wired by hand to compute anything; the connection is the lab's use of a fixed wiring diagram.
options.why: Where the weights come from is deferred to a later module and is not what the caution is about.

items.stem: The lecture says coloring the whole background rather than only the four corners is what makes the picture worth having. Why?

options.text: Because it shows what the circuit does for any input at all, including the ones between the corners.
options.why: Correct. Once the whole background is colored, a boundary appears, and its appearance is a necessity rather than an artifact of the drawing.

options.text: Because it shows which of the four corners the circuit gets wrong, which is how a faulty setting of the weights is diagnosed.
options.why: A correct circuit matches its points, and the background is not a diagnostic for individual corners.

options.text: Because it shows how confident the circuit is about each combination, with stronger color meaning a larger total.
options.why: The coloring records yes or no rather than a degree of confidence.

options.text: Because it shows how the picture would change if a third input were added, which the four corners alone cannot indicate.
options.why: Adding an input is not what the fully colored background illustrates.

items.stem: The lecture calls the two-knobs result the hardest idea in the meeting and says why it is worth holding onto. What is the reason?

options.text: It is the first time in the course that two apparently different adjustments turn out to be one adjustment described twice.
options.why: Correct. Raising the threshold and lowering the baseline both slide the boundary without rotating it.

options.text: It is the only place in the module where a result about circuits can be derived rather than demonstrated.
options.why: Nothing is said about derivation, and the result is shown geometrically like the rest of the stretch.

options.text: It is the first result that holds for a sigmoid unit but not for a threshold unit, which is why the distinction matters.
options.why: The result holds for either activation function, since both draw a single line.

options.text: It is the one adjustment a real animal can make to its own circuits, which is why it matters for the third meeting.
options.why: What an animal can adjust in its own circuits is the subject of neuromodulation later, and it is not this result.

items.stem: What does the chapter say it has shown by the end of the threshold demonstration?

options.text: That the truth table written down at the computational level is satisfied by a simple wiring diagram and two numbers.
options.why: Correct. The specification stated as a demand turns out to be met by an arrangement that can be drawn in a line.

options.text: That the truth table written down at the computational level was incomplete, and needs a third number to be satisfied.
options.why: Nothing is found wanting in the specification; it is met as it stands.

options.text: That a truth table can be derived from a wiring diagram, so the specification need not be written in advance.
options.why: Naming the target before knowing the mechanism is described as ordinary business rather than as avoidable.

options.text: That the truth table describes what the unit represents, which is what makes the account algorithmic.
options.why: A truth table says what has to be done rather than what is represented.

items.stem: What does color-coding the background of the graph, rather than only the four corners, let us see?

options.text: What the circuit does for any input at all, including the combinations that lie between the corners.
options.why: Correct. Once the whole background is colored, a boundary appears.

options.text: Which of the four corners the circuit is most confident about, since the shading is darkest where the total is largest.
options.why: The coloring records a yes or a no rather than a degree of confidence.

options.text: How the circuit would behave if a third input were added, since the extra dimension can be shown as shading.
options.why: A third input would need a third axis rather than being represented by the background.

options.text: Which settings of the weights would produce a different function, since each region corresponds to one setting.
options.why: The axes carry the inputs rather than the weights, so regions are inputs rather than settings.

pools.title: Inhibition, Choosing Exactly One, and Loops
pools.covers: reading §4.2.6, §4.2.7, §4.2.8 · lecture 4.2 slides lateral_inhibition, mutual_inhibition, loops_that_keep_running

items.stem: What is lateral inhibition?

options.text: A row of units, each receiving its own input, with every unit inhibiting its neighbors in proportion to how active it is.
options.why: Correct. The unit with the slightly stronger input inhibits its neighbors harder than they inhibit it back, so its lead grows.

options.text: A row of units in which each one inhibits the unit directly downstream of it, so that only the first in the row can fire at full strength.
options.why: Inhibition here runs sideways to a unit's neighbors rather than forward along a chain of them.

options.text: A pair of units that inhibit one another until only one of them is left firing and the other has fallen silent.
options.why: Two units suppressing each other is a different motif, and what it produces is a choice rather than a sharpened difference.

options.text: A unit that inhibits itself in proportion to its own activity, so that its output can never run away to the ceiling.
options.why: Self-inhibition would limit a unit's own output rather than exaggerate a difference between neighbors.

items.stem: Which motif turns a shallow step in the input into a steep one in the output?

options.text: lateral inhibition
options.why: Correct. It is the wiring pattern that meets the demand to exaggerate a small difference.

options.text: mutual inhibition, the two-unit contest
options.why: Mutual inhibition forces a choice between two options rather than sharpening a gradient across a row.

options.text: divergence
options.why: Divergence sends one verdict to many places and does nothing to the size of a difference.

options.text: a feedback loop
options.why: A feedback loop keeps activity running after its input has stopped, which serves persistence rather than sharpening.

items.stem: Why does a unit receiving a slightly stronger input end up with a much larger lead?

options.text: It inhibits the units beside it slightly harder than they inhibit it back, so they fall, so they inhibit it less, and it climbs further still.
options.why: Correct. The exchange is asymmetric from the start, and the asymmetry compounds.

options.text: It reaches its threshold slightly sooner than its neighbors do, and once a unit is firing its neighbors can no longer affect it at all.
options.why: Nothing makes a firing unit immune to inhibition, and the effect described works on graded activity.

options.text: It receives the same inhibition as its neighbors but starts from a higher baseline, so the same subtraction leaves it further ahead.
options.why: A shared subtraction would preserve the gap rather than widen it, which is the whole point of the arrangement.

options.text: It inhibits its neighbors for longer than they inhibit it, so the difference accumulates over the time the input is present.
options.why: The asymmetry described is in strength rather than in duration, and it works from the first moment.

items.stem: Why does an edge between a light region and a darker one look crisper than the light arriving from it warrants?

options.text: The units on the bright side are inhibited less than their neighbors and those on the dark side are inhibited more, so the bright side reads brighter and the dark side darker.
options.why: Correct. Each side's neighbors differ in brightness, which is what makes the inhibition they deliver asymmetric.

options.text: The units on the bright side saturate at their ceiling while those on the dark side fall to their floor, so the two sides are pushed apart.
options.why: Saturation would flatten both sides rather than steepen the transition between them.

options.text: The units at the edge receive input from the lighter and the darker region at once, so their output is simply the difference between the brightness of the two regions.
options.why: No unit is described as differencing the two regions; the effect arises from neighbors inhibiting each other.

options.text: The units on the dark side stop firing altogether, so the edge is where activity begins rather than where it changes.
options.why: The arrangement leaves the overall levels on either side much as they were and steepens the transition between them.

items.stem: The chapter draws one general moral from the edge case. What is it?

options.text: The nervous system is not reporting the light; it is reporting the difference, amplified, which is one of the main ways visual systems are biased to find object boundaries.
options.why: Correct. The bias is deliberate, and it will show a viewer an edge sharper than the one actually there.

options.text: The nervous system is reporting the light accurately, and the apparent crispness is a mistake introduced later in the visual system.
options.why: The effect is treated as a feature of the arrangement rather than as an error introduced downstream.

options.text: The nervous system is reporting the average light level on each side, which is why the two regions look uniform right up to the edge.
options.why: Averaging within each region is not what produces the crispness, and the chapter's point is about the transition.

options.text: The nervous system is reporting how quickly the light changes over time, which is what makes a moving edge considerably easier to see than a stationary one.
options.why: Motion is not discussed here, and the difference being reported is across space rather than over time.

items.stem: What is mutual inhibition?

options.text: Two units wired so that each one inhibits the other in proportion to its own activity.
options.why: Correct. From a near tie the lead runs away, and within a short time one unit is firing and the other is silent.

options.text: Two units that each excite the other, so that activity between them builds until both reach their ceiling.
options.why: Mutual excitation is closer to how a loop sustains itself, and it would not force a choice between the two.

options.text: Two units that inhibit a third, so that the third fires only when neither of the two is active.
options.why: An arrangement of that shape computes a logical relation rather than settling a contest between two options.

options.text: Two units that inhibit their neighbors along a row, so that a small difference between them is exaggerated.
options.why: Inhibiting neighbors along a row is lateral inhibition, which sharpens a difference rather than resolving it.

items.stem: Which term names the outcome mutual inhibition forces?

options.text: winner-take-all
options.why: Correct. One unit ends up firing and the other silent, whatever the margin between them was to begin with.

options.text: lateral inhibition
options.why: Lateral inhibition is a different motif, and it steepens a difference rather than resolving it into one survivor.

options.text: convergence
options.why: Convergence brings many inputs onto one cell, which makes combining possible rather than forcing a choice.

options.text: feedforward
options.why: Feedforward describes the direction activity runs in rather than any particular outcome.

items.stem: Walk the mutual-inhibition circuit from a near tie. What happens?

options.text: Whichever unit is momentarily ahead inhibits its rival harder, the rival falls and inhibits back less, the leader climbs further, and the lead runs away.
options.why: Correct. Something is always momentarily ahead, which is what gets the runaway started.

options.text: Both units settle at an intermediate level, since each is held down by the other in proportion to how active it is.
options.why: A stable intermediate state is exactly what the arrangement avoids, because any lead compounds itself.

options.text: The two units alternate, each taking a turn at firing while the other is suppressed, until the input stops.
options.why: Alternation is not described, and the outcome is one unit firing steadily while the other stays silent.

options.text: The unit that happens to have the higher baseline wins immediately, so the circuit is effectively decided before any of the input has even arrived.
options.why: The circuit is described as resolving a near tie in the inputs rather than being settled in advance.

items.stem: What does the circuit do with the fact that the contest was close?

options.text: It discards it: the circuit does not average the two options and does not report that the evidence was nearly balanced — it chooses.
options.why: Correct. That is a cost, and it is a cost worth paying for an animal that has one body and needs exactly one action.

options.text: The circuit preserves it, by leaving the winner firing at a rather lower rate than it would have done had the contest been a one-sided one.
options.why: Reporting the margin in the winner's rate is precisely what the arrangement does not do.

options.text: It preserves it, by leaving the loser firing weakly rather than falling silent, so the margin can be recovered downstream.
options.why: The loser is driven to silence, and that silence is described as the result rather than as a residue.

options.text: It resolves it by waiting for further evidence, so that a near tie simply delays the decision until the margin widens.
options.why: Waiting is what a near tie would otherwise force, and the runaway is what removes the need for it.

items.stem: What earlier explanation does mutual inhibition share its shape with?

options.text: The all-or-nothing action potential as a positive feedback runaway — the same runaway one level up, built of cells rather than channels, and producing a decision rather than a spike.
options.why: Correct. Once either loop starts, no intermediate setting is available.

options.text: The refractory period, which prevents a second event from starting until the first has finished, so that two of the outputs can never overlap with each other in time.
options.why: The refractory period limits repetition rather than producing a runaway, and it settles a different pair of claims.

options.text: The energy budget, in which a large share of a small total is spent on restoring what signaling has run down.
options.why: The accounting argument has a different shape and belongs to the previous module's close.

options.text: The trade between chemical and neural signaling, in which reach is given up and speed and aim are bought.
options.why: That is a comparison of two systems rather than a self-reinforcing process.

items.stem: What question left open in the previous module does mutual inhibition answer?

options.text: Why activity that is so sparse should carry information well: a circuit that suppresses everything except the winner produces a sparse pattern, because that pattern is the decision.
options.why: Correct. The silence of the losing units is not an absence of information — it is the result.

options.text: Why a brain is so expensive to run: suppressing the losing units costs energy that the winning unit does not have to spend.
options.why: The cost of suppression is not raised, and the energy accounting was settled in the previous module.

options.text: Why a neuron cannot fire a negative number of times per second: the losing unit is driven to silence rather than below it.
options.why: That limit is what the activation function addresses, and it is settled earlier in this section.

options.text: Why only a small fraction of neurons are needed to represent anything: a sparse pattern is a good deal easier for a downstream circuit to read out than a dense one would be.
options.why: Ease of readout is not the reason given, and the answer offered is that the sparse pattern is itself the decision.

items.stem: What does feedforward describe?

options.text: Connections that run in one direction, from input to unit to output, which is how every arrangement up to this point in the chapter has worked.
options.why: Correct. The word is introduced only at this point, because there was nothing to contrast it with until loops arrived.

options.text: Connections that carry excitation rather than inhibition, so that the activity always increases rather than decreasing as it passes along them.
options.why: The sign a connection carries is a separate matter from the direction activity runs in.

options.text: Connections that reach forward to units several steps ahead, skipping the ones in between.
options.why: Skipping intermediate units is not what the term picks out; it is about direction rather than distance.

options.text: Connections that run toward the front of the animal, where the sensors and the units they report to are gathered.
options.why: The word describes the direction of flow through a circuit rather than a direction in the body.

items.stem: What is a feedback connection, also called a recurrent connection?

options.text: A connection that runs a unit's output back toward its own input, either directly or around a longer path through other units.
options.why: Correct. It is called recurrent because activity can run around the loop again and again.

options.text: A connection that carries inhibition back to the unit that excited it, so that activity is damped rather than sustained.
options.why: The sign the connection carries is not part of the definition, and what a loop is credited with here is persistence.

options.text: A connection that reports the result of a computation back to the sensors, so that the animal is able to check what it has just detected against what it expected.
options.why: No verification of sensory input is described, and the loop's payoff is that activity keeps running.

options.text: A connection that runs between two units which each inhibit the other, so that one of them ends up winning.
options.why: That arrangement is mutual inhibition, and it is a different motif with a different outcome.

items.stem: A student objects that loops contradict the rule that flow runs one way. What is the answer?

options.text: Each connection within a loop still runs one way — output leaves by the axon and arrives on dendrites — and the loop is built of those one-way links.
options.why: Correct. It is the path that comes back around rather than any individual connection.

options.text: The one-way rule applies to signaling within a cell rather than between cells, so a connection between two units may run either way.
options.why: The rule covers connections between cells as well, and the answer given preserves it rather than narrowing it.

options.text: The one-way rule holds only for feedforward circuits, and a recurrent circuit is the exception the rule allows for.
options.why: No exception is granted; the whole point is that a recurrent circuit obeys the rule.

options.text: Activity in a loop runs in both directions at once, which is what allows it to sustain itself after the input stops.
options.why: Two-way flow along a single connection is not what sustains the loop; a circular path of one-way links is.

items.stem: What does a loop provide, and how?

options.text: Persistence: a unit that excites something that excites it back can keep itself going after the input that started it has stopped.
options.why: Correct. The stimulus lasts a moment and the activity lasts as long as the loop keeps running.

options.text: Amplification: activity running around the loop grows on each pass, so a weak input eventually produces a strong output.
options.why: Growth on each pass is closer to a runaway, and what the loop is credited with here is outlasting its input.

options.text: Timing: activity takes a fixed period to travel around the loop, so the circuit is able to measure how long ago a particular thing happened to it.
options.why: No clock or interval measurement is attributed to the arrangement.

options.text: Comparison: activity arriving on the second pass can be set against what is arriving fresh, so a change can be detected.
options.why: Comparison across time is how one animal steers later in the chapter, and it is not what the loop is introduced for.

items.stem: What surprising consequence does the chapter draw from loops?

options.text: An internal state does not have to be stored anywhere: a state can simply be a circuit that is still running, minutes after the thing that set it off has gone.
options.why: Correct. There need be no record, no trace, and nothing written down.

options.text: An internal state can be held indefinitely at no cost, since a loop that is already running requires no further input of any kind to keep itself going.
options.why: Whether it is free is not claimed, and the previous module's accounting says that reacting hard is expensive.

options.text: An internal state must be stored in a changed connection, since ongoing activity is too easily disrupted to be relied on.
options.why: Storage in a changed connection is named as a different thing entirely, and it is deferred to a later module.

options.text: An internal state can be read off by any unit downstream, since the loop broadcasts its activity to everything it reaches.
options.why: Who can read the state is not discussed, and the surprise named is that nothing has to be stored.

items.stem: What distinction does the chapter flag as belonging to a later module?

options.text: The difference between a state held in ongoing activity and a state held in a changed connection, which is a different thing entirely.
options.why: Correct. Loops supply the first kind, and the second is deferred rather than described here.

options.text: The difference between a state that outlasts its cause and one that ends with it, which is what separates an affective state from an ordinary reflex.
options.why: That distinction is drawn in this chapter rather than deferred, and it is what affect is defined by.

options.text: The difference between a state held in one circuit and one distributed across many, which is what makes a state hard to locate.
options.why: No question about how widely a state is distributed is raised.

options.text: The difference between a state an animal can report and one it cannot, which is where consciousness would have to enter.
options.why: Reportability is not discussed anywhere in the chapter.

items.stem: Which of the four demands does mutual inhibition answer, and how was that demand stated?

options.text: Committing — one body has to go in the one direction of its top choice, not in the average direction of its set of choices.
options.why: Correct. The chapter calls it the hardest of the four, and its justification was anatomical rather than informational.

options.text: Combining — several cues of different strengths have to be weighed carefully against one another before any single action can be chosen.
options.why: Combining is served by convergence and by weights, and it leaves the near tie unresolved.

options.text: Evaluating — what is sensed has to be sorted into good, bad and neither before a direction can be preferred.
options.why: Evaluating is answered by valence and by the labeled line rather than by a contest between two units.

options.text: Modulating — the animal's own condition has to be able to reach into the verdict and change it.
options.why: Modulation is served by loops and by neuromodulators rather than by a winner-take-all contest.

items.stem: Describe the lateral inhibition arrangement, and explain what it does to an edge in a visual scene.
items.answer: Take a row of units, each receiving its own input, and have each one inhibit its neighbors in proportion to how active it is. A unit receiving a slightly stronger input inhibits the units beside it slightly harder than they inhibit it back, so those neighbors fall, so they inhibit it less, and its lead grows. A shallow step in the input comes out as a steep one in the output. At an edge between a light region and a darker one, the units on the bright side are inhibited less than their neighbors and the units on the dark side are inhibited more, so the edge looks crisper than the light arriving from it warrants. The nervous system is not reporting the light; it is reporting the difference, amplified.
rubric: Describes the arrangement: a row of units each inhibiting its neighbors in proportion to its activity.
Explains the asymmetry that makes a lead grow.
States the shallow-step-in, steep-step-out result.
Applies it to an edge, with the bright side inhibited less and the dark side more.

items.stem: Explain how mutual inhibition resolves a near tie, and what it settles about sparse activity.
items.answer: Two units each inhibit the other. When both receive nearly equal input, whichever is momentarily ahead inhibits its rival a little harder; the rival's activity falls, so it inhibits back a little less, so the leader climbs further. The lead runs away, and within a short time one unit is firing and the other is silent. The circuit does not average the two options and does not report that the contest was close — it chooses, and the fact that the evidence was nearly balanced is discarded. It also settles a question left open in the previous module about why sparse activity carries information well: a circuit that suppresses everything except the winner produces a sparse pattern, because that pattern is the decision. The silence of the losing units is not an absence of information; it is the result.
rubric: Describes the runaway from a near tie, with the lead compounding.
States that the circuit chooses rather than averaging or reporting the margin.
Connects the motif to the question about why sparse activity carries information.
Explains that the silence of the losers is the result rather than missing information.

items.stem: The lecture says this is a motif a student can check against their own experience. What does it invite them to check, and where does it say the circuit is?

options.text: That an edge between a light and a dark region looks crisper than the light warrants — and the circuit doing it is in the retina.
options.why: Correct. The lecture insists it is not a metaphor, and adds that the bias will show a viewer an edge sharper than the one actually there.

options.text: That two objects of the same brightness look different against different backgrounds — and the circuit doing it is in the cortex.
options.why: Simultaneous contrast is a related effect, and it is not what the lecture points at or where it locates the circuit.

options.text: That a dim light is easier to see out of the corner of the eye — and the circuit doing it is in the optic nerve.
options.why: Peripheral sensitivity is not discussed, and no circuit is placed in the nerve.

options.text: That a bright edge appears to move when stared at — and the circuit doing it is in the muscles of the eye.
options.why: No motion illusion is raised, and lateral inhibition is a wiring pattern rather than anything muscular.

items.stem: The lecture adds a judgment about discarding the margin that the chapter states more flatly. What is it?

options.text: That discarding it is a cost, and a cost worth paying if you have one body.
options.why: Correct. Naming it as a price rather than as a feature is what keeps the winner-take-all outcome from looking like pure gain.

options.text: That discarding it is harmless, since a margin that small carries no information worth preserving anyway.
options.why: The lecture treats the loss as real rather than as negligible.

options.text: That discarding it is unavoidable, since no arrangement of units could preserve a margin and still produce one action.
options.why: No impossibility claim is made; the lecture presents it as a trade.

options.text: That discarding it is temporary, since the margin can be recovered from how quickly the winner reached its ceiling.
options.why: Nothing about recovering the margin from the timing is suggested.

items.stem: The lecture says why it is defining feedforward only at this point in the meeting. What is the reason?

options.text: There was nothing to contrast it with until loops arrived, since every arrangement up to then had run one way.
options.why: Correct. The word earns its keep only once a connection that runs back the other way is on the table.

options.text: The term belongs to the artificial side of the comparison, and the lecture had been working on the biological side until then.
options.why: Both kinds of connection are discussed for biological and artificial systems alike.

options.text: The term was defined in the previous module and is being recalled rather than introduced here.
options.why: The lecture presents it as a new word rather than a reminder.

options.text: The earlier arrangements had loops in them that were being ignored for simplicity, and the simplification is dropped here.
options.why: Nothing earlier is described as having had loops quietly left out.

items.stem: Which consequence of loops does the lecture single out as the one it finds surprising every time?

options.text: That an internal state does not have to be stored anywhere, and can simply be a circuit still running minutes after its cause has gone.
options.why: Correct. There need be no record, no trace, and nothing written down.

options.text: That a loop can keep running indefinitely without any further input, which makes a state free to maintain once entered.
options.why: Cost is not what the lecture singles out, and it does not claim a running loop is free.

options.text: That the same motif produces both a decision and a state, depending only on whether the connections within it are excitatory or inhibitory ones.
options.why: The two motifs are kept distinct, and the lecture does not unify them in that way.

options.text: That a state held in activity is more robust than one held in a changed connection, which is why animals use loops at all.
options.why: The comparison between the two ways of holding a state is deferred rather than resolved in favor of either.

items.stem: Which earlier demand does lateral inhibition answer?

options.text: The need to exaggerate a small difference, noted when the demands of steering were first stated.
options.why: Correct. The wiring pattern takes a shallow step in the input and produces a steep one in the output.

options.text: The need to combine cues that disagree, since inhibition is how one cue is weighed against another.
options.why: Weighing cues against one another is convergence and weights rather than a row of units inhibiting neighbors.

options.text: The need to hold a state after its cause has gone, since inhibition keeps a circuit tuned one way.
options.why: Persistence comes from a loop, and inhibition across a row does nothing to outlast its input.

options.text: The need to commit to exactly one action, since inhibition is how the alternatives are suppressed.
options.why: Suppressing alternatives is mutual inhibition, which is the next motif rather than this one.

items.stem: Which demand does the chapter introduce loops in order to meet?

options.text: The demand for states that outlast whatever caused them.
options.why: Correct. Every arrangement before it had run one way, from input to unit to output.

options.text: The demand to combine several cues that disagree into one direction of travel.
options.why: Combining is met by convergence and by weights, both of which run feedforward.

options.text: The demand to exaggerate a small difference so that a near-tie becomes a clear one.
options.why: Sharpening is lateral inhibition's job and needs no loop.

options.text: The demand to commit to exactly one action rather than a blend of two.
options.why: Committing is met by mutual inhibition, which is a contest rather than a loop.

pools.title: Where Valence Lives, and What a Fixed Circuit Cannot Do
pools.covers: reading §4.2.9, §4.2.10, §4.2.11, §4.2.12 · lecture 4.2 slides where_valence_lives, affect_as_two_numbers, the_same_motifs_in_silicon, what_a_fixed_circuit_cannot_do

items.stem: What does a sensory neuron's output actually carry?

options.text: A rate — so many spikes per second, more of them when the thing it responds to is stronger — and nothing about that rate says whether the thing is worth approaching.
options.why: Correct. It is the same claim the module opened with, arriving now with a mechanism attached to it.

options.text: A rate together with a sign, so that a downstream cell can tell an approach signal from a withdrawal signal.
options.why: No sign is carried in the signal; where the output goes is what supplies the verdict.

options.text: A pattern of timing specific to the molecule detected, which is how a downstream cell knows what has been sensed.
options.why: A distinctive timing signature would be a way of carrying identity, and the chapter denies that the signal carries one.

options.text: A rate that rises for beneficial substances and falls for harmful ones, which is much the simplest way for a nervous system to encode a verdict about something.
options.why: A cell responding to a toxin fires more when there is more of it, exactly as a food cell does.

items.stem: The chapter pushes the point about sensory neurons as hard as it can go. What is the strongest version?

options.text: Two sensory cells, one responding to a food molecule and one to a toxin, can produce output identical in every respect a downstream cell could measure.
options.why: Correct. Same rate, same timing, and nothing in the signal to distinguish them.

options.text: Two sensory cells responding to the same molecule can produce opposite outputs, depending on which part of the animal's body the two of them happen to sit in.
options.why: Location in the body is not what varies in the example, and both cells respond to different molecules.

options.text: A single sensory cell can respond to both a food molecule and a toxin, so its output is ambiguous between the two.
options.why: Ambiguity within one cell is not the case being made; two distinct cells are compared.

options.text: A sensory cell's output can be measured only downstream, so whether it carries a verdict cannot be settled either way.
options.why: The chapter settles it firmly rather than leaving it open.

items.stem: What is a labeled line, and where is the label?

options.text: A sensory cell's output routed to particular downstream machinery — and the label is not on the line but at the far end of it, in the thing the line connects to.
options.why: Correct. Route the cell to what drives the animal forward and it is a positive-valence cell; route the identical cell to withdrawal and it is a negative-valence one.

options.text: A sensory cell that carries a distinctive signal marking which kind of thing it has detected, so downstream cells can tell them apart.
options.why: A distinguishing mark carried in the signal is exactly what the chapter denies a sensory neuron has.

options.text: A connection whose weight has been set to a value that identifies the cue it carries, so the weight is the label.
options.why: Weights decide how strongly a signal counts rather than labeling what it is.

options.text: A line of cells running from a sensor to a muscle without branching, so that a signal arrives exactly where it is meant to without being mixed with any other.
options.why: Absence of branching is not what the term picks out, and the point concerns where the line terminates.

items.stem: What makes one neuron a "good-detector"?

options.text: What it is wired to: routed to what drives the animal forward it is a positive-valence cell, and the identical cell routed to withdrawal is a negative one.
options.why: Correct. Whatever the cell responds to, the animal approaches — or withdraws — according to where the output goes.

options.text: What it responds to: a cell tuned to a nutritious molecule is a good-detector and one tuned to a toxin is not.
options.why: Two such cells can produce identical output, so what they respond to cannot be what settles it.

options.text: How strongly it fires: a cell that fires hard enough to drive behavior on its own is treated by everything downstream of it as carrying a positive verdict.
options.why: Rate carries no verdict at all, however large it gets.

options.text: How many downstream cells it reaches: a cell with wide divergence carries more weight in the animal's decisions.
options.why: How widely a verdict spreads is a separate matter from what the verdict is.

items.stem: The chapter says there is no good signal, no bad signal, no pleasure molecule and no pain molecule. How is that claim scoped?

options.text: To the level of neural circuitry — which is why the chapter can spend its next section on molecules that shape value without contradicting itself.
options.why: Correct. The scope is in the sentence itself, and dropping it turns a careful claim into a false one.

options.text: To invertebrates, since a worm has no dedicated reward system of the kind the chapter goes on to find in the larger nervous systems it discusses.
options.why: No restriction by animal group is offered, and the chapter's later argument runs the other way.

options.text: To sensory neurons, since the verdict is formed further downstream rather than at the point of detection.
options.why: The claim covers the circuitry generally, not only the sensory end of it.

options.text: To artificial systems, since a network has no chemistry to carry a signal of that kind in the first place.
options.why: The claim is made about neural circuitry, and the artificial comparison is drawn separately.

items.stem: Where does the chapter say valence is a fact about?

options.text: The wiring diagram — which is the same point made in the previous module's close and in the first module's lab, where crossing two wires reversed the behavior with every part unchanged.
options.why: Correct. This section is where that claim finally gets its arrangement.

options.text: The sensory cell's tuning — which is the same point made when valence was first introduced, as a tag that a nervous system attaches to whatever it happens to be sensing.
options.why: The sensory cell is ruled out by name, both when valence was introduced and again here.

options.text: The molecule detected — which is why the chapter's next section turns to the chemistry that carries a verdict.
options.why: Locating value in the molecule is what the chapter has denied since the demand to evaluate was first stated.

options.text: The animal's internal state — which is why the same cue can be approached when hungry and avoided when full.
options.why: Internal state changes a verdict rather than being where the verdict lives.

items.stem: Stated algorithmically, what is an animal's affective state?

options.text: Two numbers — one for how good or bad things are and one for how activated the animal is — with what the animal does next a function of its position in that space.
options.why: Correct. The plane introduced earlier as a description becomes, at this level, a claim about representation.

options.text: A single number combining how good things are with how strongly the animal is reacting, since those two quantities always turn out to move together in practice.
options.why: The two quantities are explicitly independent, which is what the chapter's own pairs of states demonstrate.

options.text: A named state drawn from a fixed set, with the animal's behavior determined by which of the set it is currently in.
options.why: A list of named states is precisely what the chapter argues against.

options.text: A running record of what the animal has recently sensed, from which its current verdict can be recomputed at any moment.
options.why: Nothing is recorded; a state is a position rather than a history.

items.stem: Why a space rather than a list of named states?

options.text: A list holds only what someone thought to name, while every position in a space is a possible state — and two numbers describe a worm and a person alike.
options.why: Correct. A course built on comparing minds across species needs a description that travels, which a list of human emotion words could not.

options.text: A list cannot represent states of differing intensity, while a space allows every one of the named states to be scaled up or down by as much as the situation happens to need.
options.why: Intensity could be added to a list, and the argument given turns on what a list can hold at all.

options.text: A list has to be learned by the animal, while a space is available to any nervous system whatever its experience.
options.why: How an animal comes by its states is not what separates the two representations here.

options.text: A list would be different for every species, while a space is the same for all of them and so makes comparison unnecessary.
options.why: The space makes comparison possible rather than unnecessary, which is the opposite of the claim.

items.stem: How far does the chapter push its two-number account of affect?

options.text: Only as a claim about representation: how many dimensions are needed to describe human emotional life adequately is argued about.
options.why: Correct. The general point is that thinking of circuits as defining spaces buys a great deal of understanding about behavior.

options.text: As a complete account of affect in every animal, since the same two numbers describe a worm and a person alike.
options.why: Describing both in the same terms is a virtue of the representation rather than a claim that it is complete.

options.text: As a claim about human emotion specifically, with the worm case offered only as a simplified illustration of the human one.
options.why: The worm is not a simplification of the human case; the representation is offered as covering both.

options.text: As a claim that will be settled by the chemistry described in the chapter's next section.
options.why: The dimensionality question is left open rather than handed to the implementational level.

items.stem: What is the general point the chapter says it is making with the two-number space?

options.text: That thinking of circuits as defining spaces for decisions and preferences explains a great deal about behavior, with their activity levels defining internal states.
options.why: Correct. The claim is pitched more generally and abstractly than any particular count of dimensions.

options.text: That an animal's behavior can be predicted exactly once its position in the space is known, which is precisely what makes the account a useful one to have.
options.why: Exact prediction is not claimed, and the chapter's language is about understanding rather than prediction.

options.text: That circuits represent the world rather than the animal, so a space of preferences is really a space of environments.
options.why: The space is about the animal's own condition and verdicts rather than about the world outside it.

options.text: That any internal state can be located in the space, which is why no further representational machinery is needed.
options.why: Sufficiency of the representation is exactly what the chapter declines to claim.

items.stem: How does the comparison with artificial networks look at the scale of the circuit?

options.text: An artificial network is also built from units that take weighted inputs, sum them and pass the total through an activation function, wired into similar patterns.
options.why: Correct. It is the same arithmetic rather than an analogy, which is why one diagram serves for both.

options.text: An artificial network uses the same motifs but computes them in a different order, since its layers run strictly one way.
options.why: Recurrent connections are named among the patterns artificial networks use, so the flow is not strictly one way.

options.text: An artificial network resembles a circuit only in how it behaves, since its units have no thresholds of any kind.
options.why: Artificial units pass their total through an activation function exactly as the chapter's units do.

options.text: An artificial network resembles a single neuron closely but a circuit hardly at all, which is exactly where the comparison between the two of them breaks down.
options.why: The chapter reports the opposite: at the scale of the circuit the comparison continues to hold surprisingly well.

items.stem: Which motifs does the chapter find in artificial networks, and doing what?

options.text: Convergence and divergence make up every layer; mutual inhibition appears wherever one output has to be settled on; recurrence holds a state across time.
options.why: Correct. A fully connected layer is nothing but many-onto-one and one-onto-many, stacked.

options.text: Lateral inhibition makes up every layer; convergence appears at the output; recurrent connections supply the weights.
options.why: Weights are not supplied by any motif, and layers are built from convergence and divergence.

options.text: Convergence makes up every layer; divergence appears only in recurrent networks; mutual inhibition holds a state across time.
options.why: Holding a state is what recurrence does, and divergence is part of every layer rather than a special case.

options.text: Mutual inhibition makes up every layer; lateral inhibition settles the output; and feedforward connections are what hold a state across time.
options.why: Feedforward connections run one way and cannot hold anything after their input stops.

items.stem: What does the chapter make of one diagram serving for both biological and artificial systems?

options.text: Another example of multiple realizability, this time at the scale of the circuit rather than the cell.
options.why: Correct. The same computation runs on cells or on silicon and is described by the same drawing.

options.text: Evidence that artificial networks were designed from biological circuits, which is why the diagrams match.
options.why: How the resemblance arose is discussed for the robot vacuum rather than here, and the point made is about realization.

options.text: Evidence that the two systems face the same energy constraints, since the same arrangement is efficient in both.
options.why: Energy costs are where the two diverge, which the chapter takes up at the implementational level.

options.text: A sign that the algorithmic level is the only one at which the two systems can be compared at all.
options.why: The two are compared at the implementational level too, where the chapter finds them least alike.

items.stem: What does the chapter's audit of its own arrangements find?

options.text: Every demand raised at the computational level now has a wiring pattern that meets it — and every one of those arrangements has fixed weights, set in advance.
options.why: Correct. Those two sentences together are the section's thesis.

options.text: Every demand has a wiring pattern instantiating it, and each of those arrangements serves exactly one demand, which is why a set of only five motifs turns out to suffice.
