options.why: Motifs are reused across demands, and the property the audit turns on is that the weights are fixed.

options.text: Most demands have a wiring pattern instantiating them, with committing the one that no fixed arrangement can meet.
options.why: Committing is met, by mutual inhibition, and it is met with fixed weights like the rest.

options.text: Every demand has a wiring pattern instantiating it, and each one has been found in a real animal already.
options.why: Finding them in tissue is what the chapter's next section sets out to do.

items.stem: What are the two things the chapter says a fixed-weight circuit cannot do?

options.text: It cannot come to treat a new smell as food, and it cannot get better at telling two similar things apart by doing it a thousand times.
options.why: Correct. A circuit with fixed weights can only ever do what its weights were set to do.

options.text: It cannot hold a state after its input has stopped, and it cannot settle on one of two things when both are nearly tied.
options.why: Both of those are met by fixed-weight arrangements — a loop and mutual inhibition respectively.

options.text: It cannot combine more than two cues at once, and it cannot exaggerate any difference that happens to be smaller than its own threshold will allow for.
options.why: Neither limit is claimed, and convergence handles many cues at once.

options.text: It cannot change what it treats as good when the animal is hungry, and it cannot respond differently to the same cue twice.
options.why: Modulation by internal state is met within the section, so a fixed-weight circuit manages both.

items.stem: Scaled up to a whole animal, what would a nervous system of entirely fixed-weight arrangements mean?

options.text: The animal would meet the world with a fixed repertoire, and would meet it the same way on the thousandth encounter as on the first.
options.why: Correct. Where the weights come from, and how they can change within a lifetime, is handed to a later module.

options.text: The animal would be unable to respond to anything it had not encountered before, since no fixed weight would have been set for it in advance.
options.why: A fixed-weight circuit responds to novel input perfectly well; what it cannot do is change how it responds.

options.text: The animal's behavior would become less accurate over time, since nothing would correct the weights as conditions changed.
options.why: Nothing degrades; the repertoire simply stays as it was.

options.text: The animal would need a much larger nervous system, since every possible situation would require its own dedicated circuit.
options.why: No claim about size is made, and the limit described is about change rather than about capacity.

items.stem: How does the chapter hand its algorithmic section over to the next one?

options.text: It has all been arrows and numbers on a page, so what remains is which cells, in what arrangement, and what lets them hold a state for an hour.
options.why: Correct. The concession is made plainly rather than being smoothed over.

options.text: The arrangements have been shown to work on the page, so what remains is to test every one of them against the behavior of some real animal that steers.
options.why: Testing against behavior is not the handover; the next section supplies the tissue rather than the evidence.

options.text: The demands have been met in principle, so what remains is to show that a real animal could afford to run them.
options.why: Cost is discussed later, and the questions handed over are about cells, arrangement and duration.

options.text: The motifs have been named, so what remains is to work out which of the five a given animal actually uses.
options.why: The next section traces real circuits rather than auditing which motifs are present.

items.stem: Explain where valence lives, on the chapter's account, and state the strongest form of the claim along with its scope.
items.answer: A sensory neuron carries a rate and nothing more, and nothing about that rate says whether what it responds to is worth approaching — two sensory cells, one responding to a food molecule and one to a toxin, can produce output identical in every respect a downstream cell could measure. What makes one cell a good-detector is what it is wired to: route its output to the machinery that drives the animal forward and it is a positive-valence cell, and route the identical cell to the machinery that drives withdrawal and it becomes a negative-valence cell. That arrangement is a labeled line, though the label is at the far end rather than on the line. So valence is a fact about the wiring diagram. The strongest form of the claim is that at the level of neural circuitry there is no good signal, no bad signal, no pleasure molecule and no pain molecule — there is just a cell and where its output goes — and that claim is scoped to the level of circuitry, which is why molecules that shape value can be discussed at the implementational level without contradiction.
rubric: States that a sensory neuron carries only a rate, which carries no verdict.
Gives the identical-output case for a food cell and a toxin cell.
Explains that routing the output decides the valence, and names the labeled line.
Gives the strongest form of the claim with its scope to the level of neural circuitry.

items.stem: The chapter's algorithmic section ends by turning on its own achievement. Explain what it achieved and what it then points out.
items.answer: It achieved arrangements that evaluate, combine, sharpen, commit and persist, so that every demand raised at the computational level has a wiring pattern instantiating it. What it then points out is that in every one of those arrangements the weights are fixed: the numbers were set in advance, and nothing that happens to the circuit changes them. That is a real limit, because a circuit with fixed weights can only ever do what its weights were set to do — it cannot come to treat a new smell as food, and it cannot get better at telling two similar things apart by doing it a thousand times. An animal built entirely out of such arrangements would meet the world with a fixed repertoire, and would meet it the same way on the thousandth encounter as on the first.
rubric: States that every demand now has a wiring pattern that meets it.
Identifies fixed weights as the shared property of all of those arrangements.
Gives at least one concrete thing a fixed-weight circuit cannot do.
Draws the consequence for a whole animal: a fixed repertoire, unchanged by experience.

items.stem: The lecture tells the room to hold on to four particular words, and says why. Which words, and what do they prevent?

options.text: At the level of circuitry — because the next meeting spends an hour on molecules that shape value, which is a different level rather than a contradiction.
options.why: Correct. Dropping the scope turns a careful claim into a false one about there being no molecules involved in valence at all.

options.text: Valence is a wiring fact — because it is the sentence that the whole of this module has been building toward since its very first slide.
options.why: That claim is indeed the destination, and it is not the phrase the lecture asks the room to hold as a guard.

options.text: What it is wired to — because it is the answer to where the assignment of good and bad comes from.
options.why: That phrase is the answer itself rather than a scope marker protecting it.

options.text: Identical in every respect — because it is what makes the food cell and the toxin cell indistinguishable downstream.
options.why: That phrase belongs to the evidence for the claim rather than to its scope.

items.stem: The lecture says the name labeled line is slightly wrong in a way worth fixing. What is the fix?

options.text: The label is not on the line; it is at the far end of it, in the thing the line connects to.
options.why: Correct. The same sensory cell becomes a positive- or a negative-valence cell according to what its output reaches.

options.text: The line is not labeled by the animal but by the observer, so the name describes our description rather than the circuit.
options.why: Nothing about the name is attributed to an observer's convenience.

options.text: The label is on the line but is set by the sensory cell rather than by what it detects, so the name misplaces its origin.
options.why: Placing the label on the line at all is what the lecture corrects.

options.text: The line is not a single connection but a whole pathway, so the name understates how much machinery is involved.
options.why: How many cells the pathway involves is not the correction being made.

items.stem: The lecture gives a second reason for preferring a space to a list, and ties it to something the course cares about. What is it?

options.text: Two numbers describe a worm and a person in the same terms, and a course built on comparing minds across species needs a description that travels.
options.why: Correct. A list of human emotion words could not do that at all.

options.text: Two numbers can be measured in a worm and in a person by the same method, which is what makes the comparison empirical.
options.why: No shared method of measurement is claimed, and the reason offered is about the description rather than the technique.

options.text: Two numbers avoid attributing human feelings to animals, which is the error that any course working from a list of human emotion words would invite.
options.why: Avoiding attribution is not the reason given, and the lecture is happy to apply the vocabulary to a worm.

options.text: Two numbers can be held by a circuit with fixed weights, which a list of named states could not be.
options.why: Nothing connects the choice of representation to whether the weights are fixed.

items.stem: The lecture says how it wants students to arrive at the module where weights can change. How?

options.text: Already feeling the problem rather than being told there is one.
options.why: Correct. Which is why it takes the audit of its own achievement and then turns on it.

options.text: Already knowing which motif will solve it, so that the new module can begin with the mechanism.
options.why: No mechanism is previewed, and the door is left open rather than half-answered.

options.text: Already convinced that fixed-weight circuits are inadequate for any real animal.
options.why: The lecture credits the fixed arrangements with meeting every demand rather than dismissing them.

options.text: Already able to state the two other doors left open, since all three are resolved in the same place.
options.why: The other two doors are handed to different modules rather than resolved alongside this one.

items.stem: The lecture insists the resemblance between artificial units and the chapter's units is not an analogy. What is it instead?

options.text: The same arithmetic: weighted inputs, summed, passed through an activation function.
options.why: Correct. It is the same three-step description repaired earlier in the meeting, arriving in a different substrate.

options.text: The same wiring: artificial networks are laid out to match a biological circuit connection for connection.
options.why: Layer patterns are described as similar rather than as matching connection for connection.

options.text: The same origin: artificial units were derived from biological ones, so the resemblance is inherited.
options.why: The derivation was noted in the previous module, and what the lecture insists on here is the arithmetic.

options.text: The same limits: both kinds of unit have a floor and a ceiling imposed by their physical substrate.
options.why: An artificial unit's bounds come from its activation function rather than from any physical limit.

items.stem: What question, raised earlier and deliberately left open, does this part of the chapter answer?

options.text: Where the assignments of good and bad come from, given that they are assigned rather than inherent in the world.
options.why: Correct. The circuit answer is simpler than most readers expect, and a little unsettling.

options.text: Whether good and bad are inherent in the world or assigned by an animal, which had not been settled before.
options.why: That much was settled when valence was introduced; what was left open is where the assignment happens.

options.text: Why an animal needs to assign good and bad at all, rather than responding to whatever it detects.
options.why: Why a verdict is needed was answered when steering's demands were stated.

options.text: How an animal's internal state can change a verdict it has already assigned.
options.why: Modulation is answered by loops and by the chemistry rather than here.

items.stem: At what scale is the natural–artificial comparison made in this part of the chapter, and how does it come out?

options.text: At the scale of the circuit rather than the single cell, and it continues to hold surprisingly well.
options.why: Correct. The earlier comparison had found one artificial neuron and one real one close at the algorithmic level.

options.text: At the scale of the whole animal, and it breaks down as soon as behavior rather than computation is considered.
options.why: The whole-agent comparison was made earlier, with a machine that steers, and it held.

options.text: At the scale of the single cell again, and it comes out weaker than it did the first time.
options.why: The scale moves up rather than being repeated, and the comparison holds.

options.text: At the scale of the chemistry, and it fails because artificial systems have none.
options.why: The chemistry is where the comparison does break, and that comes later in the chapter.

items.stem: What does the chapter hand to a later module at the end of its algorithmic section?

options.text: Where the weights come from, and how they can change within a single lifetime.
options.why: Correct. The section names the material only by what fixed weights cannot do.

options.text: How a wiring diagram can be produced for an animal larger than a worm.
options.why: Connectome work is discussed in the chapter itself rather than handed forward.

options.text: How many dimensions are needed to describe human emotional life adequately.
options.why: That question is named as disputed rather than deferred to a particular module.

options.text: How an artificial network could be given something answering to neuromodulation.
options.why: That question is left open rather than assigned anywhere.

items.stem: Every circuit in this chapter has weights that never move. What is the status of that fact?

options.text: It is a simplification made on purpose: the fixed weights are ours rather than the animals', and a later module is where they start to move.
options.why: Correct. It is why the claims around it are conditional — a fixed-weight circuit, an animal built entirely out of such arrangements would.

options.text: It is a finding about small nervous systems, since the animals modeled here genuinely do have connections that never change with experience.
options.why: This is the reading the chapter states a claim to block. Real animals learn, and that includes the animals in this chapter.

options.text: It is a limitation of the diagrams, since connections can be drawn changing but not in any way a reader could follow on a printed page.
options.why: Nothing about what a diagram can or cannot show is offered as a reason anywhere in the chapter.

options.text: It is a claim about timescale: the weights do move, but far too slowly for any of it to matter within a single encounter.
options.why: No claim about how fast weights change is made. The chapter holds them still rather than describing them as slow.

items.stem: A classmate reads this subsection as the chapter's verdict on what small nervous systems are capable of. Correct the reading, and say what the subsection is a verdict on instead.
items.answer: It is a verdict on the circuits rather than on the animals. Every arrangement built in the chapter has weights that were set in advance, and nothing that happens to the circuit changes them, which is a real limit: a circuit with fixed weights can only ever do what its weights were set to do. But holding the numbers still is a simplification the chapter is making rather than something found in the biology — the fixed weights are ours rather than the animals' — which is why the claims around it are written conditionally, about a fixed-weight circuit, and about what an animal built entirely out of such arrangements would do. Real animals learn, the small ones in this chapter included. Where the weights come from, and how they change within a single lifetime, is Module 5's subject, and that is where they start to move.
rubric: Locates the limit in the circuits rather than in the animals.
States the limit itself: weights set in advance, unchanged by anything that happens to the circuit.
Identifies holding the weights still as a deliberate simplification rather than a finding about small nervous systems.
Hands the changing of weights to Module 5.

pools.title: The Tissue, the Map, and One Behavior Traced
pools.covers: reading §4.3.1, §4.3.2, §4.3.3 · lecture 4.3 slides the_tissue_that_runs_it, the_worm_whose_map_is_complete, tracing_one_behavior, two_ways_to_steer

items.stem: What does the implementational question ask?

options.text: What physically does the work, and what the doing costs.
options.why: Correct. The chapter's first section gave the capability and the second drew the arrangements; this one supplies the tissue.

options.text: What information is represented, and by what procedure it is transformed into an action.
options.why: That is the algorithmic question, which the chapter's second section asked.

options.text: What problem is being solved, and why solving it was worth what it cost.
options.why: That is the computational question. The word cost appears in both, which is why the first half has to be read.

options.text: Which cells an animal has, and how many of each kind it needs to behave normally.
options.why: An inventory of cell types is not what the question asks, and the chapter's answer is about arrangement as much as parts.

items.stem: What is a nerve ring?

options.text: A band of nerve net running around the body, thicker than the net around it.
options.why: Correct. It is one of the places where a net thickens rather than a structure of a different kind.

options.text: A ring of neurons surrounding the mouth, which coordinates the tentacles that carry stinging cells.
options.why: Coordinating tentacles is what a cnidarian's net does, and the term picks out a thickening rather than a mouth structure.

options.text: A loop of connections that carries activity round and round, so that a state can outlast its cause.
options.why: A loop that sustains activity is a recurrent circuit, which is a wiring pattern rather than a piece of tissue.

options.text: A band of muscle around the body wall, driven by the net that lies beneath it.
options.why: The term names nerve tissue rather than muscle.

items.stem: What is a ganglion?

options.text: A cluster of neuron cell bodies concentrated in one spot — a center without being a brain.
options.why: Correct. It is somewhere a great many connections happen to be, and so somewhere a great deal of processing happens to get done.

options.text: A small brain found in animals too simple to have a large one, which runs the whole of their behavior.
options.why: The word sounds grander than the thing; the chapter is careful that a ganglion is not a brain.

options.text: A bundle of axons running together from one part of the body to another, without their cell bodies.
options.why: A bundle of fibers is a different object; a ganglion is where the cell bodies are gathered.

options.text: A thickening of the nerve net into a band that runs right around the body.
options.why: That is a nerve ring, which is a further step along the same progression.

items.stem: Which term names the concentration of neurons at the front of an animal?

options.text: cephalization
options.why: Correct. It is the physical answer to a question that sounds childish and is not: why is the brain in a head?

options.text: connectome, the complete wiring diagram
options.why: A connectome is a complete wiring diagram rather than an arrangement of tissue in the body.

options.text: nerve ring
options.why: A nerve ring is a thickening that runs around the body rather than a gathering toward one end.

options.text: divergence
options.why: Divergence is a wiring pattern, one cell projecting onto many, and says nothing about where cells sit.

items.stem: Why do the largest ganglia end up at the front in bilaterians?

options.text: An animal that moves in one direction has an end that arrives first, and both the sensing and the deciding are more efficiently done at that end.
options.why: Correct. It is the same argument the chapter made about a front at the computational level, now cashed out in tissue.

options.text: The front is where the mouth is, so the tissue that controls feeding has to be close to what it operates.
options.why: Feeding is not the reason given, and the argument turns on which end meets the world first.

options.text: The front is the most protected part of a moving animal, so the tissue most costly to replace is kept there.
options.why: Protection is not discussed, and a leading end is if anything more exposed.

options.text: Ganglia form wherever the nerve net is thickest, and the net turns out to be thickest at the front in every animal that has one at all.
options.why: Thickening is how a ganglion arises rather than an explanation of where the largest ones end up.

items.stem: Why does a jellyfish cut in half leave two halves that both keep pulsing?

options.text: A nerve net has neurons spread through the body wall with nothing at the center, so there is no center to remove.
options.why: Correct. It is the tissue-level version of the point that having a nervous system is not the same as having a brain.

options.text: Each half retains a nerve ring, and a ring is enough on its own to time the contraction of the bell.
options.why: Nerve rings are thickenings found in some animals, and the reason given here is the absence of any center at all.

options.text: The muscle of the bell contracts on its own once the inhibition from the net is removed.
options.why: Nothing in the account has the net inhibiting the bell, and the halves go on pulsing rather than contracting continuously.

options.text: Cnidarian nerve nets regenerate quickly, so each of the halves rebuilds whatever connections it has lost within a few minutes.
options.why: Regeneration is not described, and the halves keep pulsing immediately.

items.stem: Along the progression from a plain net to a cephalized animal, what is added?

options.text: Nothing is added: neurons are only gathered into fewer places, so it is the same nervous system, concentrated.
options.why: Correct. The progression is about arrangement rather than about acquiring new machinery.

options.text: A layer of interneurons is added between the sensory and motor cells, which is what makes processing possible.
options.why: Interneurons appear in the worm's circuit, and they are not what the progression from net to ganglion adds.

options.text: A central controller is added, which is what allows one part of the animal to issue orders to the rest.
options.why: A ganglion is explicitly described as a center without being a brain, and nothing issues orders.

options.text: Faster connections are added between the gathered cells, which is why concentrating them is worth doing.
options.why: Conduction speed is not what changes; the efficiency argument is about where sensing and deciding happen.

items.stem: What is a connectome?

options.text: A complete wiring diagram of a nervous system: every cell, and every connection between them.
options.why: Correct. The worm's was the first of any animal to be produced in full, and for a long time the only one.

options.text: A map of which regions of a nervous system are active during a given behavior.
options.why: Activity during behavior is a different kind of map, and a connectome records connections rather than activity.

options.text: A catalog of every kind of neuron an animal has, with the function of each one of them recorded carefully beside it.
options.why: A catalog of cell types omits the connections, which is what the map is chiefly for.

options.text: A complete record of the chemicals a nervous system uses and which cells release each of them.
options.why: Chemistry is exactly what a connectome does not tell us, as the chapter goes on to argue at length.

items.stem: How was the worm's connectome produced, and on what scale?

options.text: By hand, from thousands of electron micrographs of serial slices, covering all 302 neurons of the adult hermaphrodite and the several thousand connections between them.
options.why: Correct. The map took over a decade to produce, for 302 cells.

options.text: Automatically, by tracing fluorescent markers through the living animal while it moved and behaved normally.
options.why: Live imaging is not how the map was made, and the reconstruction was done on slices rather than on a moving animal.

options.text: By recording from every neuron in turn and noting which others responded, which is how every one of the connections in the map was originally inferred.
options.why: Connections were reconstructed anatomically rather than inferred from activity.

options.text: By comparing the genomes of individual worms, since the same 302 neurons appear in every one of them.
options.why: Invariance of the cell count is a fact about the animal rather than a method for mapping it.

items.stem: What lesson does the chapter draw from how long the worm's map took?

options.text: A wiring diagram cannot simply be read off an animal; it has to be built, slice by slice.
options.why: Correct. Over a decade, for 302 cells, is the ratio that forces the point.

options.text: A wiring diagram is only worth building for animals small enough to finish, which is why the worm was chosen.
options.why: Why the worm was chosen is not argued from the difficulty, and larger connectomes have since been attempted.

options.text: A wiring diagram becomes obsolete before it is finished, since the animal's connections change while it is being mapped.
options.why: Nothing about the map going out of date is claimed.

options.text: A wiring diagram is the most informative thing that can be produced about a nervous system, which is why the effort was worth it.
options.why: The chapter argues at length that a connectome leaves a great deal out.

items.stem: How does the chapter describe connectome work beyond the worm?

options.text: It has been done for a fly and is under way in pieces for a mouse and for human tissue, the human work covering small volumes rather than whole brains.
options.why: Correct. Those maps are enormously larger, and the hedges are part of the claim rather than decoration on it.

options.text: It has been completed for a fly and for a mouse, and a complete human connectome of the same kind is expected within the next few years.
options.why: No completion for a mouse is claimed and no timetable is offered for anything.

options.text: It has been abandoned for larger animals, since the worm showed that the approach does not scale.
options.why: Work is described as under way rather than abandoned.

options.text: It has been automated since the worm, so larger maps now take less time than the worm's did.
options.why: Nothing about automation or about maps getting faster appears in the chapter.

items.stem: What are the three layers of the worm's chemotaxis circuit?

options.text: Sensory neurons in the head responding to chemicals in the water, interneurons receiving from several of them at once, and motor neurons driving the body-wall muscles.
options.why: Correct. Sense, combine, act, accomplished in three or four cells.

options.text: Sensory neurons along the body wall, a nerve ring that times the response, and motor neurons at the head.
options.why: The sensory neurons are in the head, and no ring times the response.

options.text: Sensory neurons in the head, a ganglion that stores whatever has been sensed, and then motor neurons that drive the muscles of the body wall directly.
options.why: Nothing in the circuit stores anything, and the middle layer weighs what arrives rather than recording it.

options.text: Sensory neurons on each side of the head, interneurons comparing the two sides, and motor neurons that turn the body.
options.why: Comparing the two sides is exactly what the worm's chemosensory wiring does not do.

items.stem: What are the worm's interneurons doing, in the terms the chapter has already built?

options.text: Receiving from several sources, weighing what arrives, and producing a verdict.
options.why: Correct. The section is cashing in the algorithmic account rather than restating it.

options.text: Holding the verdict reached a moment ago, so that the current input can be compared against it.
options.why: Something must hold a trace for the comparison across time, and that is not what the interneurons are credited with here.

options.text: Amplifying the difference between the strongest and the weakest input, so a near-tie becomes a clear one.
options.why: Sharpening is a separate motif, and the interneurons are described as weighing and producing a verdict.

options.text: Distributing a single verdict to muscles along the whole body, so the animal acts as one.
options.why: That is divergence, and it is the motor layer's part of the arrangement rather than the interneurons'.

items.stem: How does a worm climb toward food?

options.text: Its head sweeps side to side and it works with now against a moment ago: a rising concentration triggers no turn, a falling one makes it turn more often, roughly at random.
options.why: Correct. The intuitive picture — that the worm senses where the food is and points itself at it — is precisely what it cannot do.

options.text: It compares the concentration at the left and the right of its head as it swims, and then turns toward whichever of the two sides happens to read the higher of the two.
options.why: A millimeter of body width does not buy enough difference for that comparison, and its chemosensory cells are not wired for it.

options.text: It swims in an expanding spiral until the concentration stops rising, then reverses and repeats from the new position.
options.why: No search pattern of that kind is described; turning is triggered by a falling concentration.

options.text: It holds a memory of where the food was when it last detected it, and returns to that heading whenever the signal is lost.
options.why: Nothing is remembered about location, and steering here requires no knowledge of where the target is.

items.stem: The chapter says something strange about the worm going straight. What?

options.text: Going straight is not a behavior the worm produces; it is what happens when the rule for turning is not met.
options.why: Correct. Which is why steering here needs only a comparison across time and a rule about when to turn.

options.text: Going straight is the worm's default, which it returns to whenever no chemical is detected at all.
options.why: The absence of a cue is not what produces straight movement; an unmet turning rule is.

options.text: Going straight costs the worm more energy than turning, which is why it turns whenever conditions allow.
options.why: No energy comparison between the two is offered.

options.text: Going straight is produced by both sides of the body being equally active, which is the only case in which the animal is balanced.
options.why: Left-right balance is not what the account rests on, since the worm is not comparing its two sides.

items.stem: How do a Braitenberg vehicle and a worm differ in what they compare?

options.text: The vehicle compares two places at one instant, with its body's geometry delivering the answer; each side of the worm compares two moments at one place, now against a moment ago.
options.why: Correct. The vehicle is told which way the light is, and the worm is not — a millimeter of body does not buy a usable left-right difference.

options.text: The vehicle compares two moments at one place, while the worm compares two places at one instant using the pair of sensors it carries on either side of its head.
options.why: This inverts both halves, and it is the single easiest thing in the section to get backwards.

options.text: The vehicle compares light against darkness, while the worm compares one chemical against another arriving at the same moment.
options.why: The worm does weigh two chemicals elsewhere, and the contrast drawn here is between places and moments.

options.text: The vehicle compares its own speed against the light level, while the worm compares its rate of turning against the concentration.
options.why: Neither machine compares anything to its own movement in the account given.

items.stem: What do the worm and the Braitenberg vehicle genuinely share?

options.text: In both, which route a signal feeds is what makes that signal good news or bad news.
options.why: Correct. It is the labeled line from the algorithmic section showing up in two very different machines, one of which is not an animal.

options.text: In both, the body's geometry delivers the direction, so the arrangement of the sensors settles which way the machine turns.
options.why: Geometry delivers the answer for the vehicle only; the worm has no usable width to work with.

options.text: In both, a comparison across time is what produces the turn, with the present sample set against an earlier one.
options.why: The comparison across time is the worm's method alone.

options.text: In both, a single sensor drives a single motor, so nothing has to be combined before the action is produced.
options.why: The worm's interneurons receive from several sensory cells at once and combine what arrives.

items.stem: In tissue, what settles whether the worm crosses a strip of copper to reach food?

options.text: Copper drives avoidance and food odor approach through separate sensory cells, both converging on interneurons that produce one verdict; the worm crosses when the attractant wins.
options.why: Correct. The trade-off described at the computational level is, in tissue, a small number of cells receiving from both routes at once.

options.text: The copper-sensing cells are inhibited directly by the food-sensing cells, so a strong enough attractant silences the avoidance route entirely before the worm ever crosses.
options.why: The two routes converge on shared interneurons rather than one suppressing the other at its source.

options.text: The worm samples the copper first and then the food, acting on whichever verdict it reached most recently.
options.why: No sequence of that kind is described; the two converge and are settled together.

options.text: A ganglion in the head holds a record of previous crossings and decides on the basis of how the last one went.
options.why: Nothing is recorded, and the verdict is produced from what is arriving now.

items.stem: The worm's case strips steering down to its minimum. What is left, once everything unnecessary has gone?

options.text: A comparison across time and a rule about when to turn, with no knowledge of where the target is and no attempt to go anywhere in particular.
options.why: Correct. And the whole thing runs in an animal with fewer neurons than that sentence has letters.

options.text: A separate rule for each chemical, since the turning rule can only ever take one chemical into account at a time.
options.why: The same three layers settle the copper case, where two routes are weighed against each other.

options.text: A front end carrying the sensors, though a comparison across time of that kind would work equally well anywhere along the body.
options.why: The sensory neurons are in the head, and the chapter's argument about fronts is not withdrawn here.

options.text: A single cell making the comparison, since one cell can compare two moments as well as three or four can.
options.why: A single cell comparing two moments was the previous module's bacterium, and this circuit is three or four cells.

items.stem: Set the Braitenberg vehicle beside the worm. Say what the two share, how they differ, and why the worm cannot use the vehicle's method.
items.answer: A vehicle carries two light sensors, one on each side, each wired to a motor; whichever sensor receives more light drives its motor harder and the body swings, and whether it swings toward the light or away depends on nothing more than whether each sensor feeds the motor on its own side or the one across from it. What the two genuinely share is that which route a signal feeds is what makes that signal good news or bad news. They differ in what is compared: the vehicle compares two places at one instant, with its body's geometry delivering the answer, while each side of the worm compares two moments at one place, now against a moment ago. The worm cannot use the vehicle's method because it is a millimeter long, so the difference in concentration between one side of its head and the other is very small, and its chemosensory neurons are not wired to compare left against right.
rubric: Describes the vehicle's two sensors and the crossed-or-uncrossed wiring.
States what they share: the route a signal feeds decides whether it is good or bad news.
Gets the contrast the right way round — the vehicle compares places, the worm compares moments.
Explains the worm's constraint from its size and from how its chemosensory cells are wired.

items.stem: Trace the tissue from a plain nerve net to a cephalized animal, defining each step, and say what changes along the way.
items.answer: A nerve net is neurons spread through the body wall, each connected to its neighbors, with nothing at the center. A net is not perfectly even, and where it thickens into a band running around the body it is a nerve ring. Where cell bodies gather into a cluster concentrated in one spot, that is a ganglion — a center without being a brain, in the sense that it is somewhere a great many connections happen to be and therefore somewhere a great deal of processing happens to get done. In bilaterians the largest ganglia end up at the front with the sensors, because an animal that moves in one direction has an end that arrives first and both the sensing and the deciding are more efficiently done there; that concentration is cephalization. Nothing is added along the progression: the neurons are only gathered into fewer places.
rubric: Defines the nerve net as spread through the body wall with nothing at the center.
Defines a nerve ring as a thickened band running around the body.
Defines a ganglion as a cluster of cell bodies, and notes it is a center without being a brain.
Names cephalization and gives the efficiency reason for the front.
States that nothing is added — the neurons are only gathered.

items.stem: The lecture says it wants to be careful about one of its terms because the word sounds grander than the thing. Which term, and what is the caution?

options.text: Ganglion — it is a center without being a brain, somewhere a great many connections happen to be and therefore where a great deal of processing happens to get done.
options.why: Correct. The looser reading would make every animal with a ganglion an animal with a brain.

options.text: Connectome — it is a map of connections rather than an explanation of behavior, and having one of them settles a good deal less than the word makes it sound.
options.why: That caution is made elsewhere in the meeting, and it is not the one attached to a word sounding grander than the thing.

options.text: Cephalization — it names where neurons sit rather than any increase in what they can do.
options.why: That point is made with the figure's caption rather than as a caution about the word itself.

options.text: Nerve ring — it is a thickening of a net rather than a structure built separately from it.
options.why: The ring is described plainly rather than as a term liable to be over-read.

items.stem: The lecture deliberately sets up a wrong answer before taking it away. What is the wrong answer?

options.text: That the worm senses where the food is and points itself at it — the intuitive picture, which the animal cannot in fact do.
options.why: Correct. Feeling the wrong answer being removed is what makes the actual mechanism land.

options.text: That the worm turns at random until it happens to find food, with no comparison involved at all.
options.why: Random turning is half of the real mechanism rather than the picture being dismantled.

options.text: That the worm's interneurons store what it has sensed, so that its route can be planned in advance.
options.why: Planning from a stored map is the robotics tradition discussed in an earlier meeting.

options.text: That the worm needs many more than three or four cells to steer, since steering had been presented up to that point as a demanding thing to do.
options.why: The small cell count is offered as a finding rather than as an error to be corrected.

items.stem: The lecture asks the room to sit with a particular ratio. What is it, and what does it force?

options.text: Over a decade of work, for 302 cells — which forces the lesson that a wiring diagram has to be built slice by slice rather than read off an animal.
options.why: Correct. The enterprise has moved on since, but the human work covers small volumes rather than whole brains.

options.text: Several thousand connections among 302 neurons — which forces the point that even a small nervous system is densely wired.
options.why: Density is real and it is not the ratio the lecture stops on.

options.text: One millimeter of animal against thousands of micrographs — which forces the point that the slices have to be very thin.
options.why: Slice thickness is not what the lecture asks the room to dwell on.

options.text: 302 cells against the three behaviors left unexplained — which forces the point that very few cells can go on to produce a great deal of behavior.
options.why: That point is made elsewhere in the meeting, and the ratio named here is about the cost of the map.

items.stem: The lecture says one thing on this slide is what the vehicle and the worm genuinely share, and connects it to an earlier meeting. What is it?

options.text: That which route a signal feeds is what makes it good news or bad news — the labeled line, showing up in two very different machines, one of which is not an animal.
options.why: Correct. Everything else on the slide is a difference rather than a shared feature.

options.text: That both use two sensors placed apart on the body, which is what any steering arrangement requires.
options.why: The worm's method does not use its two sides at all, which is the slide's main contrast.

options.text: That both produce a turn whose size is proportional to the difference detected, which is what makes the steering of both of them come out smooth.
options.why: Proportional turning is not attributed to the worm, whose turns are roughly at random when conditions worsen.

options.text: That both were built by the students in a previous lab, which is why the comparison can be made carefully.
options.why: The vehicle was built in the lab; the worm was not.

items.stem: What makes the worm worth the attention the chapter gives it?

options.text: Its wiring is complete — every neuron and connection reconstructed — and it was the first nervous system of any animal mapped whole.
options.why: Correct. Which is what lets one behavior be traced end to end.

options.text: It is the smallest animal that has a nervous system at all, so there is nothing simpler available to be studied.
options.why: No claim that it is the smallest is made anywhere.

options.text: Its neurons are unusually large, which is what made the reconstruction possible at all.
options.why: Cell size is not what the chapter credits; the reconstruction was done from serial slices.

options.text: It is the only animal whose behavior can be predicted from its wiring alone.
options.why: Its behavior explicitly cannot be predicted from its wiring, which is the chapter's next point.

items.stem: What is connectomics?

options.text: The attempt to produce complete wiring diagrams of nervous systems.
options.why: Correct. It has been done for a fly, and is under way in pieces for a mouse and for human tissue.

options.text: The study of how the connections in a nervous system change as an animal learns.
options.why: Changing connections belong to a later module, and the enterprise here maps them as they are.

options.text: The comparison of wiring diagrams across species to establish how nervous systems are related.
options.why: Comparison is something a set of maps makes possible rather than what the enterprise is defined as.

options.text: The reconstruction of a nervous system's activity from recordings made while an animal behaves.
options.why: Activity is a different kind of map; this one records connections.

pools.title: The Two Ends of the Circuit, and the Molecules That Modulate It
pools.covers: reading §4.3.4, §4.3.5, §4.3.6 · lecture 4.3 slides the_two_ends_of_the_circuit, what_a_connectome_does_not_tell_us, four_molecules, directions_not_locations

items.stem: What is transduction?

options.text: Converting an event in the world into a change in membrane voltage, which is the one thing a sensory neuron does that no other neuron does.
options.why: Correct. Once the channel has opened, touch and smell are the same, and the cell behaves like any other neuron from there.

options.text: Converting a change in membrane voltage into a train of action potentials that can travel the whole length of an axon without weakening.
options.why: Turning a voltage into a signal that travels is what any neuron does rather than the sensory cell's distinctive job.

options.text: Converting a chemical signal arriving at a synapse into an electrical change in the receiving cell.
options.why: That is ordinary synaptic transmission, which every neuron on the receiving end performs.

options.text: Converting a verdict inside the nervous system into a force that moves the body.
options.why: That happens at the far end of the circuit, where the verdict stops being a voltage and becomes a force.

items.stem: How do touch and smell differ at the sensory end, and where do they converge?

options.text: A touch pulls a channel open mechanically; an odor binds a receptor and a short chain of steps opens one a moment later. After that both are the same: ions cross and the voltage moves.
options.why: Correct. Different keys and different locks, converging immediately afterward.

options.text: A touch opens a channel by binding a receptor while an odor molecule pulls one open mechanically; after that, both of them go on to produce an action potential of exactly the same size.
options.why: The two mechanisms are the other way round, and what follows is a voltage change rather than a guaranteed spike.

options.text: A touch is transduced in the skin and an odor in the head, so the two converge only once their signals reach the interneurons.
options.why: Convergence happens inside the sensory cell itself, as soon as the channel opens.

options.text: A touch produces a graded signal and an odor an all-or-none one, which is why the two are handled by different kinds of neuron.
options.why: Neither is tied to one kind of signaling, and the worm's cells are largely graded whatever the sense.

items.stem: What does the chapter correct about what the previous module said, and how is the correction scoped?

options.text: In C. elegans and a number of other small invertebrates, output is mostly not all-or-nothing: the worm has no voltage-gated sodium channels and signals largely in graded voltage.
options.why: Correct. The scope matters — jellyfish do have those channels and fire ordinary sodium spikes.

options.text: In invertebrates generally, neurons turn out not to fire all-or-none spikes at all, so the previous module's account of signaling turns out to hold only for the vertebrates among them.
options.why: Jellyfish are invertebrates and do fire sodium spikes, so the correction cannot be drawn that broadly.

options.text: In every animal, the all-or-nothing description was an approximation, since all real signals are graded to some degree.
options.why: The chapter keeps all-or-none signaling as real, and corrects a claim about one lineage rather than about neurons everywhere.

options.text: In C. elegans, spikes occur but are carried by calcium rather than sodium, so the signal is all-or-none with a different ion.
options.why: One smell neuron has a calcium-based spike, and most of the worm's neurons are graded rather than spiking.

items.stem: What rescues the broader point about thresholds despite the correction?

options.text: A threshold is a claim about a function — below some level nothing happens and above it something does — and an all-or-none spike is only one way to build one.
options.why: Correct. A graded signal that stays too small to release any transmitter until the input is large enough builds exactly the same thing.

options.text: A threshold can be restored by treating the peak of a graded signal as a spike, so the two claims made about thresholds turn out to be equivalent after all.
options.why: Redescribing a graded swing as a spike is not the move; the functional claim survives without it.

options.text: A threshold is supplied downstream by the muscle, which contracts only once the voltage reaching it is large enough.
options.why: The threshold in question belongs to the signaling cell rather than to the muscle at the end of the chain.

options.text: A threshold is not needed for the arrangements built at the algorithmic level, since a graded unit can compute the same functions.
options.why: The chapter keeps the thresholds intact rather than declaring them unnecessary.

items.stem: Which hedges does the chapter attach to the graded-signaling claim?

options.text: Jellyfish do fire sodium spikes, one worm smell neuron has a calcium-based spike, and graded signaling still fades with distance — which matters less in a very small animal.
options.why: Correct. It may be that there was not evolutionary pressure to pay for perfectly discrete signals in a creature that size.

options.text: Graded signaling is found only in the worm, its disadvantages disappear entirely at small scales, and no spikes of any kind at all are ever found anywhere among the nematodes.
options.why: One calcium-based spike has been found, the disadvantages still hold, and other small invertebrates share the pattern.

options.text: Graded signaling is an adaptation to life in soil, and it appears in any animal whose body is under a millimeter long.
options.why: No connection to habitat is drawn, and no size threshold of that kind is stated.

options.text: Graded signaling carries more information than spiking, which is why small animals were selected to adopt it.
options.why: The chapter treats it as a cost not worth paying rather than as a gain in information.

items.stem: What is a neuromuscular junction?

options.text: The junction where a motor neuron ends on a muscle cell, across which acetylcholine crosses and opens channels so the muscle depolarizes much as a neuron would.
options.why: Correct. What happens after that is what makes a muscle a muscle rather than another neuron.

options.text: The junction between two motor neurons, at which the verdict is passed along one last time before it finally reaches the muscle cell at the end of the chain.
options.why: Both sides of the junction named here are not neurons; one of them is muscle.

options.text: The point at which a sensory neuron converts a mechanical stimulus into a change in membrane voltage.
options.why: That is transduction, at the other end of the circuit entirely.

options.text: The band of tissue in which the worm's body-wall muscles are joined to one another along its length.
options.why: The junction is between nerve and muscle rather than between muscle cells.

items.stem: What happens in a muscle cell after it depolarizes, and how does the chapter describe the result?

options.text: Calcium floods in, filaments slide past one another and the fiber shortens, pulling on adjacent attached cells — the verdict stops being a voltage and becomes a force.
options.why: Correct. That sequence is what makes a muscle a muscle rather than another cell that depolarizes.

options.text: Sodium floods in and the muscle fires an action potential, which travels along the fiber and causes it to lengthen.
options.why: Calcium is what enters, and the fiber shortens rather than lengthening.

options.text: Acetylcholine is released from the muscle onto the next cell in the strip, so the contraction spreads along the length of the body from one cell to the next.
options.why: Acetylcholine crosses onto the muscle rather than being released by it.

options.text: The muscle holds its depolarization until the opposing muscle relaxes, so that the two never contract at once.
options.why: The alternation is produced by the motor neurons rather than by the muscle waiting.

items.stem: How is the worm's body-wall arrangement an instance of something already built at the algorithmic level?

options.text: Excitatory motor neurons release acetylcholine onto one side while inhibitory ones release GABA onto the other, so the body bends and the two swap — mutual inhibition in musculature.
options.why: Correct. The chapter cashes in the motif rather than introducing a new arrangement for the worm.

options.text: Several sensory neurons converge on a small number of interneurons, so the trade-off between two competing cues is settled in a single place — convergence, implemented in musculature.
options.why: Convergence is a real part of the worm's circuit, and it is not what the body-wall muscles instantiate.

options.text: The motor neurons excite one another around a loop so that the bending wave sustains itself — a recurrent circuit, implemented in musculature.
options.why: The wave is driven by alternation between opposed sides rather than by a self-sustaining loop in the muscle.

options.text: Each motor neuron inhibits its neighbors along the strip in proportion to its activity — lateral inhibition, implemented in musculature.
options.why: Inhibiting neighbors along a row sharpens a difference, which is a different motif and a different job.

items.stem: Which two sides of the worm does the alternating contraction oppose?

options.text: Its back and its belly — a worm lies on its side, so a bend that looks from above like a sweep left and right is really upward and downward.
options.why: Correct. This is the most repeated error in the chapter's drafting history, and the left-right appearance is an artifact of how the animal is watched.

options.text: Its left and its right, which is exactly why a bend viewed from above appears to sweep across from the one side of the animal to the other.
options.why: The left-right appearance is exactly what the chapter corrects; the opposed sides are back and belly.

options.text: Its head end and its tail end, with the wave of contraction passing between them as the animal moves.
options.why: The wave does travel head to tail, and the opposed pair being contracted and released is back against belly.

options.text: Its inner and its outer surface, since the muscles lie in strips wrapped around the body wall.
options.why: The muscles lie in strips along the animal's length rather than in concentric layers.

items.stem: Where is the worm's rule about when to turn?

options.text: Nowhere written down: it is which of two mutually inhibiting groups of interneurons — one driving the forward wave, one the backward — currently has the upper hand.
options.why: Correct. Turning is the same circuit motif one layer up from the muscles.

options.text: In a small ganglion at the head, which holds the rule and applies it whenever the sensory comparison comes out badly.
options.why: Nothing in the worm holds a rule; the outcome is which group of cells is winning.

options.text: In the sensory neurons themselves, which fire only when the concentration is falling and so trigger a turn directly.
options.why: The sensory cells report concentration, and the turn is settled by the contest between the two interneuron groups.

options.text: In the strength of the connections onto the muscles, which are set so that a turn follows automatically whenever the input arriving is a weak one.
options.why: Connection strengths are fixed and do not encode a rule of that kind.

items.stem: What limitation of connectomes does the chapter identify?

options.text: The worm's wiring has been completely known for decades, and its behavior still cannot be predicted from that wiring.
options.why: Correct. That limit is the reason the chapter does not finish at the end of a wiring diagram.

options.text: The worm's wiring is known only for the adult hermaphrodite form, so the behavior of any other form cannot be predicted from what has been mapped.
options.why: No restriction by form is offered as the limitation, and the problem holds for the animal that was mapped.

options.text: The worm's wiring changes over the course of its lifetime, so a map built from one animal will not describe a second one accurately.
options.why: The chapter's point depends on the connections not changing, which is what makes something else the variable.

options.text: The worm's wiring is far too dense to trace by eye, so any prediction from it is limited by how accurately the map was reconstructed.
options.why: Accuracy of the map is not what the limitation rests on.

items.stem: What is the evidence that the diagram is not the whole machine?

options.text: A worm that has just eaten and one that has gone hungry for hours respond to the same molecule in opposite ways, with the same 302 neurons wired the same way.
options.why: Correct. Since the connections are not what is changing, something else must be varying.

options.text: A worm's response to the same molecule weakens with repeated exposure, which shows the connections are being adjusted.
options.why: Adjusted connections would make the diagram out of date rather than incomplete, and that is a different module's subject.

options.text: Two worms of the same age respond differently to the same molecule, which shows that no two connectomes are alike.
options.why: The chapter's case is about the same animal at two times rather than two different animals.

options.text: A worm with part of its nervous system removed still behaves normally, which shows that the map records a good deal more than the animal actually needs.
options.why: No lesion evidence is offered anywhere in the chapter.

items.stem: What is a neuromodulator?

options.text: A chemical released into the surrounding tissue rather than a single synapse, reaching many cells at once and acting over seconds to minutes.
options.why: Correct. The category is defined by how the chemical is released and what it does rather than by what molecule it is.

options.text: A chemical released into a single synapse that makes the receiving cell more or less likely to fire.
options.why: Release into one synapse is what a neurotransmitter does, and it carries a message rather than changing how others are handled.

options.text: A chemical that carries a message to many cells at once, so that a verdict can reach the whole body quickly.
options.why: Reaching many cells is right, and carrying a message is exactly what the chapter denies of it.

options.text: A chemical that changes the strength of a connection permanently, so that the circuit goes on computing something new from that point onward.
options.why: A lasting change in a connection is a different thing entirely and belongs to a later module.

items.stem: What separates a neuromodulator from a neurotransmitter, in this chapter's terms?

options.text: A neuromodulator does not carry a message; it changes what the cells receiving it do with the messages they are already getting.
options.why: Correct. It turns a neuron's sensitivity up or down, temporarily making one pathway easier and another harder.

options.text: A neuromodulator is a different class of molecule, built for slow signaling rather than fast.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter says they are a different class of molecule; the category is about release and effect.

options.text: A neuromodulator acts on muscle rather than on neurons, which is why its effects appear as changes in behavior.
options.why: Neuromodulators act on the cells of the circuit, changing what those cells do with their inputs.

options.text: A neuromodulator is released by the body rather than by the nervous system, which is part of why it manages to reach so very many cells at once.
options.why: Where it is released into — tissue rather than one synapse — is the point, not which system produces it.

items.stem: What follows from neuromodulation for the relationship between a wiring diagram and a circuit?

options.text: One wiring map can behave as several circuits depending on what chemicals are nearby; the worm's connections do not change when it gets hungry, but the chemistry does.
options.why: Correct. Which is why a complete map still leaves the animal's behavior unpredicted.

options.text: One wiring map describes several animals at once, since it is the chemistry rather than the connections that distinguishes any one individual animal from another.
options.why: The chapter's case concerns one animal at two times rather than differences between individuals.

options.text: One wiring diagram becomes several as an animal develops, since new connections are added when its needs change.
options.why: Connections are explicitly said not to change; that is what makes chemistry the variable.

options.text: One wiring map is enough to predict behavior provided that the animal's internal state has also been recorded as part of it.
options.why: The chapter stops short of that, and treats the diagram as not being the whole machine.

items.stem: How does neuromodulation relate to the trade the previous module described?

options.text: The old way did not go away: the body still uses chemical signaling, and that signaling can affect the firing of neurons.
options.why: Correct. A neuron gave up the cheap, everywhere-at-once reach of chemistry, and the reach survives alongside it.

options.text: The trade was reversed, since neuromodulation shows that chemical signaling turned out to be faster than neural signaling after all.
options.why: Neuromodulation acts over seconds to minutes, which is slower rather than faster.

options.text: The trade applies only within a circuit, since between circuits the animal still relies entirely on diffusion.
options.why: No such division of labor between within and between circuits is drawn.

options.text: The trade was completed, since neuromodulators are how the nervous system finally replaced chemical signaling altogether.
options.why: The point is the opposite: chemical signaling persists and does work neurons cannot.

items.stem: How does the chapter frame the four neuromodulators?

options.text: Not as four unrelated chemicals but as four ways of moving an animal around the two-dimensional affective space built earlier.
options.why: Correct. That framing is why the direction each one moves an animal is worth tabulating at all.

options.text: As four stages in a sequence, with each of them taking over from the last as an animal's state changes over a stretch of time.
options.why: No sequence among them is described; each is a direction rather than a stage.

options.text: As four molecules that between them carry every message a nervous system needs to send slowly.
options.why: A neuromodulator carries no message, which is what distinguishes it from a transmitter.

options.text: As four chemicals each dedicated to one of the four demands steering makes of a nervous system.
options.why: The four molecules are not matched one to one against the four demands.

items.stem: What is the contrast the chapter draws between dopamine and the endorphins?

options.text: Dopamine drives pursuit — wanting a thing and going after it — while endorphins and the other opioids carry relief and satisfaction: liking rather than wanting.
options.why: Correct. Which is precisely why the two can come apart, and treating dopamine as the chemistry of enjoyment is a common misperception.

options.text: Dopamine carries enjoyment once a thing arrives, while endorphins sustain the effort of going after it in the first place.
options.why: That reverses the pair, and the first half is the misperception the chapter names explicitly.

options.text: Dopamine raises arousal while endorphins raise it further, so the two work together to keep an animal pursuing something.
options.why: Endorphins lower arousal, and the contrast drawn is about wanting against liking.

options.text: Dopamine acts in vertebrates and endorphins throughout the animal kingdom, which is part of why only one of the two of them turns out to appear in the worm at all.
options.why: No such split is drawn, and the scoping the chapter does make concerns a different molecule.

items.stem: What does serotonin do, and what is the worm evidence for it?

options.text: It tracks satiety and the overall tone of the system: a hungry worm that finds bacteria to eat slows almost to a stop, and that slowing depends on serotonin.
options.why: Correct. It is one of the places where the chapter's chemistry is tied to a specific worm behavior.

options.text: It sets vigilance: a worm exposed to a threatening stimulus becomes a good deal more responsive to everything around it, and that heightening depends on serotonin.
options.why: Vigilance is what norepinephrine is credited with, and the chapter scopes that claim to vertebrates.

options.text: It drives pursuit: a hungry worm speeds up when it detects food odor, and that speeding depends on serotonin.
options.why: Pursuit is dopamine's role, and the worm's serotonin-dependent response to finding food is to slow down.

options.text: It carries relief: a worm that has escaped a noxious substance settles, and that settling depends on serotonin.
options.why: Relief and satisfaction are what the opioids carry, and the worm evidence concerns feeding rather than escape.

items.stem: What does norepinephrine do, and how does the chapter scope the claim?

options.text: It sets arousal and vigilance — the dial for how strongly an animal reacts to anything at all — and the claim is scoped to vertebrates.
options.why: Correct. That scoping matters later, when the chapter turns to which molecules are conserved in the worm.

options.text: It sets arousal and vigilance in every animal with a nervous system, a claim which is part of why it appears in the worm as well as in ourselves.
options.why: The claim is made for vertebrates, and what the worm does with it is taken up separately.

options.text: It signals satiety and lowers arousal toward contentment, which is why it is a common target of medication.
options.why: Those are serotonin's entries rather than norepinephrine's.

options.text: It drives the effort spent pursuing something, which is why arousal and motivation rise together.
options.why: Pursuit belongs to dopamine, and norepinephrine raises arousal at either valence.

items.stem: Where does dopamine move an animal on the valence–arousal space?

options.text: It raises arousal, and raises expected valence rather than current valence.
options.why: Correct. The word expected is the whole content of the claim, and it is what keeps dopamine on the wanting side of the contrast.

options.text: It raises arousal and raises current valence, which is why pursuing something feels good while it is happening.
options.why: Current valence is what the claim carefully avoids, and raising it would collapse wanting into liking.

options.text: It lowers arousal and raises valence, settling an animal once the thing it wanted has been obtained.
options.why: That direction belongs to the endorphins rather than to dopamine.

options.text: It raises arousal at either valence, which is why it accompanies both pursuit and alarm.
options.why: Raising arousal at either valence is norepinephrine's direction.

items.stem: The chapter gives one instruction about how to read where each modulator moves an animal. What is it?

options.text: Read it as a direction of travel rather than a location: a modulator shifts an animal's state, and where it ends up depends on where it started.
options.why: Correct. The same chemical arriving at a quiet animal and an already agitated one does not produce the same state.

options.text: Read it as the state an animal reaches when the chemical is at its highest concentration, which works out the same way for every animal that receives it.
options.why: Treating it as a destination is exactly what the instruction warns against.

options.text: Read it as the average position of animals with that chemical present, since individuals vary a good deal around it.
options.why: No claim about averages or individual variation is made.

options.text: Read it as the state the chemical prevents rather than the one it produces, since each modulator works by suppression.
options.why: Nothing describes the modulators as working by suppression of a state.

items.stem: The chapter corrects something the previous module taught. State the correction with its scope and its hedges, and explain what survives it.
items.answer: The correction is that a neuron's output is not always all-or-nothing. The C. elegans genome contains no voltage-gated sodium channels at all, and most of the worm's neurons signal with graded changes in voltage, a larger input producing a larger swing continuously. The scope is C. elegans and a number of other small invertebrates, not invertebrates in general: jellyfish do have those channels and fire ordinary sodium spikes, and one of the worm's smell neurons has a calcium-based spike, so the picture is not uniform. What survives is the threshold. A threshold is a claim about a function — below some level of input nothing happens and above it something does — and an all-or-none spike is only one way of building one; a graded signal that stays too small to release any transmitter until the input is large enough builds exactly the same thing.
rubric: States that the worm has no voltage-gated sodium channels and signals largely in graded voltage changes.
Scopes the claim to this animal and other small invertebrates rather than to invertebrates generally.
Keeps at least one of the chapter's hedges — the jellyfish, or the one calcium-spiking smell neuron.
Explains that a threshold is a functional claim, so it survives the correction.

items.stem: Explain why a complete connectome still leaves the worm's behavior unpredicted, and what fills the gap.
items.answer: The worm's wiring has been completely known for decades and its behavior still cannot be predicted from that wiring: give the same animal the same input twice and it may do different things, and a worm that has just eaten and one that has gone hungry for hours will respond to the same molecule in opposite ways with the same 302 neurons wired the same way. Since the connections are not what is changing, the diagram is not the whole machine. What fills the gap is neuromodulation. A neuromodulator is a chemical released into the surrounding tissue rather than into a single synapse, so it reaches many cells at once and acts over seconds to minutes. It does not carry a message; it changes what the cells receiving it do with the messages they are already getting, turning sensitivity up or down. So one wiring diagram can behave as several different circuits depending on what chemicals are nearby.
rubric: States that the wiring is fully known and behavior is still unpredictable from it.
Gives the fed-versus-hungry case with the connections held constant.
Defines a neuromodulator by its release into tissue, its reach, and its timescale.
States that it carries no message but changes what cells do with the messages they get.

items.stem: The lecture makes a point of how it handles the correction to the earlier module. What does it say about that?

options.text: That it would rather correct it out loud than let students find the discrepancy later.
options.why: Correct. The correction is delivered as a correction rather than folded quietly into the new material.

options.text: That the earlier claim was a deliberate simplification, flagged at the time as something to be revised here.
options.why: Nothing is described as having been flagged in advance; the correction arrives as news.

options.text: That the earlier claim remains true for teaching purposes, so students should keep using it until a later module.
options.why: The lecture treats the correction as real rather than as something to be set aside.

options.text: That the discrepancy is a disagreement among researchers rather than a settled correction to the earlier account.
options.why: The worm's lack of voltage-gated sodium channels is presented as established rather than disputed.

items.stem: The lecture frames neuromodulation as a move in an argument begun in the previous module. What is the move?

options.text: That the old way did not go away: chemical signaling was slow, unaimed and unswitchable, and animals built neurons instead — and the chemistry persists alongside them.
options.why: Correct. Which is why a complete wiring diagram still leaves the behavior unpredicted.

options.text: That the old way was improved: chemical signaling became a great deal faster and more precisely targeted once there were neurons available to release it.
options.why: Nothing describes chemical signaling as having been improved by the arrival of neurons.

options.text: That the old way was replaced within circuits but kept between them, so diffusion still carries signals over long distances.
options.why: No division between within and between circuits is drawn.

options.text: That the old way was never a real alternative, since diffusion could not carry a verdict at all.
options.why: The previous module treated chemical signaling as a genuine and still-used option.

items.stem: The lecture frames the four molecules before naming them, and gives a reason. What is the reason?

options.text: A list of four chemicals is exactly the kind of thing that gets memorized and never understood, so the framing comes first.
options.why: Correct. The framing is that they are four ways of moving an animal around one space rather than four unrelated chemicals.

options.text: The names are harder to remember than the effects, so the effects are introduced first as an aid to recall.
options.why: Ease of recall is not the reason offered, and the framing is about understanding rather than memory.

options.text: Two of the four appear in the worm and two do not, so the scoping has to be settled before any of them is named.
options.why: The scoping question is deferred by the lecture rather than settled in advance.

options.text: The four were discovered in a different order than they are presented, so the framing offered here quietly corrects the historical sequence.
options.why: No history of when the four were discovered is given, and the framing offered is about how to understand them rather than about their order.

items.stem: The lecture calls the arrow-rather-than-point drawing a second dividend from an earlier argument. What was the argument, and what is the dividend?

options.text: That a space beats a list because a list holds only what someone thought to name — and the dividend is that a chemical can be described as a direction.
options.why: Correct. Dopamine reaching a quiet animal and an agitated one does not produce the same state, because the arrow starts from different places.

options.text: That two numbers describe a worm and a person in the same terms — and the dividend is that the very same four arrows turn out to apply to both of those species equally.
options.why: Describing a worm and a person in the same terms is the other reason given for preferring a space, and it is not the dividend the arrows illustrate.

options.text: That affect outlasts its cause — and the dividend is that an arrow shows how long a modulator's effect persists.
options.why: Duration is not what an arrow records; it shows which way a modulator shifts a state rather than how long the shift lasts.

options.text: That valence and arousal are independent — and the dividend is that each molecule moves exactly one of the two.
options.why: Several of the four move both quantities at once, which is part of what makes them roughly span the space between them.

items.stem: What did the account of one neuron talking to the next leave out?

options.text: How a stimulus gets into the system at all, and how a verdict inside it becomes a body that bends.
options.why: Correct. Both ends of sense, combine, act had been left alone until this point.

options.text: How a signal travels the length of an axon without weakening, and how it crosses to the next cell.
options.why: Both of those are covered by the account of one neuron talking to the next.

options.text: How several inputs are weighed against one another, and how a single action is chosen from them.
options.why: Weighing and choosing are what the algorithmic section supplied.

options.text: How a state can outlast its cause, and how an animal's condition changes a verdict.
options.why: Persistence and modulation are addressed elsewhere rather than being the two ends of the sequence.

items.stem: What is distinctive about the sensory end of the circuit?

options.text: The stimulus itself is the key, and different kinds of senses use different biological mechanisms to turn it into a voltage.
options.why: Correct. Different keys and different locks, converging as soon as the channel opens.

options.text: The stimulus arrives as a chemical in every case, which is why one mechanism serves for all the senses.
options.why: Touch pulls a channel open mechanically rather than arriving as a chemical.

options.text: The stimulus is amplified before it reaches the cell, so that even a weak event produces a full response.
options.why: No amplification stage is described ahead of the sensory cell.

options.text: The stimulus is compared against what was sensed a moment earlier, which is what makes sensing informative.
options.why: Comparison across time is how one animal steers rather than a general feature of the sensory end.

pools.title: Where the Comparison Breaks, What a State Costs, and Why This Is About Us
pools.covers: reading §4.3.7, §4.3.8, §4.3.9 · lecture 4.3 slides where_the_comparison_finally_breaks, what_a_state_costs, conservation_is_partial, motivation_mood_and_alertness

items.stem: The chapter identifies a second divergence between natural and artificial systems. How does it differ from the first?

options.text: The first was about materials — the same algorithm implemented in radically different stuff — and this one sits higher up.
options.why: Correct. The second divergence is about what the systems have at all, rather than about what they are made of.
