options.text: The first divergence was about speed and this one is about cost, so the two of them together price the difference between tissue and silicon.
options.why: Speed and cost belong to the previous module's comparison of a neuron with a transistor.

options.text: The first was about what the two systems compute and this one about how accurately they compute it.
options.why: What the two compute has been found to match closely throughout, which is why the chapter can use one set of diagrams.

options.text: The first was about single cells and this one about whole agents with a job to do.
options.why: Moving from a cell to a whole agent happened at the computational level with the robot vacuum.

items.stem: What does an artificial network have, and what does it lack?

options.text: It has weights and activations, and that is all it has; nothing in it corresponds to a chemical released into the space between units.
options.why: Correct. Nothing in it wears off either, which is the third of the three things that follow.

options.text: It has weights, activations and thresholds, and what it lacks is any way of settling on one output among several.
options.why: Settling on one output is what mutual inhibition does, and the chapter finds that motif in artificial networks.

options.text: It has weights and activations, and what it lacks is any way of holding a state across time.
options.why: Recurrent connections are named as how such a network holds a state across time.

options.text: It has weights, activations and a global parameter as well, so nothing at all turns out to be missing from the comparison.
options.why: A global parameter exists in some systems, and the chapter is careful about why it is not the same thing.

items.stem: Engineers sometimes set a global parameter that changes a whole network's behavior at once. Why is that not the same as neuromodulation?

options.text: It is set from outside, by whoever runs the system, rather than released by the network into itself in response to what happens to it.
options.why: Correct. The chapter takes the nearest analog seriously before explaining where it falls short.

options.text: It changes every unit by the same amount, where a neuromodulator affects only the cells with the right receptors.
options.why: Which cells respond is not the distinction drawn, and the analog fails on where the change comes from.

options.text: It changes the weights rather than how the units respond, so it alters what the network computes permanently.
options.why: A global parameter is not described as changing weights, and permanence is not the issue.

options.text: It is applied before the network runs rather than during, so it cannot respond to anything the network encounters.
options.why: The timing is not what the chapter objects to; the objection is that it comes from outside the system.

items.stem: What does the chapter conclude about the implications of this asymmetry?

options.text: That they are unclear in both directions: it is not obvious that such systems lack something they need, nor obvious that they do not.
options.why: Correct. The chapter stops rather than resolving, which is the point of the subsection.

options.text: That artificial systems are missing something they will need before they can hold a state across time.
options.why: Holding a state is something artificial networks already manage with recurrent connections.

options.text: That artificial systems are not missing anything, since a global parameter supplies whatever neuromodulation would.
options.why: The global parameter is examined and found not to be the same thing.

options.text: That the question cannot be settled until artificial systems are built with a chemistry of their own.
options.why: No condition for settling the question is offered; it is simply left open.

items.stem: How does a small animal maintain a state that outlasts its cause?

options.text: A chemical released into the tissue keeps a circuit tuned one way for minutes, long after the event that set it off.
options.why: Correct. Persistence is what lets an animal keep fleeing after the scent has thinned and keep searching after some of the food is gone.

options.text: A loop of excitatory connections simply keeps running, which is the one mechanism available to an animal with so few neurons.
options.why: A loop is one way to hold a state, and the chapter credits neuromodulators as an important part of how a small animal does it.

options.text: The connections between the relevant cells are strengthened, so the circuit stays biased until they weaken again.
options.why: A changed connection is a different thing entirely and belongs to a later module.

options.text: The sensory neurons continue firing after the stimulus has gone, so the input itself outlasts the event.
options.why: Nothing in the account has the sensory cells sustaining their own activity.

items.stem: Holding a state has a metabolic consequence that the wiring leaves invisible. What is it?

options.text: Reacting strongly is expensive, so staying keyed up is spending, and ceasing to respond where nothing can be escaped is conserving.
options.why: Correct. It is the implementational level's second question — what the doing costs — asked about persistence.

options.text: Holding a state costs nothing once it is entered, so an animal loses nothing by staying keyed up indefinitely.
options.why: Staying keyed up is described as continuous spending rather than as free.

options.text: Holding a state costs more than reacting, so an animal saves energy by responding immediately and letting the state go.
options.why: The expense is in reacting strongly, which is what a sustained state commits the animal to.

options.text: Holding a state draws on the same budget as growth, so an animal that stays alert grows more slowly.
options.why: No trade against growth is drawn anywhere in the chapter.

items.stem: What does the chapter call the non-pathologizing way to understand a great many behaviors?

options.text: Giving up is a thing bodies do to save energy, not simply a thing that goes wrong.
options.why: Correct. A behavior that looks like failure from the outside can look like an accounting decision from the inside.

options.text: Giving up is always the correct response when conditions cannot be escaped, since conserving is what the budget requires.
options.why: The chapter does not say giving up is always adaptive, and it makes no recommendation of that kind.

options.text: Giving up is a sign that a neuromodulator has been depleted, which is why the behavior can be reversed chemically.
options.why: Depletion is precisely the chemical-shortage reading the chapter rejects a little later.

options.text: Giving up is a failure of the wanting system, which the chapter goes on to describe as a hijack.
options.why: The hijack account is about pursuit being captured rather than about an animal ceasing to respond.

items.stem: Which of the four neuromodulators are the strong cases for conservation, and on what evidence?

options.text: Dopamine and serotonin: both are present in the worm and in us, acting through receptor families recognizably related across that distance.
options.why: Correct. A worm slowing on a bacterial lawn and a person losing interest in a meal are not the same event, though the machinery is not unrelated.

options.text: All four, since each is found in the worm and in human beings and each acts through related receptors.
options.why: The worm does not appear to make norepinephrine at all, so the four are not four ancient constants.

options.text: Norepinephrine and dopamine: both set how strongly an animal reacts, which is the oldest requirement a nervous system has.
options.why: Norepinephrine is the weak case rather than a strong one.

options.text: Serotonin alone, since it is the only one for which a specific worm behavior has been traced.
options.why: Dopamine is named alongside it, and the receptor-family evidence covers both.

items.stem: What does the chapter say about norepinephrine and the worm?

options.text: The worm does not appear to make it at all, and uses two other amines, octopamine and tyramine, in roles that overlap with the vertebrate system.
options.why: Correct. The hedges are the chapter's own, and stripping them turns a careful claim into a false one.

options.text: The worm makes it in much smaller quantities than a vertebrate does, which is why its own arousal responses are correspondingly weaker.
options.why: No quantitative comparison is drawn; the chapter's claim is that the worm does not appear to make it.

options.text: The worm uses octopamine and tyramine to do exactly the job norepinephrine does in vertebrates, so the system is conserved in function.
options.why: The chapter says the roles overlap and the details are still being worked out, which is weaker than doing exactly the same job.

options.text: The worm makes it but has no receptors for it, so the molecule is present and does nothing.
options.why: Nothing of that kind is described; the chapter's claim is that the molecule is absent rather than present and unused.

items.stem: How does the partial conservation of the four molecules bear on the comparative method?

options.text: Shared machinery is evidence of shared ancestry, different machinery doing a similar job of something else, and telling them apart is comparative work.
options.why: Correct. Which is why the chapter treats the sorting of the four molecules as a result rather than as a caveat on the comparison.

options.text: Partial conservation shows that the comparative method cannot usefully be applied to chemistry at all, but only to anatomy and to behavior.
options.why: The chapter applies the method to the four molecules directly and treats the outcome as informative.

options.text: Partial conservation shows that shared machinery is unreliable as evidence, since a similar job can perfectly well be done by two quite unrelated molecules.
options.why: Similar jobs done by different machinery is evidence of something else rather than a reason to distrust shared machinery.

options.text: Partial conservation shows that the worm is too distant a relative for any comparison with human beings to be useful.
options.why: The chapter's whole point is that two of the four do run deep enough for the comparison to matter.

items.stem: How does the chapter describe addiction, anhedonia and anxiety in the vocabulary it has built?

options.text: Addiction as the wanting system captured by something that does not feed it; anhedonia as valence stuck low; anxiety as arousal held high.
options.why: Correct. Each is a structural description — where in the space something has gone, or which direction has been hijacked.

options.text: Addiction as the valence axis stuck high; anhedonia as the wanting system suppressed; anxiety as the liking system captured.
options.why: This shuffles all three, and anhedonia is about valence rather than about wanting being suppressed.

options.text: Addiction as arousal set high and staying there; anhedonia as the wanting system captured; anxiety as the valence axis stuck low.
options.why: Arousal held high is the anxiety reading, and the other two are swapped as well.

options.text: Addiction as a shortage of dopamine, anhedonia as a shortage of serotonin, and anxiety as an excess of norepinephrine in the tissue.
options.why: A shortage account is exactly what the chapter rejects in the next breath.

items.stem: What two retractions does the chapter attach to those readings?

options.text: That none of them is a complete account of any of those conditions, and that none of the conditions is a simple chemical shortage.
options.why: Correct. The phrase chemical imbalance suggests a level that has dropped and could be topped up, and that is not what anyone finds when they look.

options.text: That none of them applies to worms, and that none has been demonstrated experimentally in human beings.
options.why: The chapter says explicitly that none is a complete account in humans or in worms.

options.text: That none of them is settled among researchers, and that each will be revised once the chemistry is better understood.
options.why: No prediction about future revision is offered.

options.text: That none of them applies outside a clinical setting, and that no reader should apply the vocabulary to themselves.
options.why: The chapter makes no such instruction, and it presents the readings as ways of understanding.

items.stem: What does the chapter offer in place of a chemical-shortage account?

options.text: Systems with feedback, states and histories, which go wrong in ways that match their structure.
options.why: Correct. It is a harder thing to say and a much more useful one.

options.text: Systems with fixed weights, which go wrong only when the weights themselves have been set badly.
options.why: Fixed weights are the algorithmic section's limitation rather than an account of how these systems go wrong.

options.text: Systems too complex to describe, so that no account at the level of mechanism is currently possible.
options.why: The chapter offers a structural account rather than declining to give one.

options.text: Systems whose chemistry varies a good deal between individuals, so that what counts as balanced differs from one person to the next.
options.why: Individual variation in a baseline level is still the level-based picture the chapter is rejecting.

items.stem: What does the chapter conclude about the four molecules as a set?

options.text: They are not four ancient constants: only two of them run deep, and the others are more recent or more variable.
options.why: Correct. Dopamine and serotonin are the deep pair, and norepinephrine is the case that does not carry across.

options.text: They are four ancient constants, which is what allows a chapter about a worm to bear on human motivation at all.
options.why: Partial conservation is what the chapter argues for, and it is enough for the worm to be relevant.

options.text: They are four recent inventions of the vertebrate line, with the worm's chemistry only loosely analogous.
options.why: Two of the four are present in the worm and act through recognizably related receptor families.

options.text: They are four names for what is really a single system, since each of them moves an animal through the very same space.
options.why: Moving an animal through one space is how they are framed, and they remain four distinct molecules.

items.stem: Why does the chapter say the human end is where the conservation matters most?

options.text: Because motivation, mood and alertness in ordinary human life run on these systems.
options.why: Correct. Which is why the shapes of things going wrong turn out to be recognizable in the terms the chapter has been building.

options.text: Because the human versions of these systems are better understood than the worm's, so they anchor the comparison.
options.why: The worm is the better-understood case in this chapter, with its complete wiring and traced behaviors.

options.text: Because human beings are the only animals in which all four molecules are present at once.
options.why: No claim of that kind is made, and the worm is missing one of the four altogether.

options.text: Because the human systems can be studied without the comparative work the rest of the chapter depends on.
options.why: The comparative work is what licenses applying the worm's chemistry to human life at all.

items.stem: "The conservation is partial." Explain what that means for the four neuromodulators, keeping the chapter's hedges intact.
items.answer: Dopamine and serotonin are the strong cases: both are present in the worm and in human beings, and both act through receptor families that are recognizably related across that evolutionary distance. Norepinephrine is the weak case — the worm does not appear to make it at all. Instead the worm uses two other amines, octopamine and tyramine, in roles that overlap with the vertebrate arousal system, in ways that are still being worked out. So the four molecules are not four ancient constants: two run deep, and the others are more recent or more variable. The hedges matter — does not appear to, overlap, still being worked out — because stripping them turns a careful claim into a false one.
rubric: Names dopamine and serotonin as the conserved pair, with the receptor-family evidence.
States that the worm does not appear to make norepinephrine.
Names octopamine and tyramine as overlapping in role rather than doing the same job.
Concludes that two run deep and the others are more recent or more variable.

items.stem: Where does the comparison between biological and artificial systems finally break, and how far does the chapter push the conclusion?
items.answer: An artificial network has weights and activations, and that is all it has. Nothing in it corresponds to a chemical released into the space between units, and it typically has no mechanism for reaching all the units at once, changing how every one of them responds for a stretch of time, and then wearing off. The nearest analog is a global parameter that changes a whole network's behavior at once, but it is set from outside by whoever is running the system rather than released by the network into itself. The chapter pushes the conclusion no further than the asymmetry: the implications are unclear in both directions, since it is not obvious that artificial systems are missing something they need, and not obvious that they are not.
rubric: States that an artificial network has weights and activations and nothing corresponding to a released chemical.
Notes the absence of a mechanism reaching all units at once and wearing off.
Considers the global parameter and explains why it is not the same — it comes from outside.
Leaves the implications unresolved in both directions.

items.stem: The lecture says it is doing something here that it has tried to do throughout the course when warranted. What?

options.text: Stopping rather than resolving, because the asymmetry is real and its implications are unclear in both directions.
options.why: Correct. It is not obvious that artificial systems are missing something they need, and not obvious that they are not.

options.text: Naming a disagreement among researchers rather than taking a side, so students can weigh the evidence themselves.
options.why: No disagreement among researchers is reported here; the question is simply open.

options.text: Correcting something said in an earlier module rather than letting students discover the discrepancy later.
options.why: That is done on an earlier slide, about all-or-nothing signaling.

options.text: Deferring a question to a later module rather than half-answering it now.
options.why: Nothing here is handed to a later module; the question is left open rather than postponed.

items.stem: The lecture is careful about how far the giving-up point goes. How does it draw the boundary?

options.text: It is not a clinical claim; what it says is that a behavior looking like failure from outside can look like an accounting decision from inside.
options.why: Correct. The chapter makes no clinical claim either, which is why the lecture matches it.

options.text: It is making a claim about human depression specifically, and leaving the animal case standing only as an illustration of that claim.
options.why: The claim is pitched across animals and humans alike rather than being about one condition.

options.text: It is claiming that conserving is always the better strategy when conditions cannot be escaped.
options.why: Nothing says giving up is always adaptive; the point is that it is an accounting decision rather than a malfunction.

options.text: It is claiming that the wiring diagram would show the cost if it were drawn in enough detail.
options.why: The consequence is described as one the wiring does not show at all.

items.stem: The lecture points at three particular words in one of its own sentences. Which, and why?

options.text: Does not appear to, overlap, still being worked out — the chapter's own hedges, and stripping them makes a careful claim false.
options.why: Correct. The sentence they belong to is the one about the worm, norepinephrine, octopamine and tyramine.

options.text: Recognizably, related, and across that distance — they are what keep the dopamine and serotonin case from being overstated.
options.why: Those words belong to the strong case rather than to the sentence the lecture stops on.

options.text: Ancient, constants, and variable — they are what separate the two deep molecules from the other two.
options.why: That sentence draws the conclusion rather than carrying the hedges the lecture flags.

options.text: Partial, interesting, and complexity — they are the framing the whole slide is organized around.
options.why: The framing is stated plainly; the words singled out are the hedges inside one specific claim.

items.stem: The lecture notes a feature the three clinical readings share. What is it?

options.text: Each is a structural description, saying where in the space something has gone or which direction has been hijacked.
options.why: Correct. That is what it looks like to describe a condition with the machinery built across the three meetings.

options.text: Each of the three is drawn from the worm rather than from human research, which is part of why they are offered only as ways of understanding.
options.why: The three are given for human life, using vocabulary the worm work supplied.

options.text: Each of them names a single molecule as the one whose level has gone wrong, which is part of what makes the three of them testable.
options.why: Naming a molecule whose level has dropped is the account the lecture goes on to reject.

options.text: Each describes a condition that can be produced experimentally in an animal, which is the evidence for them.
options.why: No experimental production of these conditions is described.

items.stem: The lecture says the sorting of the four molecules is a result rather than a caveat. Why?

options.text: Because it is what the comparative method is for: shared machinery evidences shared ancestry, different machinery doing a similar job something else.
options.why: Correct. Telling those two apart is the whole business of comparative work, and here it has been done on four molecules.

options.text: Because it shows that the worm is a rather better model for human chemistry than anyone had assumed, which is a finding in its own right.
options.why: The sorting cuts both ways, with two molecules running deep and two not.

options.text: Because it settles which of the four molecules will be the most useful target for medication.
options.why: No claim about targets for medication is drawn from the sorting.

options.text: Because it establishes that the four molecules evolved at four different times, which dates the arousal system.
options.why: No dates are attached to any of the four.

items.stem: What mechanism do artificial networks typically lack?

options.text: Any way of reaching all units at once, changing how each responds for a stretch of time, and then wearing off.
options.why: Correct. The hedge is typically — nothing says no artificial system has ever had such a mechanism.

options.text: Any way of settling on a single output when several are nearly tied with one another.
options.why: Mutual inhibition turns up in artificial networks wherever that has to be done.

options.text: Any way of holding activity going after the input that started it has stopped.
options.why: Recurrent connections do exactly that in an artificial network.

options.text: Any way of weighting some inputs more heavily than others before summing them together.
options.why: Weights are one of the two things such a network is described as having.

items.stem: Holding a state chemically has a consequence of a particular kind. What kind?

options.text: A metabolic one, and it is something the wiring does not show at all.
options.why: Correct. Reacting strongly is expensive, so staying keyed up is continuous spending.

options.text: A computational one, which shows up as a loss of precision in the verdicts the circuit reaches.
options.why: No loss of precision is described as a cost of holding a state.

options.text: A structural one, which shows up as a change in the connections once the state has been held long enough.
options.why: Connections do not change here; that is what makes the flexibility a near miss rather than learning.

options.text: A temporal one, which shows up as a delay before the animal can respond to anything new.
options.why: No delay of that kind is attributed to holding a state.

pools.title: A System That Can Be Hijacked, and What Wiring Made Possible
pools.covers: reading §4.3.10, the unnumbered Close · lecture 4.3 slides a_system_that_can_be_hijacked, what_wiring_made_possible

items.stem: What one last consequence does the chapter draw from everything above it?

options.text: A system that assigns value is a system that can be fooled about value.
options.why: Correct. It follows from the whole chapter rather than introducing anything new into it.

options.text: A system that assigns value is a system that can change what it values over time.
options.why: Changing what is valued would require the weights to move, which is exactly what these circuits cannot do.

options.text: A system that assigns value is a system that needs a separate mechanism for checking its own verdicts.
options.why: No checking mechanism is described, and nothing in the chapter calls for one.

options.text: A system that assigns value is a system whose verdicts other animals can learn to predict and exploit.
options.why: Exploitation by other animals is not the hijack the chapter describes.

items.stem: What does anything acting directly on the wanting chemistry produce?

options.text: The pull toward a thing, without the thing — which is what addictive substances do, and why wanting and liking can come apart.
options.why: Correct. The pursuit is manufactured where pursuit is decided rather than arriving through the senses from something in the world.

options.text: The satisfaction of having a thing, without the thing — which is why the pursuit stops before anything has been obtained.
options.why: Satisfaction belongs to the liking side, and the hijack described works on wanting.

options.text: A general rise in arousal, which makes every available option look more attractive than it otherwise would.
options.why: The effect described is specific to pursuit rather than a uniform lift in how strongly the animal reacts.

options.text: A lasting change in what the animal treats as good, since the wanting chemistry sets the weights in the circuit.
options.why: Weights do not move here; the chemistry retunes the circuit temporarily and leaves nothing behind.

items.stem: Why does the chapter say that wanting and liking coming apart is not a curiosity?

options.text: Because it is the center of the problem: the pursuit can grow while the satisfaction shrinks.
options.why: Correct. A person in that state is not enjoying anything more; they are wanting it more.

options.text: Because it shows that the two systems were never really separate, so the distinction was always artificial.
options.why: The chapter keeps the two distinct, which is what makes their coming apart describable at all.

options.text: Because it happens in every animal with a wanting system, so it is a general feature rather than a rare failure.
options.why: No claim about how widely it occurs is made.

options.text: Because it is the clearest evidence that dopamine carries enjoyment as well as pursuit.
options.why: Treating dopamine as the chemistry of enjoyment is the misperception the chapter names and rejects.

items.stem: How far does the chapter extend the hijack beyond substances, and how is the claim hedged?

options.text: Any arrangement that reliably triggers pursuit can sit on the same circuit, and things designed to hold attention sit on it, intended or not.
options.why: Correct. The hedge keeps it a claim about what the circuit responds to rather than an accusation about anyone's intentions.

options.text: Only substances that act on dopamine receptors can produce the effect, so nothing outside pharmacology is at issue.
options.why: The chapter says explicitly that it is not only substances.

options.text: Any arrangement that reliably triggers pursuit can sit on the same circuit, and those who design such things do so knowingly.
options.why: Attributing intent is what the hedge is written to avoid.

options.text: Any arrangement that raises arousal can sit on the same circuit, which is why alarming things are as compelling as rewarding ones.
options.why: The circuit at issue is the one that decides pursuit rather than the one that sets arousal.

items.stem: What does the chapter say it has now done with steering?

options.text: Answered it at all three levels: why it was worth having, what arrangements compute it, and what tissue and chemistry run it.
options.why: Correct. One object — an arrangement of neurons — examined three times.

options.text: Answered it at two levels, with the implementational account deferred to the module on vertebrate brains.
options.why: All three are answered here, and the vertebrate scale-up is a separate matter handed to a later module.

options.text: Answered it for the worm, with the general case left open until more connectomes are available.
options.why: The answers are pitched generally, with the worm as the worked case rather than the limit of the claim.

options.text: Answered it at all three levels for animals, with the artificial comparison left for a later module.
options.why: The comparison with artificial systems runs the length of the chapter and is closed out in it.

items.stem: Why did neurons come to be wired into circuits at all, on this chapter's answer — and what does that answer then demand?

options.text: An important answer, perhaps the answer, is steering: an animal that moves in a direction has to settle which, which demands evaluating, combining, committing and modulating.
options.why: Correct. The hedge — perhaps the answer — is the chapter's own.

options.text: The answer is coordination: a body of specialized cells has to act as a single thing, which is what the earliest neurons were built to make possible in the first place.
options.why: Coordination is what the earliest nervous systems were for, and steering is this module's addition on top of it.

options.text: The answer is speed: an animal that senses, decides and acts faster than its rivals is the animal that eats rather than being eaten.
options.why: Speed is the previous module's answer for why neurons exist at all.

options.text: The answer is persistence: an animal whose states outlast their causes can keep acting after the evidence has gone.
options.why: Persistence is one of the four demands rather than the answer the whole chapter turns on.

items.stem: Which wiring patterns make up the chapter's algorithmic answer?

options.text: Convergence, divergence, weights against a threshold, lateral and mutual inhibition, and recurrent feedback loops.
options.why: Correct. Each of them helps meet one of the demands listed at the computational level.

options.text: Convergence, divergence, transduction, cephalization, and the neuromuscular junction.
options.why: Three of those are pieces of tissue rather than wiring patterns, and they belong to the implementational answer.

options.text: Weights, thresholds, activation functions, decision boundaries, and labeled lines.
options.why: Those are properties of a single unit or ways of describing one, rather than the patterns units are wired into.

options.text: Lateral inhibition, mutual inhibition, feedforward connections, and the two-number affective space.
options.why: Feedforward is the absence of a loop rather than a motif, and the affective space is a representation.

items.stem: What physically implements the computations this chapter describes?

options.text: A net of neurons condensing into rings and ganglia and then a front end, plus chemicals released into the tissue that retune the arrangement for minutes.
options.why: Correct. The worm whose entire wiring is known is the worked case within that answer.

options.text: A net of neurons condensing into a brain, together with the connections between those neurons changing as the animal goes on encountering the world.
options.why: Connections changing is exactly what this chapter's animals cannot do.

options.text: A set of units taking weighted inputs and passing the total through an activation function, wired into recurring patterns.
options.why: That is the algorithmic answer, given in arrows and numbers rather than in tissue.

options.text: A complete wiring diagram of one animal, which is all the implementational level can currently supply.
options.why: The chapter's implementational answer includes the chemistry, which is precisely what a wiring diagram leaves out.

items.stem: The whole chapter elaborates a single idea. What is it, and what two things does the value of an input derive from?

options.text: Good and bad are verdicts an arrangement assigns, not properties the world provides; value comes from what a cell is wired to and from the chemistry in the circuit.
options.why: Correct. The chemistry decides how much any of it matters at this moment.

options.text: Good and bad are verdicts an arrangement assigns; the value of an input comes from what a cell is wired to, and from how strongly the sensory cell is firing.
options.why: Firing rate carries no verdict, which the chapter has insisted on since the demand to evaluate was raised.

options.text: Good and bad are properties of the world that an arrangement detects; the value of an input comes from the molecule and from the receptor that fits it.
options.why: Locating value in the molecule is the reading the chapter has denied throughout.

options.text: Good and bad are verdicts an arrangement assigns; the value of an input comes from what a cell is wired to, and from what the animal has learned about it.
options.why: Nothing in this chapter is learned, which is the last point the chapter makes.

items.stem: Across the three levels, how does the comparison with artificial networks come out?

options.text: The demands are the same and the wiring patterns very nearly so, which is why one set of diagrams served both; the chemistry is not, and whether that absence is a deficiency nobody can say.
options.why: Correct. The comparison came out differently at each level, which is why it was worth running the length of the chapter.

options.text: The demands and the wiring patterns are both different, which is why the artificial comparison had to be dropped at the implementational level.
options.why: One set of diagrams served for both, which would be impossible if the patterns differed.

options.text: The demands, the wiring patterns and the chemistry all turn out to be very nearly the same, which makes this the strongest case of multiple realizability anywhere in the course.
options.why: The chemistry is exactly where the two come apart.

options.text: The demands are the same and the chemistry is nearly the same, though the wiring patterns differ a good deal between the two.
options.why: This inverts which layers match: the patterns match and the chemistry does not.

items.stem: Neuromodulation looks at first like the flexibility every arrangement in this chapter lacks. Why is it not that?

options.text: None of it is learned: once the chemistry wears off the modulation has left nothing behind — the weights do not move, and nothing about that episode is kept.
options.why: Correct. It is a near miss on purpose, because the same wiring really does produce different behavior from one hour to the next. Note the scope: what keeps nothing is the modulation, not the animal.

options.text: None of it is fast enough: neuromodulation acts over seconds to minutes, so it cannot supply the flexibility a circuit needs within a single encounter.
options.why: Speed is not the objection; the objection is that nothing persists afterward.

options.text: None of it reaches the whole animal: a chemical released into tissue affects only nearby cells, so the flexibility is local rather than general.
options.why: A neuromodulator is described as reaching many cells at once.

options.text: None of it is under the animal's control: the chemistry is set by the body rather than by the circuit, so it is not flexibility of the right kind.
options.why: Where the chemistry comes from is not the issue; whether anything is kept afterward is.

items.stem: Nothing in this chapter's circuits changes with experience. What follows for how those circuits meet the world?

options.text: They meet it with a repertoire that was set before the encounter began, and meet it the same way on the thousandth encounter as on the first.
options.why: Correct, and the subject is the circuits rather than the animals they model. It is the same limitation the algorithmic section reached, arriving from the implementational side.

options.text: They meet it with a repertoire that broadens as the chemistry running through them varies, though it returns to its starting point each time.
options.why: The repertoire itself does not broaden; the same circuit runs with different chemistry.

options.text: They meet it with a repertoire the animals themselves can never alter, since nothing a worm or a jellyfish encounters is ever kept.
options.why: This is the reading the chapter added a claim to block. Real animals do learn, C. elegans included; the fixed weights are ours rather than theirs.

options.text: They meet it with a repertoire set by the animal's internal state, which is why a hungry animal behaves as if it were differently wired.
options.why: Internal state changes the verdict without changing the repertoire the circuit was built with.

items.stem: The fixed-weight limitation is argued twice in the chapter, from two different directions. What are they?

options.text: From the algorithmic side, that fixed weights can only do what they were set to do; from the implementational side, that the chemistry leaves nothing behind once it wears off.
options.why: Correct. The two are not interchangeable, and the algorithmic statement is where the limitation is introduced.

options.text: From the computational side, that steering demands more than a fixed repertoire; and from the algorithmic side, that no arrangement of fixed weights can meet all four demands.
options.why: Every demand is met by a fixed-weight arrangement, which is what makes the limitation surprising.

options.text: From the implementational side, that a worm has too few cells to hold anything; and from the algorithmic side, that a weight is a number rather than a memory.
options.why: Neither argument is made anywhere in the chapter.

options.text: From the algorithmic side, that fixed weights cannot represent a state; and from the implementational side, that chemistry cannot hold one either.
options.why: Both a loop and the chemistry hold states perfectly well; what neither does is keep anything afterward.

items.stem: What does the chapter hand forward, and to where?

options.text: How a weight changes within a lifetime; the vertebrate brain; what one decision boundary cannot separate; and value, once decisions stop being reflexive.
options.why: Correct. Four doors, opened deliberately and left for four later modules.

options.text: How a weight changes within a lifetime, and nothing else, since the other questions raised are all settled inside the chapter.
options.why: Several other questions are handed forward explicitly in the same paragraph.

options.text: How a connectome can be produced faster, how neuromodulators are synthesized, and how affect is measured in human beings.
options.why: None of those three is among the questions the chapter defers.

options.text: How a nerve net became a brain, how valence became conscious feeling, and how the behavior of a worm might be predicted in full from its wiring.
options.why: None of those is handed forward, and the chapter makes no claim about conscious feeling anywhere.

items.stem: Neuromodulation is a near miss for the flexibility this chapter's circuits lack. Explain what it nearly is, and the test that shows it is not.
items.answer: It nearly is the flexibility that every arrangement in the chapter has been missing, because the same wiring produces different behavior from one hour to the next and the animal's own condition is what decides which. The test is what is left afterward. A hungry worm and a fed worm run the same circuit with different chemistry, and once the chemistry wears off the modulation has left nothing behind: the weights have not moved, and nothing about that episode is kept. So none of it is learned, and the circuits built in this chapter still meet the world with a repertoire that was set before the encounter began, the same way on the thousandth encounter as on the first. The scope matters: real animals do learn, C. elegans among them, and holding the weights still is a simplification the chapter makes rather than a claim about the biology.
rubric: States what makes neuromodulation look like the missing flexibility — same wiring, different behavior.
Gives the test: what is left once the chemistry wears off.
States that the weights do not move and nothing about the episode is kept.
Concludes that the circuits' repertoire is unchanged from the first encounter to the thousandth, without extending the claim to the animals.

items.stem: Summarize the chapter's three answers about a neural circuit, and the one idea they elaborate.
items.answer: The computational answer is steering: an animal that moves in a direction has to settle which direction, and settling it demands evaluating what arrives, combining signals that disagree, committing to one action, and letting the animal's own condition change the verdict. The algorithmic answer is a short list of wiring patterns — convergence, divergence, weights against a threshold, lateral inhibition, mutual inhibition, and recurrent feedback loops. The implementational answer is a net of neurons condensing into rings and ganglia and then into a front end, a worm whose entire wiring is known, and a handful of chemicals released into the tissue that retune the arrangement for minutes at a time. All three elaborate one idea: good and bad are verdicts an arrangement assigns rather than properties the world provides.
rubric: Gives steering as the computational answer, with the demands it makes.
Lists the wiring patterns as the algorithmic answer.
Gives the tissue and the chemistry as the implementational answer.
States the one idea: good and bad are assigned by an arrangement rather than found in the world.

items.stem: The lecture says the pursuit in a hijacked system is manufactured somewhere particular. Where?

options.text: At the point where it is decided, rather than arriving through the senses from something in the world.
options.why: Correct. That is what produces the pull toward a thing without the thing.

options.text: At the sensory end, where a substance mimics whichever molecule the animal would otherwise have been detecting there.
options.why: The hijack acts on the wanting chemistry rather than on what the senses report.

options.text: At the muscles, where the action is produced whether or not any verdict has been reached upstream.
options.why: Nothing bypasses the verdict; the verdict itself is what gets manufactured.

options.text: In the wiring, which is rearranged so that a new cue comes to drive approach.
options.why: Rewiring is exactly what these circuits cannot do.

items.stem: The lecture adds a caution to its remark about things designed to hold attention. What is the caution?

options.text: It is a claim about what the circuit responds to rather than an accusation about anyone's intentions.
options.why: Correct. The chapter's own hedge is whether or not anyone intended it, which keeps the claim about the circuit rather than about anybody's purposes.

options.text: It is a claim about digital media specifically rather than about designed things in general.
options.why: No industry or medium is named anywhere. The claim covers any arrangement that reliably triggers pursuit, which makes it broader rather than narrower.

options.text: It is a claim that holds only for substances, since nothing else acts directly on the receptors.
options.why: The lecture makes the point precisely in order to extend it beyond substances.

options.text: It is a claim awaiting evidence, since no study has tested the connection directly.
options.why: No appeal to missing evidence is made, and the caution concerns what is being claimed rather than how well established it is.

items.stem: The lecture calls its closing move a near miss on purpose. What is the test it offers?

options.text: A hungry worm and a fed worm run one circuit with different chemistry, and once it wears off the modulation has left nothing behind.
options.why: Correct. The weights have not moved and nothing about that episode is kept — and the lecture is careful to add that real animals do learn, so the fixed weights are ours rather than theirs.

options.text: A worm that has crossed a copper barrier once crosses it more readily the second time, which is the kind of change this module's circuits cannot produce.
options.why: A fixed-weight circuit cannot produce that change, which is why it is not the test on offer. Real worms do learn, though — the module sets learning aside rather than denying it.

options.text: A worm with its neuromodulatory chemistry removed behaves identically to one with it intact.
options.why: Removing the chemistry is not an experiment the chapter or the lecture reports.

options.text: A worm's connectome looks different before and after a period of hunger, which shows the wiring has changed.
options.why: The connections explicitly do not change, which is the whole basis of the argument.

items.stem: The lecture closes by naming where four open questions go. Which pairing is right?

options.text: Weights come next; the vertebrate brain after that; what one boundary cannot separate later; and value once decisions stop being reflexive.
options.why: Correct. Four doors, each opened somewhere in the module and each handed to a different place.

options.text: How a weight changes comes next; what one decision boundary cannot separate follows immediately after it; and the vertebrate brain is left for the end of the course.
options.why: The scale-up to a vertebrate brain is the very next thing after weights rather than the last.

options.text: The vertebrate brain comes next, and how a weight changes is handed to the modules where value returns.
options.why: Weights are the immediate next subject, and value returning is a separate and later matter.

options.text: All four are handed to the same later module, since each of them concerns what a fixed circuit cannot do.
options.why: They go to four different places rather than to one.

items.stem: A student finishes the chapter concluding that a worm cannot learn. Where has the student gone wrong?

options.text: Real animals do learn, the animals in this chapter included; leaving learning out was a choice, made because a circuit is easier to understand while its numbers hold still.
options.why: Correct. What meets the world with a repertoire set in advance is the circuits the chapter builds, not the animals they are models of.

options.text: The conclusion holds for the worm but not for the cnidarians, whose nerve nets are the one arrangement in the chapter that can be altered by experience.
options.why: Both groups learn, and no arrangement in the chapter is described as alterable by experience.

options.text: The conclusion holds only while the animal is hungry, since an internal state suspends the fixed weights for as long as the state lasts.
options.why: An internal state changes the verdict a circuit reaches without touching the weights at all.

options.text: The conclusion is right about the worm and wrong only about what follows from it, since nothing in the chapter turns on whether an animal can learn.
options.why: A great deal turns on it: the chapter adds a claim specifically to stop this conclusion being drawn.
